Counter-signal: SPOWV/SPINE (sparsify a dense/distributional signal, not local-competitive learning) show parity-or-improvement over dense on real text. P_deflated=0.45; recommend V2-A (PPMI/SVD-sparsified code, forward-only, cheap) over a 2nd from-scratch competitive-Hebbian variant.
plain_language: We asked the outside ML literature whether a simple word-fragment baseline beating our brain-inspired sparse memory mechanism on real dictionary-style data is a known problem or something new. Answer: the GENERAL shape (simple keyword matching beating fancy learned representations on new/unseen data) is well-known and documented across many papers. But nobody has ever tested THIS SPECIFIC brain-inspired mechanism on THIS SPECIFIC kind of real word data before, so it is new information, not proof the whole approach is dead. The literature suggests a cheap fix: build the sparse code from word co-occurrence statistics instead of from local brain-like competition, which has worked for others on real text.

summary: 5x-drill 3/5 neuroscience: monolithic sparse-competitive-Hebbian at k=2% is DG-CA3 territory running an ATL-hub task; MISSING VWFA-analog + ATL-hub-analog dense amodal convergence + semantic-control gating; v2 needs 3-stream A+B+C parallel-cascade; NO published existence proof of pure sparse-competitive-Hebbian on real-corpus synonym retrieval; P_deflated=0.48
plain_language: The brain actually solves the exact synonym-retrieval task our encoder is failing at, but it uses 3+ different brain regions working in parallel (VWFA for letters, ATL for meaning, IFG/pMTG for control). We built one region (the hippocampus-like sparse memory) and asked it to do all four jobs. Fix is not tuning; it is adding two more brain-inspired components — a dense semantic hub and a surface-letter n-gram bank — and letting them work in parallel like the brain does. A 30-minute test can arbitrate: concat a dense PPMI hub with char-trigrams and see if it beats trigrams alone by 5+ points on WordNet held-out synonyms.

summary: task-regime reframe (5x drill 5/5): WordNet held-out-synonym-retrieval at N=100/4-sent is encoder-confounded, not unfair-per-se. CharPositionalEncoder (absolute char-position HRR bind) has near-zero substring-shift-invariance vs CharTrigramEncoder (shift-invariant bag-of-trigrams). Char-trigram wins via inductive-bias match to WordNet gloss orthographic overlap, not more data (identical training text confirmed by code read). Component-C readout-swap HARD_FAIL is a TRUE negative (readout cannot manufacture substring signal absent from stored prototypes). Validates in-flight V2 P1 (VWFA n-gram front end) with a concrete mechanistic reason. Recommends analogy-completion / compositional-generalization as the next cheap decisive test to decouple encoder-defect from concept-mechanism quality.
plain_language: We dug into why a simple bag-of-letter-chunks trick keeps beating the brain-inspired concept encoder on a word-matching test. Answer: the concept encoder currently spells out words by binding each letter to its exact position, so it cannot recognize a related word unless it starts with the exact same letters in the exact same slots -- while the simple trick just checks for shared letter-chunks anywhere in the word, which is exactly what this WordNet test rewards. So the test was not unfair, but it was quietly testing the wrong layer (the spelling front-end) instead of the concept-understanding layer we care about. This confirms the team is already fixing the right thing (the VWFA-style front-end swap in flight) and points to a follow-up test (analogy completion) that would test the concept layer without the letter-spelling confound.

summary: Component C modern-Hopfield readout HF (commit 4cd1d30ba, r@5=0.05 vs cosine 0.16): ML-lit 5x-drill-4/5 confirms verdict (I) with geometry-scoped caveat. Millidge 2022 Universal Hopfield Networks is the closest controlled comparison and finds hard-max beats softmax at fair-comparison beta on retrieval-capacity task. Canonical HDC/VSA lit (Plate/Kanerva/Rachkovskij/Kleyko survey) unanimously recommends cosine/Hamming argmax cleanup, not softmax. No paper found doing the exact 3-way (cosine vs Hopfield vs magnitude-weighted) comparison on equal-norm sparse storage. Caveat: substrate own 2026-07-01 Cell D v2 result (dense continuous Hebbian tape + direct attention read, recall 1.000) plus 3 independent literature threads jointly show modern-Hopfield attention advantage is storage-geometry-contingent (dense continuous), not present for sparse-bipolar equal-norm storage -- consistent with, not contradicting, todays negative. Recommendation: close Component C in current sparse-bipolar form; keep Cell D v2 dense-tape+attention path as the sanctioned M3 attention-readout mechanism.
plain_language: We asked the published AI/ML literature whether attention-style readout (the modern-Hopfield mechanism used in transformers) should have beaten simple cosine-similarity lookup on the substrates sparse memory, since our own test showed it losing badly (5 percent vs 16 percent accuracy). The literature says no: the closest matching published experiment found plain nearest-neighbor lookup beating this kind of attention readout under similar conditions, and the whole hyperdimensional-computing field independently recommends cosine lookup as the standard. So this is not a bug, it is expected. There is one useful nuance: attention-style readout DOES work well elsewhere in our system (a different test yesterday got perfect recall) because that test used a dense continuous memory, not the sparse memory format tested here. So the lesson is: use attention readout only with dense memory, use cosine lookup with the sparse memory -- exactly what we already do elsewhere in the plan.

summary: 5x drill 2/5 modern-Hopfield readout physics scope: Ramsauer Theorem 5 beta_needed=ln(2M/eps)/Delta_cos ~ 80-450 for this config, matching independently the Skunkworks max_cos/sqrt(N) proxy by coincidence (thin Delta_cos ~ noise floor). Proved softmax attention-WEIGHT ranking is provably identical to cosine ranking at any beta (monotonicity) -- so measured HF implies readout is scoring the blended one-step-update OUTPUT vector (sub-critical metastable smear), not weight. Neyman-Pearson fixed-sufficient-statistic ceiling argument confirmed correct long-run (encoder Delta_cos is the lever) but overclaims near-term -- current gap is recoverable regime artifact, not floor.
plain_language: Studied why the memory-lookup mechanism (modern-Hopfield/softmax attention) scored much worse than a simpler cosine-similarity lookup on the same stored patterns. Found the collapse is very likely a fixable setup mistake (wrong strength dial + wrong thing being compared), not a hard mathematical wall -- a cheap follow-up test (three settings of the strength dial) should confirm and recover it to parity with the simple method, after which improving the pattern-encoder (not the lookup rule) is the real long-term lever.

summary: component_c_hopfield_readout_prior_arc: substrate empirical mining finds no prior evidence Hopfield mechanism is unsuited to task; instead surfaces a concrete beta/temperature-scaling bug (reused beta=4/8 from a raw-dot-product cell applied on top of already-bounded cosine/sqrt(N), crushing softmax to near-uniform, collapsing attractor to corpus centroid). Cheap decisive test (remove /sqrt(N) or rescale beta by sqrt(N)) proposed to discriminate bug-fix vs genuine mechanism mismatch before Option A composition or Option 2 storage-lever swap is dispatched.
plain_language: We dug through our own past experiments (not outside literature) to understand why the brain-analog Hopfield-style memory readout scored near-random on the word-meaning retrieval test. We found the team reused temperature/beta constants from an earlier unrelated test that used a different math convention -- when combined with the new formula the softmax essentially goes blind and just returns the average of everything, which looks like random guessing. This is a fixable configuration bug, not proof the mechanism is broken. We proposed a 5-minute re-run to confirm before spending effort on more expensive fixes.

summary: 2x-drill CA3 auto-associator anti-signal at cluster-correlated codebook (cluster_cos~0.90, 75pct dim-zero cue): 4-axis convergence (neuro/math/ML external + substrate-internal Cycle178+free-prob prior arc) shows this is a KNOWN attractor-network failure class (structure-blind Hebbian decoder + tight clustering -> crosstalk/prototype-attractor dominance), not substrate-novel. Hypothesis C (DG-side competitive-Hebbian preprocessing upstream of CA3) is most literature-favored fix P=0.55 (Foldiak 1990 + arXiv:2301.02196 direct architecture match); B (Storkey storage rule) P=0.28 partial only; A (iteration count) P=0.15 weak; D (fundamental/unfixable) P=0.10 as stated, refuted by 3 independent upstream fixes existing in lit. SCOPE SELF-CORRECTION: substrate own Cycle 178 result (rho=0.5 recall=0.93 BONUS vs rho=0.9 recall=0.33 COLLAPSE, inverted-U not monotonic) bounds the CG_HN_ARCHITECTURAL claim to cluster_cos>~0.8-0.9, NOT >0.5 as might be loosely extrapolated. T-F capacity check confirms K=500 well under C_TF~1047 -- failure is correlation-structure not capacity-overload. 3 ready-to-dispatch SMOKE probes proposed (A/B/C arbitration + combined-arm D stretch test).
plain_language: We asked the outside science literature and our own past experiments why the brain-inspired CA3 memory-completion step was making retrieval WORSE, not better, when the stored memories were very similar to each other (like many near-duplicate photos). Four independent sources -- neuroscience papers, physics-of-memory papers, AI papers, and our own month-old internal test -- all agree on the same explanation: this specific memory-completion trick blindly averages everything it has stored, so when memories are very similar it blends them into a single blurry answer instead of finding the right one. The fix the science point to is not to change the completion trick itself, but to sharpen the memories BEFORE handing them to it (the way the brains dentate gyrus sharpens memories before the hippocampus tries to complete them). We also caught and corrected an overclaim: our own past test showed that MILD similarity between memories actually helps (a bonus), and only VERY HIGH similarity hurts -- so the failure only applies to near-duplicate memories, not moderately similar ones. We wrote three cheap, ready-to-run tests to confirm which specific fix works best.

Real headroom is in compositional/multi-hop retrieval (recall@2hop plateau ~0.55-0.65 across all current SOTA per prior June drills), which the substrate rerank layer already covers regardless of encoder choice. Recommend stella_en_1.5B_v5 (MIT, Matryoshka, 8192ctx) as default replacement, snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0 (Apache-2.0) as conservative fallback, Qwen3-Embedding-4B for the compositional lane. Empirical bake-off proposed: 4-5 arms, N=500-1000 subset, ~half-day CPU/single-GPU wall time.
plain_language: We compared the current Wikipedia-search encoder (bge-large, from 2023) against everything newer released through mid-2025, scored on 11 different practical dimensions (not just raw search quality -- also speed, cost, license, article-length handling, and how easy it is to customize later). The surprising finding: our current encoder is already doing almost as well as physically possible on the Wikipedia search task itself, so chasing a fancier model for pure search quality would barely help. Where it IS worth upgrading: the current model can only read the first 512 words of an article (about one paragraph), which may be silently dropping most of every long Wikipedia article -- we flagged this as a real risk to check. We also caught that two of the strongest-scoring alternative models are legally restricted to non-commercial use, which would have been a licensing trap if adopted. Recommended replacement: a newer open-license model with no such length limit and no licensing risk, plus a cheap same-day test to confirm it in practice before switching.

summary: VSA-selector-vs-LLM-rerank drill: USER claim true but narrower than stated; regime boundary corroborated by 2 independent lit axes (COGS/CFQ/MetaQA hop-scaling + IR cost tables); bge_substrate_compositional_verify_v1 code-read shows it is NOT VSA bind/unbind (dense whitening+Rocchio+MMR proxy); +0.027 explained by known PRF/MMR precedent not compositional binding; one external paper shows true HRR binding failing at chance on 2-hop KG composition matching substrate d=25 cliff; 3 cheap decisive tests proposed with HP/HF thresholds; P_deflated=0.42
plain_language: We checked whether our hyperdimensional-computing selection method really should beat an LLM at picking relevant facts, as the user hypothesized. The literature says yes, but only in specific situations (facts with explicit structure, multi-step lookups, cost-constrained systems, or when you need to show your reasoning) -- and it turns out the actual experiment we ran (+0.027 F1 gain) did not test the real hyperdimensional binding mechanism at all, it tested a simpler embedding trick that happens to have modest, well-known precedent in the search literature. We proposed 3 cheap follow-up tests to find out if the real mechanism does better.

summary: optimal retrieval architecture for Director-KB: dense-seeded PPR graph-walk over existing KGStore (B=graph-walk backbone + A=MDR-style hop-trigger + C=dense-hybrid seeding), no external LLM anywhere; neither bge->stella swap nor fine-tuning alone fixes the RAG-composition bridge-surfacing HARD_FAIL -- it is a structural retrieval-architecture gap, not an encoder-quality gap
plain_language: Studied how to fix the KB retrieval bug where the substrate cannot find the connecting fact between two pieces of info (bridge chunks) for multi-step questions. Found the substrate already secretly has a knowledge-graph database (KGStore) sitting unused for this purpose -- it just needs a cheap graph-walk step added on top, seeded by the existing dense search. Published research on near-identical systems (HippoRAG, BridgeRAG) shows this specific fix works, but only for the specific failure pattern seen here, not a universal fix. Recommends 3 cheap same-day CPU tests before any real engineering commitment, and confirms that swapping or retraining the search encoder alone will NOT fix this -- it needs the architecture change.

plain_language: Studied how other systems (old-school expert systems, modern AI memory architectures, and the brain) automatically check their own stored rules before acting, since our substrate currently stores learned rules but never consults them automatically. Found a well-established pattern (three independent research lineages agree): a cheap tag-based filter followed by a similarity check, not a fancy learned router, since checking 99 stored facts is nearly instant either way. Proposed a concrete starting design (advisory-only, fully audited, easy to disable) plus a strict test for telling real effect from decorative-only retrieval, and handed a ready-to-build first experiment to the experiment-development lane.

plain_language: We asked whether the SHARDED (per-item) storage mode pinning at 100% accuracy across two different test sweeps today was a bug or a gap in what we tested. Outside research shows this is expected: per-slot memory schemes (like hash tables or Kanerva sparse memory) stay saturated until you push the items-per-slot ratio near a sharp cliff -- fan-out and dimension are not the covariates that matter. We already have one internal probe (Probe 6) that found the edge of that cliff. The cheap next step is to fill in a handful of points around that already-found edge rather than opening new territory.

summary: multi-round retry theory + composed-retrieval failure ontology: cross-lit synthesis (VSA/EVSI/SPRT/BAI/SDT) collapses to one universal inequality (gap*info<=cost) predicting single-shot argmax wins at high SNR/near-ceiling baseline; 7-mode failure ontology with mutual discriminators; 6-axis anti-drift regime signature framework; noise x ceiling-headroom identified as load-bearing pair
plain_language: Study of when a composed multi-round retrieval architecture (retry+clarify) should beat a single-guess baseline. Four independent bodies of theory (from VSA capacity, Bayesian sequential decision theory, best-arm bandits, and signal-detection+dialog theory) all give the same rule: retry only helps if the gap between top-two candidates times the informativeness of a second look exceeds the retry cost. The recent low-noise negative result is now predicted (not a killed direction): the baseline sat near the accuracy ceiling so retry had no room to earn back its cost. Delivered 7 mutually-distinguishable failure modes with prereg-detectable numeric discriminators, and a 6-axis regime-signature framework that must be swept before any composed-retrieval architectural claim earns regime-invariant status. Rank-1 follow-on: noise x ceiling-headroom sweep, 5-10 CPU-hours, cheap and decisive.

plain_language: We researched how production rule-engine systems (like OPA and Rete-family engines) safely transition rules from advisory (log only) to enforcement (actually apply). Best practice is a per-rule graduation flag (shadow/warn/live) plus a cryptographic nonce that proves a downstream module actually READ the modified parameter, combined with a null-A/B test that proves the change actually affected output distribution. This gives Phase 2 a concrete architecture and first-probe cell design with pre-registered hard-fail bands.

summary: teacher_free_semantic_bootstrapping_sparse_kb: 2x drill (4-way parallel lit-scan + synthesis) on R3 (internal self-teacher, wean off BGE) viability at ~1.6 atoms/entity. VERDICT NOT VIABLE NOW: every method family (KGE, random-walk, GNN-SSL, graph self-distillation, classical distributional semantics) has a tested floor above current KB density or has never been tested this sparse. Classical-distributional noise floor (Antoniak & Mimno 2018; Wendlandt et al 2018) is 100-400 atoms/entity, i.e. 60-250x current density -- the sharpest quantified gate found. KGE degree-stratification (KG-Mixup, WWW 2023) shows low-degree bins fail even at WN18RR density (~4.24-4.5 avg, 2.7x ours). Corrected a pre-supplied lead: WN18RR avg degree is NOT ~2.19 as speculated, actual computed value ~4.24-4.5 (mode 2). Verdict: grow-into-it foundational bet, 2-stage milestone ladder (Stage1 ~5-10/entity clears field tail-cutoff; Stage2 ~100-400/entity clears distributional noise floor), reinforces D1-now/R3-later sequencing from prior brain-grounded drill (D2 P revised 0.25->0.15 now, D3 0.30->0.25 now, both capped 0.40 after-milestone).
plain_language: Checked whether the substrate could teach itself the meaning of concepts from its own sparse knowledge base alone, with no outside AI teacher. Answer: not yet -- published research on similar methods needs roughly 60 to 250 times more facts-per-concept than we currently have before that kind of self-taught meaning stops looking like noise. This does not kill the long-term goal (the brain does something like this with no outside teacher either), but it turns a vague someday into a concrete two-step growth target for the knowledge base, and confirms staying with the current outside-AI-model bridge for longer than previously assumed.

summary: sparse-code semantic fidelity frontier: 2%-active is NOT the binding constraint on 0.85 cosine. Direct 4x-expansion SAE anchor (Morelli CLIP, FVU 0.22 at 0.78% active, spot-verified) clears 0.85-equiv at a TIGHTER sparsity; sparse-JL kurtosis penalty negligible at 2%; sparse-VSA end-task parity. 0.85-at-2% feasible IFF dense readout reaches ~0.88+; if dense tops ~0.80 the miss is objective-bound not sparsity-bound. plain_language: We asked whether making the concept-encoder code very sparse (only ~2% of units active) is what blocks the 0.85 quality target. Answer: no. Published sparse-autoencoder and random-projection results show sparser codes than ours already hit ~0.88 quality at our exact settings, so 2% is a comfortable, not risky, choice. The real bottleneck is upstream in the training objective (which recently crashed even with zero sparsity). Recommendation: fix and validate the dense objective first (read that one number, it is free), keep the 2% target, and run the sparsity sweep only as a cheap confirmation.

plain_language: Studied how the brain keeps a concept-encoding useful even though it never stops changing, and whether our encoder should do the same. Finding: the brain does not keep a frozen readout stable for free -- it periodically re-syncs (like a nightly memory tune-up), and our already-in-progress fix (anchoring every concept to a fixed reference frame) turns out to be the exact same trick a totally different field (upgrading search-engine embedding models without re-indexing everything) already uses. So this is good confirmatory news: no new build needed right now, a cheap free test is queued for next, and the long-term plan to eventually drop the outside teacher is unaffected.

plain_language: We shrank an expensive training test down to save compute, keeping the crowding ratio the same, expecting to see the same failure in miniature. It did not show up -- not because the shrink was wrong, but because the code has a second, always-on near-neighbor-teaching channel that behaves the same regardless of batch size (confirmed by reading the actual training loop), and because a separate ingredient already known to hurt (a nitpicking comparison term) was left on at full strength throughout the test, swamping any real signal. There is also a live possibility that the real driver is just the sheer number of distinct things being taught, not any batch-size ratio at all. Bottom line: do not spend the expensive full-scale test on the fancier fix yet -- run one more free variant first (simple objective, nitpicking term off) since current evidence favors it.

summary: cardinality_capacity_ceiling_0.85_reachability: 4 parallel lit-scans (sign-rank/LIMIT paper fetched, generalized-neural-collapse fetched, ANN anisotropic-quantization fetched, VSA-bundling-capacity fetched) converge: no hard info-theoretic wall below 0.85 (JL + sign-rank on natural structure predict d=4096 comfortably oversized for N=177899; raw combinatorial capacity ~640 bits/item vastly exceeds ~17.4 bits needed for distinctness) but current rigid block-WTA code is mathematically Product Quantization and pays a real axis-misalignment tax that compounds with N, plus training uses reconstruction-MSE loss instead of a rank-aware objective (ScaNN anisotropic-quantization literature shows this costs real ranking fidelity for free to fix). Top lever = rank-aware/anisotropic loss reweight (zero structural cost, P=0.50 capped); 2nd = OPQ-style learned rotation before block-argmax (P=0.45); widening d/K is real but insufficient alone per two disagreeing scaling proxies (2.3x-3.9x needed vs 2x proposed). Cheapest diagnostic = teacher-embeddings-direct-through-same-sparsifier bypass (zero training) to cleanly separate code-capacity-bound from student-bound before the NCE-fix FULL run even needs interpreting.
plain_language: We asked outside research whether a small, sparse code can ever faithfully represent 178,000 distinct concepts, or whether there is a hard mathematical wall below the 85%-match quality target. The answer: no hard wall -- the code has far more raw capacity than needed -- but the way the code is currently built (like a jigsaw cut into fixed pieces that do not line up with the real picture) and the way training is scored (matching the whole picture rather than preserving which pairs are more/less alike) are both leaving real quality on the table for free-to-fix reasons. We found two near-zero-cost fixes worth trying (change the scoring rule; add one learned realignment step before the jigsaw cut) before considering the more expensive option of making the code bigger, and a free one-step test (feed the untouched original picture through the same jigsaw-cutting step, no training needed) that will tell us immediately whether the jigsaw itself is the problem.

plain_language: We figured out exactly what the encoder 0.85 target metric means and how close we honestly are. The literal goal (does the code agree with the teacher on which things are similar) is basically hit already. A second, more practically-important question (does it actually return the RIGHT memory out of many neighbors) is still weak, and we proved with a cheap zero-training test that widening the code helps a little but is not the main fix needed -- the training process itself is the bigger lever, and that fix is already in flight.

Closest systems (IBM NVSA Nature MI 2023 88.1pct I-RAVEN, IBM in-memory PCM-HDC 760k-device classifier, Eliasmith SPAUN 2.5M-neuron fixed cognitive demo, Loihi HDC) are all narrower-scope solvers/classifiers/demos, not general memory substrates -- real but modest systems-integration gap (P=0.35). Encoder (distill BGE into block-sparse WTA code) is closest to OPQ/anisotropic-quantization + Frady-Kleyko Sparse-Block-Codes fusion; same-day internal algebra-gate=1.000-without-explicit-objective result further deflates the one candidate novel-combination (P=0.35->0.20) since SBC structurally preserves algebra by code-format construction, not training objective. Glass-box/audit framing already independently discovered by two 2025 papers (Attention-as-Binding arXiv 2512.14709, Hyperdimensional-Probe arXiv 2509.25045); once KG-provenance/circuit-tracing counted as competing, VSA-algebra-as-audit is not clearly more lay-legible (P=0.15); narrow algebraic-erasure-certificate sub-claim remains genuine white space (P=0.40, crypto/statistical unlearning literature has zero VSA-specific overlap). Director read (not novel, not yet an AI system, modest incremental value in crowded niche) judged BASICALLY CORRECT, arguably not harsh enough on combination-novelty; confirmed by convergence with internal SUBSTRATE-KNOWS-NOTHING anchor.
plain_language: The user asked for an unflinching gut-check: is any of this actually new, or has it all been done before? Outside research says the core math (the bind/combine/clean-up-memory operations) is 30+ year old, thoroughly published textbook material -- no novelty there, confirmed not a close call. The closest real-world systems (IBM, a brain-simulation project, Intel neuromorphic chips) are all narrower than what we are attempting -- they solve one puzzle-type or run one fixed demo, not a general memory system -- so there is a real but modest gap in assembling known pieces into one working system, not a scientific gap. The concept-encoder idea (compressing a big AI language model into a tiny sparse code) turns out to be a close cousin of two already-known compression tricks, and a same-day internal test result suggests even that combination is not doing real work -- the useful property comes for free from the code shape, not from anything we invented. The interpretable-memory pitch has already been independently proposed by two 2025 academic papers we were not first to think of, and a skeptic has a fair point that our version is not obviously easier for a real auditor to understand than the existing alternatives. Bottom line: the harsh read the user was given is basically right and, if anything, could be stated even more plainly on one specific point -- this is currently a well-engineered but non-novel component, not yet an AI system, with two narrow honest opportunities (assembling the pieces nobody else has, and a specific algebra-based deletion-proof idea) worth pursuing at modest, not breakthrough, value.

plain_language: We asked: exactly what should deep multi-step reasoning over our own stored memory look like, and how does the brain actually do it? Five completely different fields of study (brain science, psychology, our own vector math, modern AI chatbot research, and information theory) all pointed to the same one answer: fix the noisy intermediate result back to something clean after every reasoning step, using a separate scratch-memory, instead of letting small errors pile up hop after hop. This is the same trick phone-line repeaters use to keep a signal clean over long distances. We have never actually built and tested this combination on our own substrate, so we specced the cheap, one-afternoon experiment that tests it directly, with clear numeric pass/fail lines. No wall was found that rules this out -- the only real limit is a point where the trick stops working if you push too far, and we have one small, unconfirmed hint at roughly where that point might be for us.

plain_language: Ran 5 independent research angles on how to make the substrate SPEAK (turn a stored thought into ordered words). Four of five angles (brain science, psycholinguistics, and the substrate math theory) all independently point to the SAME mechanism we already designed: tag each word with its position, then use an iterative solver to unbind position+content together. Modern AI language models do it differently, but that is because AI has not solved this exact problem either, not because our approach is wrong. No hard mathematical wall was found blocking it. This does not change our build plan, it confirms it, and adds one promising alternative approach to try if our current test comes back negative.

Schema-formation (full goal) untested across ~80 CL-adjacent cells -- c3 landed data shows transfer=0.000 EVEN AFTER forgetting is fixed, confirming forgetting-prevention and abstraction are separate mechanisms (converges with all 5 lit angles: CLS neuro, schema cogsci, VSA bundling math, ML continual-learning surveys, info-theory stability-plasticity). Decisive next cell schema_bundle_structural_transfer_v1 (bundle bound episodes per relation-type into a segregated one-way schema store, test recall on held-out novel entity pairs vs random baseline) proposed, P_deflated=0.32.
plain_language: We confirmed the substrate genuinely does not forget old knowledge when new knowledge arrives (proven four separate times, including with the brain-correct dual-store architecture) -- that half of continual learning is done and real, not smoke. But the other half -- turning many individual facts into a general reusable pattern (a schema), the way the brain turns repeated experiences into generalized knowledge -- has never been tested, and a landed experiment from this week shows that fixing forgetting did NOT also produce that generalization (it stayed at zero). We designed the exact experiment to test it next, using math that mirrors how the brain forms schemas during sleep.

summary: 5x_drill_memory_spec_and_brain_mechanism: 5 independent lit-scans (hippocampal neuro, cognitive psych fan-effect, VSA/HDC theory, modern-ML associative memory, info theory) converge on ONE mechanism -- protect a compact index/pointer separate from content, rather than making raw superposition/bundling robust directly. Matches hippocampal indexing theory (Teyler and Rudy) exactly, and matches our own hub-rescue win (PROTECTED/INDEX binding deg5+ 0.261->0.727) as an independent re-discovery of the same fix. VSA lit (Clarkson/Ubaru/Yang 2023 arXiv:2301.10352) gives explicit O(K^2) capacity-cost formula in hub-degree K -- formal explanation for why plain bundling punishes hubs. Info-theory scan quantifies capacity at N=8192: true combinatorial wall (Gardner/Cover) approx 16384, classical-Hopfield-cost-curve approx 1130, our measured empirical operating point (capacity_alpha~0.30 at N=16384) approx 2458 -- already beating the classical reference, 6.7x below the true wall -- remaining gap is compute/engineering cost not physics. Genuine open gaps flagged honestly: (1) whether protection taxes non-hub capacity is untested, (2) whether protection generalizes across full hub-degree spectrum + load is untested (only one bucket/one load point measured), (3) resonator-not-helping-hubs (+0.056) has no direct VSA precedent, only an analogous explanation via Modern-Hopfield correlated-pattern spurious-state theory. Single decisive next experiment pre-registered: joint capacity x hub-degree CPU sweep with explicit HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL bands. P_deflated=0.50 (capped, novel-synthesis-generalization claim) per calibration discipline; mechanism-direction confidence higher (~0.65) but capped number governs.
plain_language: We asked five completely different fields of science (how the brain physically avoids getting confused by a person or place that shows up in thousands of memories, human psychology of forgetting, the specific vector math we use, modern AI memory systems, and pure information theory) the same question: how do you reliably remember a heavily-connected concept without every memory about it blurring together. All five gave the same answer: keep a small separate tag/pointer to the memory instead of trying to make the memory content itself resist crowding -- and that is exactly the fix that already worked once in our own system (a hub-recall test jumped from about 1-in-4 correct to about 3-in-4 correct using this exact idea). The brain has done this for real, for over a thousand million years-equivalent of evolution, so this is a proven-safe target, not a guess. We also found real numeric headroom: our current memory capacity is already better than the textbook baseline and still far below the true mathematical ceiling, meaning more compute (not new physics) is the main path to more capacity. Honestly flagged gaps: we have not yet tested whether protecting hub memories costs capacity elsewhere, or whether the fix holds up at realistic scale and across all degrees of connectedness -- one specific, cheap, computer-only experiment is proposed next to settle exactly that.

It tests whether cleaning up (snapping to the nearest clean concept) after every reasoning hop keeps a multi-hop memory chain accurate, versus carrying a fuzzy running vector that drifts. Full-N smoke already HARD_PASSed on 2 seeds: above a crosstalk-load line (M/N ~ 1) the clean-every-hop mechanism degrades gracefully while the fuzzy-carry method collapses -- a +0.50 accuracy gap at depth 5, with the clean method perfectly faithful (its answer is mechanically reproducible from its discrete trace) and a shuffled control at chance. plain_language: We dug into why teaching the substrate general facts (like where things are usually located) failed to transfer to a brand-new example, even though the underlying reasoning trick was proven to work on clean toy data. Outside research points at a specific, fixable cause: the substrate guessed the relationship pattern by simple averaging over examples, and averaging is a documented weak method whenever a fact has many valid answers (a sofa can be in a house, room, or store) no matter how good the word-meaning encoding is. The fix (train that pattern properly, comparing right answers against wrong ones, instead of averaging) has ALREADY worked once before on this same system for a similar analogy task -- so this is not starting from zero, it is finishing a fix that is half-built. The brain does something structurally similar: it keeps a separate, dedicated pattern-learning system apart from its store of specific facts, rather than hoping raw meaning alone does the job. We propose a next cheap test, but flag honestly that our test is a slightly harder version (a truly unseen example, not just a new combination of familiar ones) than the case where the fix worked before, so success is likely but not guaranteed.

plain_language: Shipped the make-or-break follow-up to the failed schema-transfer experiment to the remote CPU runner (now running). It asks a sharp question: when we teach the substrate a relation (like 'is located at') from real facts and then test it on a brand-new subject it has never seen, does it actually transfer the specific subject->object mapping, or is it just guessing the relation's typical answer? The quick preview showed meaning-based encoding beats spelling-based encoding, but troublingly, scrambling which subject goes with which object barely changed the score -- a sign the ~0.21 accuracy is 'name the usual place' guessing, not real per-subject transfer, and that training the transform did not clearly beat plain averaging. The full run uses many more held-out test entities (150 vs 60) and 3 seeds so the real-vs-scrambled gap -- the load-bearing metric -- is statistically firm, answering honestly whether ANY relation/encoding/estimator combo shows genuine subject-conditional inductive transfer above the 0.20 bar, or whether it is relation-prior guessing everywhere.

plain_language: We dug into why the substrate cannot yet answer new questions about things it has never directly stored a fact about (e.g. guessing where a brand-new object would typically be kept). The honest finding: the last test was inconclusive, not a proof of failure -- its own built-in sanity check did not work correctly, so we cannot yet say whether training harder helps or not. What we learned from outside research is that the field-proven fix is not training the relation-rule harder, but training the way the system reads an object description itself, jointly with the rule -- nobody has tried this exact combination in our kind of vector math before, so it is a real, promising, and currently untested next step, not a known dead end.

plain_language: We converged on the most brain-faithful next attempt at the deepest open problem: teaching the substrate to guess a new fact about something it has never directly learned about, using only what the new thing resembles. Instead of copying a generic machine-learning trick, we designed the version that mirrors how the brain actually does this (the hippocampus/entorhinal system) -- group similar things into a small number of known types (something the substrate already does perfectly, PP-254), then let a brand-new thing slot into the closest known type and refine from there. This reuses a capability we have already proven works, which is why this is a genuinely promising next experiment rather than a shot in the dark, though it remains unproven until run.

plain_language: We figured out WHY the substrate finally showed genuine (if modest) ability to guess facts about never-seen things: it started conditioning its guess on what the specific thing IS (its content), not just averaging over everything it had seen for that fact-type. That is exactly the trick well-known relational-AI models use, so this is a real, literature-grounded finding, not a fluke. We also found -- by directly counting the underlying fact database -- that one of the three fact-types tested (CapableOf) has almost no repeated answers to learn from (each thing has its own unique capability), so it may never generalize well no matter what; the other two have real room to improve with more training examples, which is a cheap next test to run. The brain-inspired version tested here was a simplified stand-in, not the full brain mechanism, so this does not mean brain-inspired approaches lost -- it means our simple version left performance on the table, with a clear next step to close the gap.

plain_language: We dug into the one open memory weak spot: very-high-degree hub concepts (referenced 8+ times) only recall correctly 42-47%% of the time even with our best current fix, versus 93-98%% for moderately-referenced ones. Good news found: a redundancy trick (storing several independent backup copies and averaging them before cleanup) already fully fixed this exact problem TODAY in a clean lab-style test, up to very high degree -- and that trick is grounded in a real, well-established brain mechanism (how populations of neurons average out noise, the same math used in motor-cortex direction coding). The catch: that fix has only been proven on clean synthetic data, not yet on our real messy data, and there is a real risk real hub interference does not behave as cleanly as the lab test assumed. We also corrected an earlier claim: the brain mechanism we thought was doing this (multiple-memory-trace theory) actually does not support constructive averaging in the literature; the better-grounded citation is population coding. Next cheap test: apply the validated fix to the real data and see if it holds.

plain_language: We asked whether the substrate pieces we already proved (reading text into concepts, storing and recalling facts, chaining reasoning hops, speaking an answer back out) actually snap together into one working pipeline, the way senses, memory, thinking, and speech snap together in a brain. Two of the three joints check out clean: the memory and reasoning pieces already speak the exact same internal language, so no translation is needed there. The third joint, handing a reasoning result to the speaking-out-loud step, has never actually been tried end to end, because the two best speaking mechanisms we have each speak a slightly different internal dialect than what reasoning currently produces. We researched how the brain solves this exact kind of dialect-mismatch problem (it builds an explicit trained translator between brain regions rather than forcing one shared language everywhere), and outside math and engineering literature says the same thing: a quick untrained translator loses real accuracy, a trained one does not. So this is not a dead end, it is a well-understood, buildable next step, and we laid out the cheap test that tells us exactly how much translation is needed.

plain_language: The richer-content experiment failed because the test asked the substrate to guess ONE specific correct answer when relations like AtLocation often have several valid answers (a dog can be at-location house, yard, or park). We measured how often this really happens (about 10-30% of the time) and found it only explains a small part of the failure. The bigger cause: when we let the model list its top-10 guesses instead of just its single best guess, the right answer shows up much more often (roughly 3x more often for one relation). This means the substrate is closer to knowing the answer than the strict single-guess test gave it credit for. We designed a new test that scores it the way the scientific field normally does for this kind of problem (ranked guesses, not one shot), and a quick preview run suggests it will land as a partial win, not a clear pass or fail -- worth running for real.

plain_language: The reframe cell that just landed showed the substrate usually gets the right answer into its top-10 guesses but rarely picks it first. We diagnosed why: a small set of frequently-seen answers act like magnets and keep winning the top spot regardless of the actual question, a well-known effect in high-dimensional similarity search (hubness) mixed with plain popularity bias from training. We spec'd a cheap, no-retraining fix (rescore the existing guesses to cancel out the magnet effect) and pre-registered pass/fail bands for it -- not run yet, just designed.

The ensemble-of-reward-estimators option wins because it directly targets the one number (noise across random seeds) that kept our just-passed trained gating experiment from reaching a clean pass. plain_language: We dug through the full history of the encoder (the substrate's weakest part, the layer that turns a word or concept into the memory's internal code) to find where it really stands and what has been holding it back. We found something valuable that had been overlooked: a training run from a few days ago actually already hit the accuracy target set for it (0.85), with the memory's algebra (the combine/undo operations) working perfectly -- but this good result was buried inside a run that got labeled an overall failure because a different variant tested in the same batch broke the algebra. The real blocker is not that the encoder is too small or too dependent on the borrowed teacher model -- it's that one of the training recipes used was subtly corrupting itself at full scale. Going fully teacher-free (no borrowed model at all) is confirmed not realistic yet at our current data size, so borrowing-then-specializing remains the right approach, and it may be closer to done than we thought. We spec'd the next, near-free experiment: run the already-trained winning version through the last two pipeline steps to confirm it holds up on real test questions, not just the practice-round metric.

Turns out we already fed it one real knowledge base (ConceptNet, 133 thousand facts) weeks ago and it is sitting in storage, verified intact -- but nobody has actually checked whether the substrate can FIND and USE those facts through its normal question-answering path (only an isolated test harness proved the underlying trick works, on a different dataset). So the cheapest, smartest next move is not adding more data -- it is checking whether the data we already have is actually reachable. We spec'd that check (no new download, no rebuild needed) and separately confirmed it does not need to wait on the other integration work in flight.

plain_language: We designed the decisive test for whether the substrate brain components truly work together under hard, realistic conditions (not just the easy test that already passed). Looking at data already on disk, we found that when the substrate cleans up its answer at a hand-off point (like a mental relay station), errors do not pile up out of control -- but when it skips that cleanup, errors compound badly. The new test chains four proven brain-like parts together (understanding roles, multi-step memory recall, a goal-checking gate, and speech output) under hard conditions to see if this good behavior holds for a real chain, not just one hand-off, and to check for a subtle risk: a stage confidently giving a wrong answer that silently poisons everything downstream.

plain_language: We re-checked which missing brain-inspired components are worth building next now that the memory/reasoning/generation/control pieces all work and connect end to end. We found something concrete hiding in the code: the multi-hop reasoning result that has been our headline win actually cheats at one step -- it is told the right answer-bucket to search in, rather than figuring it out itself -- and that gap has been flagged and waiting since a week and a half ago. Fixing it (using the same clean addressing trick that just made word-generation work at large scale, rather than training an opaque new network) is now the single best next build, because it upgrades an existing proven result from cheat-assisted to fully real, not just adds a nice-to-have. Separately, we found that the trained control gate gets much worse the deeper the reasoning chain goes, which is a textbook case for a brain-style forward-model corrector (predict and fix drift before it compounds, the way the cerebellum corrects movement before you feel the error) -- promising but needs a fresh experiment design rather than reusing an existing one. Two other candidate brain parts (a slow memory-consolidation system and a predictive-coding cortex layer) stay deprioritized -- nothing new makes them worth the compute right now.

The harder part is genuine arithmetic (actually computing 2+3=5, not just recognizing patterns) -- but a fresh look found the substrate already has three separate proven building blocks for representing exact numbers (the same trick grid cells in the brain use for space, repurposed for numbers) and outside research pinpointed exactly the one small missing piece needed to make ADDITION work, much smaller than previously estimated. Designed (not yet built) two concrete test cells: one for real arithmetic plus a built-in self-check for whether an answer is exactly right, and one free add-on testing the grammar-rule-to-algebra transfer. Also flagged why this matters beyond math: an exact right/wrong check (not a fuzzy similarity score) is exactly the missing ingredient for the substrate to eventually check its own reasoning for consistency.

What nobody tried is the much easier, already-proven version: use the same memory-retrieval trick that already works great on outside knowledge bases, but point it at the substrates own status records, to answer questions like which of my claims is the current one and do any two of my records disagree. We designed that experiment (did not run it, just designed it) -- it is cheap, reuses tools already proven to work, and is grounded in how the brains own conflict-detection circuit works (a very simple mechanism: if two competing answers both light up about equally, that IS the disagreement signal, no extra machinery needed). summary: math_arithmetic_basis_next_primitives: envelope-push on MATH capability post exp_math_rns_add_chain_v1 FULL HARD_PASS (verified: acc_A=1.000 all 3 regimes, controls collapse 0.000-0.012, 10-step chains hold, equality-check 1.000/1.000). Ranked build order for {subtract, compare, multiply}: (1) SUBTRACT is essentially free -- conjugate-phasor is the additive-group inverse of the already-certified exact homomorphism, no new mechanism, P=0.85. (2) COMPARE needs a magnitude-decode step (confirmed by lit-scan: RNS residues carry no order info by construction) -- recommended mechanism is half-range sign-detection (decode (a-b) mod M via already-proven CRT-decode, threshold vs M/2), a classical RNS-hardware trick with ZERO prior VSA/HDC precedent (genuine novel-synthesis, P_deflated=0.45 capped), directly closing the numeric-threshold-logic gap flagged in the 07-05 self-reasoning audit. (3) MULTIPLY has a NAMED mechanism in the substrate own primary reference (Kymn et al. 2024 arXiv:2311.04872 star operator: decode one operand via existing per-subblock argmax, exponentiate the other operand phasor by that residue, CRT-decode result) but requires all-PRIME moduli (current regimes are not prime) and an asymmetric decode-mid-pipeline step; lit-scan narrows the 06-23 drills 500-1000-line joint-RHC estimate down to ~150-250 lines for multiply-alone, P_deflated=0.40. A discrete-log/LNS re-encoding alternative for multiplication was investigated and explicitly REJECTED: it would require a Zech logarithm lookup table to restore addition in log-domain, i.e. would undo the just-proven free-addition mechanism rather than extend it. 4 parallel Sonnet lit-scans (LNS/Zech-log 15 sources; RNS magnitude-comparison 14 sources; brain log-magnitude coding 9 sources incl Schwartz log-polar cortex, Dehaene logarithmic mental number line, Greenwood cochlear tonotopic map; VSA/RHC multiply-and-compare mechanics re-confirming Kymn/Hanley/qFHRR + 1 new resonator-network citation) = 38 verified external sources this drill.
plain_language: The substrate just proved it can do exact addition (2+3=5, verified perfectly). We checked what math operation to build next. Good news: subtraction is basically free -- it is the mirror-image of addition we already proved, just flip a sign, no new mechanism needed. Comparison (is A bigger than B) is more interesting: the way the substrate stores numbers has no built-in sense of order (a well-known limitation of this style of number encoding), so we found a classical trick from computer-hardware number theory (subtract the two numbers, then check which half of the range the answer falls in) that should work, but it has never been tried in this style of substrate before, so it counts as a genuinely new step, not a guaranteed one. Multiplication is the interesting one: the exact paper this substrates addition trick came from ALREADY describes a way to do multiplication too, but it is a different, more involved recipe (you have to briefly read out one of the two numbers instead of keeping both fully hidden inside the math, and the moduli have to be prime numbers) -- so it is buildable and well-documented, but costs more engineering than addition or subtraction did, and is ranked third. We also checked and ruled out an alternative multiplication trick (encoding numbers as logarithms) because it would require a lookup-table fix to make ADDITION work again, which would undo what we just proved -- not a good trade. Recommended build order: subtraction first (free), comparison second (closes a specific gap we flagged earlier about the substrate checking its own confidence/claims against thresholds), multiplication third (completes basic arithmetic but is not needed for the self-checking goal specifically).

That is actually how human brains do it too (the part of the brain that picks a word and the part that adds endings to it are demonstrably separate systems, connected by a simple handoff, not one continuous process). We wrote a full test plan (a sample sentence, what would count as pass/fail, and a brand-new check nobody has run yet: does the ending-adding mechanism and the word-order mechanism actually agree on which word they are each talking about). Nothing was built or run this cycle -- this is the blueprint for the next build step.

We designed (but did not yet run) a fair test: the substrate builds a map of how one state leads toward another using its own trained memory, then tries to pick a useful middle stepping-stone on its own. We also found a subtle but important risk: the practice worlds we test on are built randomly, so they may not have natural shortcut-through-here states at all, which would make some of the fancier discovery methods pointless -- so the test includes a built-in check for exactly that. Our honest guess: partial success is more likely than a clean win or a clean failure. This is a narrow step toward the substrate reasoning about how to solve a problem, not general self-improvement.

summary: thalamic_router_RC2_mechanism_RC3_decision: 2x revival drill on exp_multihop_router_crt_residue_addressed_v1 clean structural HARD_FAIL (oracle e2e=0.980, crt e2e=0.147 vs naive 0.237, crt_minus_naive=-0.088, address-size sweep confirmed fundamental across 4 points). MECHANISM: hard-decision non-redundant per-modulus CRT decode is a textbook-fragile classical configuration (Li/Xia 2009 IEEE TSP, Wang/Xia 2010 IEEE TSP, RRNS lit Szabo-Tanaka 1967/Barsi-Maestrini 1973) -- a single residue error causes an unbounded reconstruction jump with no graceful degradation; the known fixes (redundant check-moduli RRNS, or joint/maximum-likelihood decoding) are genuine redesigns not a resize, explaining why the address-size sweep held fundamental at every point tested (wrong knob). Grid-cell literature (Sreenivasan and Fiete 2011 Nat Neurosci) confirms the brains own residue-like modular code needs BOTH large per-module neuron populations AND downstream attractor cleanup (hippocampal CA3) to be robust -- RC2 has neither ingredient. RC3 (learned router) feasibility: internal track record is 6/6 HARD_FAIL on a structurally analogous noisy-routing problem already tried in this codebase (MoE cosine-anchor/Hebbian-anchor/ReLU/gradient/capacity-aware routers); an independent external lit-scan converges on the same negative (Ng and Jordan 2001, Bickel covariate-shift: non-stationary Hebbian crosstalk undercuts the usual discriminative-classifier advantage). P_deflated(RC3 beats naive_centroid)=0.20. STRATEGIC CALL: SHELVE dedicated thalamic routing (both an RC2 redesign and RC3) as a build priority -- no current consumer (integration already composes end-to-end via regenerative cleanup without a router, logged separately), RC3 prior is low and converges from two independent evidence sources, and RC2 known fixes are substantive redesigns with nothing waiting on them. Framed as a legitimate, evidence-backed brain-component-inventory finding: regenerative cleanup IS the substrates working router-analog (parallel to hippocampal pattern completion), not a gap papered over. RC1 (relation-typed router, sidesteps the noisy-address-decode problem entirely since relation identity is clean side-channel input) flagged as the one not-yet-falsified backlog candidate if a future need arises. Concrete RC3 cell spec provided for the backlog (exp_multihop_router_rc3_learned_v1, arms/bands/non-stationarity discriminator) but NOT recommended for dispatch now.
plain_language: We dug into WHY the algebraic thalamic-style router (the one that failed last cycle) actually failed, and decided whether to build a learned (trained) version instead. The mechanism answer: the router tried to read an address by looking at two small, dedicated pockets of the memory vector and combining them with a strict math rule (like reading two dials and multiplying) -- and it turns out this exact approach is a well-known weak spot in classical number-theory engineering (the same problem hardware engineers solved decades ago for fault-tolerant computer arithmetic): a single misread dial throws the whole answer off with no partial credit, and simply making the dials bigger (which we tried, 4 sizes) does not fix that -- you need either extra backup dials or a smarter, softer way of combining the readings, both of which are much bigger redesigns. Interestingly, the brains own version of a similar dial-based code (grid cells that map space) avoids this exact trap by using huge crowds of cells per dial PLUS a cleanup step afterward -- our version had neither. Then we asked: would training a smart router (instead of hand-designing an algebraic one) do better? We found this project already tried 6 different trained/smart routers for a related problem and ALL 6 failed, and outside research agrees that trained routers usually only help when the background noise pattern stays stable over time -- and our noise pattern (from thousands of overlapping memories) keeps shifting, which is exactly the condition where trained routers do not reliably help. Bottom line recommendation: do not spend more building effort on a dedicated router right now -- the system already gets its reasoning chains to complete another way (a self-cleanup step at each stage) without needing one, so this becomes a shelved, well-understood item on our inventory list rather than a blocking problem.

plain_language: We dug into WHY the substrate failed to invent its own step-by-step plan (waypoints) when the plan needed 3+ sequential guesses at deep, high-branching regimes, even though the same mechanism worked fine with just 1 guess. The answer, confirmed both by our own numbers and by outside research: this is the exact same well-known problem as a student who copies each step off their own previous (possibly wrong) answer instead of checking against the real solution -- small errors compound multiplicatively the more sequential guesses are chained, regardless of how good each individual guess is. This is a famous, well-studied problem in machine learning (not a mystery), and it comes with well-known fixes: solve a coarser, simpler version of the plan first then fill in details (like sketching a route before adding street-level turns), and double-check each guess against a cheap sanity test before trusting it for the next step, instead of blindly chaining guesses. We wrote up a ready-to-build follow-up experiment that adds exactly those two fixes (reusing almost all existing code) to see if they rescue the deepest, hardest case. Recommended building it, both because the fixes are cheap and well-precedented, and because it doubles as a real test of a brain-inspired anticipate-and-correct mechanism (cerebellum-style) that a separate finding today also flagged as worth building.

Local smoke (2 seeds x N_DIM {2048,4096}, wall 95.6s): content=0.143 > exact=0.110 (lift +0.033, recall-within-recoverable 0.913) BUT margin-gated precision=0.687 < 0.75 -> HARD_FAIL; naive flat-tau precision 0.55 (the refuse-gate lifts it +0.14 but not enough); scrambled control collapses to 0.0; op-agreement guard 1.0; capacity_sensitive=FALSE. This is the honest CROSS-CELL-LAW noisy-readout bound. Committed 52cb73135; >=5-seed FULL (5 seeds x N_DIM {4096,8192,16384}, timeout 1800s) staged to remote_cpu_queue via queue_add.sh, REMOTE-VERIFIED (exit 0, self-test 10.2s on remote, PROT-022 referent resolved, entry present in queue.json).
outcome: experiments/exp_cert_ledger_retrieval_coverage_v1.py + preregs/cert_ledger_retrieval_coverage_v1_2026-07-06.md + data/exp_cert_ledger_retrieval_coverage_v1_smoke/metrics.json (smoke HARD_FAIL bound); canonical FULL pending on remote_cpu_queue
plain_language: The substrate's self-audit could only find a backing certified record for ~3% of the numbers it checks. We built a smarter, content-based lookup - using the substrate's own text-to-vector encoder to connect each cited number to the right record by the experiment's name-meaning instead of an exact string match, plus a confidence gate that refuses ambiguous matches. It genuinely recovers more records (about 91% of the ones that actually exist, a real improvement over exact matching), but it is NOT trustworthy enough to rely on: roughly 3 in 10 of its confident matches land on the WRONG near-identically-named experiment, and adding more dimensions does not fix this. The deeper reason coverage stays low is structural: about 83% of the cited numbers come from throwaway/smoke experiments that were never certified into the ledger, so there is simply no record to find. The honest fix is to make experiments record their own pass/fail numbers in a machine-clean field and certify more of them - not a cleverer search. This is a narrow glass-box monitor step: the substrate only reads and checks its OWN records, never edits the ledger or any code.

summary: cert-ledger self-audit coverage HARD_FAIL 2x-drilled: root cause is the ledger WRITER SCHEMA (no field for structured gate-claims), not retrieval quality -- 1/5822 cells adopt record_gate(), and even that adopter data never reaches cert_ledger.jsonl (grep: 5/1467 rows mention it in prose, 0 carry actual claim data). Demonstrated retrieval-free direct entailment recovers all 15 real claims on the one adopting cell with 0 mismatches and 0 retrieval steps, vs 0 regex hits in that same file verdict_msg. Ranked revival: #1 retrieval-free direct-entailment audit cell (cheap, reuses VETd comparator, no capacity axis); #2 additive gate_claims field on cert_ledger_writer.py + cell-template adoption convention; #3 regex retrofit-backfill NOT recommended (lit-confirmed retrospective-parse error risk). LOAD-BEARING, flagged for 3x follow-on.
plain_language: The self-audit experiment that just failed did NOT fail because the search mechanism is bad -- it failed because the permanent record-keeping file has no place to store the actual numbers behind a certification decision, only a text description of it. We found this by directly inspecting the files: only 1 out of 5822 experiment records has been upgraded to store numbers cleanly, and even that one record has its numbers silently dropped when it gets filed into the permanent ledger. We proved a fix works on that one record (checked all 15 of its numbers correctly, instantly, with no fuzzy search needed) and ranked three ways to fix this broadly, recommending the cheapest and safest one first. This is important because it directly blocks the goal of having the substrate meaningfully check its own work.

summary: generation_decode_correlated_collision_exact_margin: PR-transfer MIDDLE_BAND drilled to mechanism. Deep-regime generation decode collapse (gsbc D48, p1=0.37-0.62) is NOT a continuous clumped-exceedance process (3 lit-scans confirm extremal-index/Chen-Stein declumping is threshold-dependent, needs auxiliary parameters, and cannot be derived from bulk/trace stats like PR -- an acknowledged open problem for strongly-correlated continuous variables per Majumdar-Schehr arXiv:1910.10667). Instead: GSBC block-local codes are bounded-magnitude k-sparse bipolar (self-overlap = max possible overlap), so collision degenerates to an EXACT duplicate-codeword tie, resolved by argmax first-index tie-break. Derived p1_exact = n_distinct(codebook)/V -- exact, parameter-free, verified 0.961-1.016x ratio-fit (worst-case 1.04x) across all 9 non-saturated smoke cells (both gsbc/corr families, both mild D26 and deep D48 regimes), vs PR-gaussian 1.6-2.7x off and naive-independent 10-20 orders of magnitude off. CHAIN_GRADE candidate.
plain_language: The substrate previously found that its comprehension self-prediction trick partially, but not fully, worked for predicting generation-decode errors. This drill found the real reason and the right fix: because generation codes are literally either identical or not (a strict yes/no match, not a fuzzy similarity), decode errors only happen when two concepts got assigned the EXACT SAME code by accident. That means the substrate can predict its own generation reliability perfectly just by counting how many of its codes are exact duplicates of each other -- no statistics or approximation needed, and it is a fifth exact self-margin candidate, cheaper to compute than the ones that came before it.

summary: encoder_nce_margin_tradeoff_2x_drill: Stage-2 encoder v2 FULL HARD_FAIL 3-way triangulated (v2 const-NCE, v3b MID ablation, v3c FULL 5-seed NCE=0) as a margin-vs-geometry trade-off, not capacity/distill-target/JL-wall. NCE=0 recovers DENSE spearman 0.816-0.916 (5/5 seeds, beats prior P=0.20 estimate) but collapses keyed-algebra decodability 0.033-0.317 (need >=0.90). Top lever: sequenced NCE curriculum (reuse 5 landed NCE=0 checkpoints, short terminal NCE-relock) grounded in 2 freshly-fetched papers (arXiv:2605.06870, arXiv:2603.22304). Cheap smoke recommended, not a GPU-day. P_deflated=0.40 for joint recovery; 0.75 for semantic-alone (already effectively proven).
plain_language: We dug into why the encoder training run failed its meaning-accuracy target. Turns out two training goals were fighting each other: teaching it to rank meanings correctly, and teaching it to reliably decode an exact answer after combining concepts algebraically. Turn off the second pressure and meaning-accuracy is basically solved (close to or above target, 5 times in a row); leave it on (what actually ran) and decoding is perfect but meaning-accuracy caps out around a third to a half. This is not a dead end -- outside research on similar systems shows a fix: teach meaning first, then apply the decoding pressure only briefly at the very end. That test is cheap (reuses training already done, no fresh GPU-day) and is the recommended next experiment.

summary: self-margin taxonomy synthesis + CG_META assessment: 3-family classifier (order-statistic / collision-count / product-law-chain) keyed on decode-regime confirmed across 5 CG + 1 MIDDLE + 2 MM + 3 resistors; 2 tiers (generation dupclass CHAIN_GRADE, control-branching MEASURED_MECHANISM) finalized during this drill and matched ex-ante predictions; verdict CG_META-CANDIDATE not yet cert-tierable pending a held-out test (sketched, 2 predictions pre-registered) due to in-sample circularity in taxonomy construction.
plain_language: I pulled together everything the self-margin research thread found this session into one map: the substrate predicting its own failure points splits into 3 families depending on how it decodes, and two of the last pending results (generation, control) just landed exactly as predicted. I checked honestly whether this deserves to be certified as a general law and concluded not yet -- every capability used to build the pattern was also used to test it, which is circular. I wrote out a concrete, cheap next test (two new capabilities, predictions committed in writing before the fit is run) that would resolve this either way.

summary: self_margin_taxonomy_held_out_validation_resonator: pre-registered order-statistic/product-law-chain prediction for exp_resonator_capacity_gpu_v1 (K2/K3/K4 factorization) HARD-FAILS -- all 4 model variants tried miss K4 by 3.4x-7.1x (aggregate mean-ratio 4.24, outside [0.60,1.70] HARD-FAIL band); taxonomy remains DESCRIPTIVE-only, no CG_META atom minted.
plain_language: We asked whether the self-margin prediction rule (which classifies how a capability breaks down) could correctly predict a NEW, never-before-tested case (the resonator memory-factorization cliff) before we looked at the answer. It could not -- the predicted collapse curve was 3 to 7 times too optimistic at the hardest setting. This means the rule is a good description of the cases used to build it, but not yet a proven general law; we are keeping it as reference documentation, not promoting it to a certified capability claim.

summary: resonator K-collapse 2x negative-revival: mechanism=convergence-basin/spurious-joint-fixed-point proliferation (AGS/TAP/K-SAT annealed-counting family), cross-validated 3 lit-scans + substrate own 2026-05-19 history (Frady-Sommer + Karunaratne-Langenegger ACF paper family). Self-predictability=NO ready closed form this cycle (effort-boundary not fundamental-boundary, unlike row 8b); own derivation verified z_init=16.8 to <1pct, combinatorial-count check HARD-FAILs by ~10x informatively. No 4th CG_META family minted. Concrete actionable: transfer substrate own validated ACF rescue (cap_map row 51) to untested factor-count axis.
plain_language: We dug into WHY the resonator (the part of the substrate that solves multi-piece puzzles by iterative guessing) collapses so badly when asked to resolve 4 things at once instead of 2 or 3. The cause is a well-known phenomenon in neural-network theory: as more interlocking pieces are added, the number of self-consistent WRONG answers the search can get stuck on grows much faster than the number of RIGHT answers, so the search increasingly falls into a wrong-but-stable trap. This matches published theory and even matches this project own two-month-old research that already spotted the right papers. We could NOT derive a formula this cycle that predicts exactly how bad the collapse will be from first principles -- that remains an open, but plausible, math project, not a dead end. The good news: we already have a proven fix (called ACF) for a closely related version of this same problem, validated elsewhere in this project, that has never been tried on this exact variant -- that is a concrete, low-risk next experiment.

summary: brain_component_consumer_ranking: re-audited all missing/weak brain-component candidates (thalamus, cerebellum x2, basal-ganglia, neuromodulation, CLS, cortical-microcircuit) for a PROVEN consumer post-thalamic-router-shelving. 4/6 confirmed still lack a present consumer (unchanged from 07-06). Waypoint-decomposition cerebellum target now CLOSED (FULL HARD_FAIL, DELTA=0.004). TOP PICK: cerebellum-class SR-rollout anticipatory-bias for the already-built, already-HARD_PASS-at-d4 PFC-BG gate own measured depth-degradation (gonogo_lift 0.653->0.075 d4->d6). Prior multi-gamma/branching lever smoke-negative for being the driver; 2 fresh lit-scans confirm gamma-only insufficiency externally and find zero direct precedent for anticipatory-forward-model-fixing-gating-horizon-degradation specifically (novel synthesis, P capped 0.20-0.28). Full 3-arm CPU smoke spec delivered inline.
plain_language: We asked: of all the brain parts the substrate is still missing (thalamus, cerebellum, basal ganglia training signal, neuromodulation, memory consolidation, cortex microcircuit), which ONE has a real, already-existing job waiting for it -- learning from the mistake where we almost built a thalamus-like router nobody needed. Most (4 of 6) still do not have a genuine waiting job, confirming what we found two days ago. But one does: the substrate already has a working goal-directed control gate that is excellent at shallow reasoning depth but falls off a cliff at deeper depth, and a cerebellum-style anticipate-then-decide mechanism (predicting the outcome before committing, not just cleaning up after) has never actually been tried on it -- only a different, already-disproven fix (widening how far ahead the gate looks) was tried. Outside research backs this up: simply looking further ahead does not fix this kind of problem in general, but nobody has directly tested the predict-before-committing trick on this exact kind of gate either, so this is a real but honestly uncertain next experiment, not a sure thing. A cheap, CPU-only test design is ready and handed off in the note.

summary: 2x drill on 3-cell converging noise-compounding negative (resonator K-way, waypoint compounding-error, cerebellar SR-rollout): diagnosed TWO distinct sub-mechanisms (no-reset coupled search vs self-referential decision-feedback-style correction), neither fundamental. Fresh on-disk finding: waypoint verify-gate retry_rate_combo=0.0/fallback_rate_combo=0.0 at deepest FULL regime proves the rescue never actually verified against independent ground truth. Reasoning-depth survives via regenerative-repeater property (hard argmax vs fixed external codebook each hop). Top rescue candidate: finite-T Glauber relaxation + redundant-restart plurality vote on resonator K4, converges with field-advisor D1 candidate.
plain_language: We dug into why three different capabilities all get NOISIER, not better, when they chain multiple reasoning/decode steps together, while a fourth (reasoning-depth) chains fine. Found the fourth one resets to a clean, exact answer after every step (like a digital repeater), while the three failing ones either never reset or double-check a guess against the same shaky signal that made the guess in the first place -- so the check never catches anything. This is fixable, not a hard wall; we have a concrete, cheap next test (add controlled randomness plus multiple independent tries, then vote) targeted at the clearest case.

summary: ingest_arc_scoping: encoder joint solution (INBATCH-RKD, dense 0.897/0.887, keyed@J5=1.0, shuffled-key control 0.0 clean) independently re-verified on disk both seeds HARD_PASS at n=177899 (the CURRENT real live-store scale, not synthetic) -- but this is 18pct of the 970069-entity production KB target (wc -l verified), a genuine untested scale gap. Bigger finding: the near-term ingest pilot does NOT need to wait on this gate at all -- it splits into path A (retrieval/composition via existing BGE space + proven CHAIN_GRADE Hebbian-bind mechanism, zero encoder dependency) vs path B (native substrate bind/unbind reasoning, what the joint solution actually gates). Staged plan: Stage0 exp_ingest_knowledge_integration_verify_v1 (dispatch-ready today, CPU-only, reuses already-committed ConceptNet content + live query path, zero new ingest) -> Stage1 N8 cert (pre-registered 06-22, never dispatched) -> Stage2 50-200-note dogfood pilot (BGE space, no re-encode) -> Stage3 encoder scale-test at >=400K before trusting 970K production claim -> Stage4 relation-vocabulary consolidation loop (only needed for open-corpus ingest beyond curated sources). Added a shuffled-2nd-hop firing control to the ingest test design (imported from the 07-06 self-audit vacuous-retrieval lesson) that was missing from the 07-05 spec.
plain_language: I scoped out how we would actually feed the substrate real outside knowledge once the encoder is trustworthy, and found the plan does not need to wait as long as it seemed. The part of the encoder that lets it do algebra-style reasoning on its own memory really did pass its test today, cleanly, and I checked the raw numbers myself rather than trusting the summary -- but it was only tested on the amount of knowledge already loaded in today, not the much bigger final target (about 5 times more). Separately, and more importantly, I found that the FIRST real test of ingest -- can the substrate actually find and correctly combine facts it already has stored -- does not depend on that encoder work passing at all, and can be run right now, cheaply, this cycle, using machinery that already exists. I wrote out the exact staged plan, in order, with the first cheap test fully specified.
