plain_language: The reasoning-engine test failed and we needed to know WHY before building the proposed fix: is the answer-information genuinely lost when many candidates get mashed into one signal (in which case splitting the signal = 'sharding' is the right fix), or was the reader just not given enough tries to dig the answer out? We re-ran the EXACT same failed signal but only turned the reader's effort dial up (20 up to 100 passes), changing nothing else. Result: giving the reader more passes DOES progressively dig out the correct answer -- from 62% up to 87% of the reachable answers get surfaced by 100 passes -- so the information was NEVER lost; it is in there. The headline recall number stayed flat only because of HOW the reader ranks what it finds (it rewards whatever it grabs first and a safety gate throws away the ones it finds late). So the wall is on the READER side (ranking + gate + effort), not the storage side. That means the sharding rebuild is NOT the justified next step -- we should fix the reader's ranking and gate first. This was a cheap seconds-scale check, not a burned overnight run.

plain_language: We tried the fix the last experiment pointed at: teach the reader to rank answers by how confidently it recognizes each one, rather than by which it happened to grab first, and give it plenty of tries. On a clean textbook example it worked perfectly. On the real data it did NOT: the correct answer, even after the reader digs it out, comes out with such a faint match-strength (because it is buried under a lot of overlapping cross-talk from all the other candidates crammed into one signal) that ranking by confidence still cannot lift it above the louder wrong answers. In fact the simplest possible reader beats the fancy one here, and even that simplest reader loses to just guessing by popularity. So this sharpens the diagnosis: the answer is not truly lost, but it is packed in too weakly to read out no matter how clever the reader. The real fix is upstream -- stop cramming so many candidates into one signal (the 'sharding' rebuild), which is exactly the next step that was on hold. This was a cheap 65-second local check; we did NOT burn an overnight GPU run on a fix we could see fails.

summary: DEEP DRILL (USER-requested, deepest of arc): brain beats frequency-guessing not via smarter weighting but via a structurally SEPARATE geometric/relational map (Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine: structure-code factorized from content-code), BUILT OFFLINE by hippocampal replay/systems-consolidation (CLS theory; replay demonstrably generates never-traveled shortcut sequences, Gupta et al 2010 Neuron, falsifying a simple-experience-frequency account of replay itself), and ARCHITECTURALLY caps frequency influence to a bounded DDM starting-point offset while structural evidence sets an uncapped drift-rate (Mulder et al 2012 J Neurosci double-dissociation) -- a strictly stronger claim than the prior notes plain residualization fix. Mapped to substrate: compose/bind CG = hippocampal episode-storage (proven); ranker = perirhinal familiarity (all we have); MISSING = factorized structural code, offline map-builder, and architectural (not additive) frequency cap. 4 ranked courses w/ deflated P: A hardened-residualization-ranker (P=0.28, in flight) > D relation-type meta-property closure layer (P=0.30-0.35, cheap/narrow) > B corpus density (P=0.15-0.20 standalone) > C replay-built geometric map-builder (P=0.20-0.25, highest ceiling, must confront on-substrate stage3_hrr_involutive_systematic_generalization_v1 HARD_FAIL precedent first, sequence after D).
plain_language: We asked: how does a brain figure out a fact it was never directly told, beating the lazy strategy of just guessing whatever is most common? The answer has three parts. First, the brain keeps a completely separate mental map of HOW THINGS RELATE (like a subway map showing which stations connect, with the station names removed) instead of mixing that up with how often it has seen any particular fact -- this map can be read like a ruler to measure a distance it was never shown, the way a lookup table never can. Second, that map is not built instantly: it is built OFFLINE, during sleep and rest, when the brain replays and recombines memories -- and we can prove this isnt just replaying old footage, because sleep-replay in animals has been caught generating shortcut routes the animal never physically walked. Third, even when the brain does use a familiarity/popularity gut feeling, it is walled off so that popularity can only give a small head start in a race, never let a popular-but-wrong answer out-run strong real evidence. Our system currently only has the popularity-flavored gut feeling and nothing else -- we are missing the separate map, the sleep-time map-builder, and the wall between popularity and evidence. We laid out four ways to build these, ranked from cheapest-and-readiest to deepest-and-riskiest, each with an honest chance-of-success estimate and the biggest risk named -- including flagging that we already have one failed past experiment that looks uncomfortably similar to the riskiest, highest-payoff option, so that option should be attempted last and carefully.

plain_language: Before the big verification run lands, mapped out exactly what to do next no matter how it turns out. Looked at the real history of how this class of AI reasoning method has improved over a decade and found that a huge chunk of past progress came from cheap training tweaks, not fancy new architecture -- so the very first thing to try, win or lose, is those cheap tweaks, before building anything exotic. Also found an honest, humbling calibration: our own best-possible target for this task is roughly equivalent to an old, first-generation method from 2013 in absolute terms, because our task is harder (two-step reasoning, not one-step) -- so hitting our own ceiling is a real win but should never be described as matching the best AI systems in the world. summary: abstract_grounding_relational_role_vs_attribute_reframe: brain-first drill on the reframe that abstract concepts ground via relational/map-ROLE not attributes. Garvert/Behrens 2017 eLife proves pure-relational graph-communicability coding is real and neurally dissociable from attribute coding, BUT every other headline abstract-map result (Constantinescu 2016, Park 2021/2024) is actually a 2-3D attribute-coordinate code in disguise. Symbol-grounding literature (Harnad, Taddeo-Floridi, Bender-Koller octopus) rules out pure relational structure with no reachable exogenous anchor -- exactly what HARD_FAIL_FAIRNESS caught (any edge inflated it = missing must-fail control, not proof relational grounding fails). Reconciles all 3 attribute-negatives with different mechanisms each. Unifying claim: relational grounding is PARASITIC on exogenous anchoring via composition-reachability, not a free byproduct of building the reasoning map -- sharpens (does not contradict) the grounding-is-the-verifier convergence note. Explains why 6 on-substrate relational-code negatives kept failing: built over a closed relational island (zero grounded data), the exact regime the literature says cannot ground. P_deflated=0.30 refined-claim / 0.12 strong-form.
plain_language: Dug into how brains actually ground abstract ideas like math and social relationships -- is it by attaching properties (like a number having a size), or by where a concept sits in a mental map of relationships? Found it is a bit of both, and crucially: a pure relationship-map only counts as real grounding if it eventually connects back to something concrete and experienced -- a map thats just relationships-about-relationships with nothing real underneath is a well-known trap in cognitive science (the same trap language models fall into). This explains why three earlier attempts to ground abstract concepts each failed for a different, fixable reason, and gives a specific redo test plus a likely explanation for why past relational-reasoning experiments here kept losing to simple frequency-guessing.

plain_language: We asked: can we tell, with real math, whether an idea like justice or multiplication is actually connected back to something concrete and real (like a hand or a rock) inside our knowledge graph, or whether its floating disconnected? Turns out network scientists already have exactly the right tools for this (the same math used to study epidemics spreading and internet robustness), and other researchers have already used it for exactly this grounding question on dictionaries. Our commonsense graph (CSKG) is already downloaded and already dense enough for reasoning -- now we designed a cheap, no-training test to check if it is ALSO well-connected enough to ground abstract ideas back to concrete ones, with built-in trick-detectors so the test cannot fool itself. We also found a neat, verified surprise: the most well-connected hub words in a dictionary graph are actually the LEAST concrete ones (words like be/have/do), not the most concrete ones -- so well-connected does not mean grounded, they are different things and must be checked separately. The actual test itself is designed and ready to run next session; nothing was run yet, this was research and design only per the current safety lock.

plain_language: We built and shipped the actual test that the last research note designed: does our commonsense knowledge graph actually connect concrete, real-world words (like 'rock' or 'hand') to abstract ideas (like 'justice' or 'probability')? The test drops a set of 'concrete' starting points into the graph and walks outward step-by-step to see how quickly it reaches the abstract words. Crucially it has three built-in cheat-detectors so it cannot fool itself: it compares against random starting points, against a shuffled version of the same graph that keeps each word's number-of-connections but scrambles WHO connects to whom, and against just picking the most-connected hub words. A dense graph reaches everything easily, so only beating those controls counts as real grounding. It is a pure graph walk -- no training, no new data, all inputs already on disk. A quick self-check on a tiny hand-built graph passed on the remote machine in 3 seconds, confirming the walker and the cheat-detectors all work. The full run is now queued and will start automatically once the machine finishes its current job.

summary: how-others-beat-frequency: RotatE Table1 proves TransE cannot represent CSKG dominant relation mix (SYNONYM symmetric + IS_A 1-to-N) at any dim/training; on-disk read confirms CSKG fit (all 3 variants: margin_fb/margin_mb/anchor1) is additive-Euclidean TransE in the FIT step, RotatE-equivalence claim true only of FPE readout kernel -- operator-gap: substrate already has validated rotation-native FHRR-bind (PP-275 Hits@1=0.899) but course-C cells never call it. plain_language: We found the likely root cause of why our knowledge-graph reasoner underperforms: it uses an addition-based relationship representation that is mathematically proven unable to handle synonym (same-as) and category (is-a) facts, which are exactly our two most common fact types. We already built and proved a rotation-based fix elsewhere in the system but never applied it here. We also found our internal pass/fail bar (90% correct) was set far above anything ever achieved in this research field at this data size, so we recommend a fairer, still-honest target: beat the popularity-guessing baseline specifically on rare facts, which is both the real prize and the standard the field itself uses.

summary: next-form-decision: 4-way lit scan (form-by-degree, best-form-for-commonsense, popularity-leakage, brain direction+magnitude) on first CSKG fair-test result (ROTATE=0.077 beats POP=0.044 on fair low+mid stratum; ADDITIVE=0.104 beats rotation there; rotation wins high-degree 0.396 vs 0.321 + aggregate MRR). Recommendation: build HAKE-style phase+modulus hybrid next -- theoretically matched to our mereological/causal relation mix, real verified gains over plain RotatE on hierarchy-heavy benchmarks (never tested on commonsense graphs -- open gap). Leakage flag (r=0.31, failed g_backdoor) does NOT invalidate the stratified beat-POP claim (stratification IS the field-standard remedy) but DOES flag aggregate MRR as not-yet-trustworthy, and raises a NEW risk: a scalar modulus term is the component most likely to re-encode degree -- must pre-register a hard-fail band on r-increase for the next build.
plain_language: Researched why our simple encoder wins on rare facts while our fancier rotation encoder wins on popular facts, and whether a combined direction+size design (seen in both AI knowledge-graph literature and how the brain maps space) would get the best of both. Recommendation: build that hybrid next, using the exact same fair test, with a built-in tripwire so we cannot fool ourselves if the new size component just re-measures popularity.

summary: Scaling-law drill (does glass-box relational reasoning scale to bigger KGs): current CSKG result (N=25752) is MIDDLE_BAND_PARTIAL not clean win -- additive TransE beats rotation on the fair stratum, backdoor correlation r=0.31 fails the <0.20 gate. No dim-vs-N law exists in KGE literature, but newest KGE rank-bottleneck theory (arXiv:2506.22271) AND classical Treves-Rolls hippocampal capacity theory independently converge: capacity is governed by LOCAL DEGREE/connectivity, not global N. Frequency baseline moat likely GROWS as a share of total graph mass with scale (Barabasi-Albert skew growth) even as the fair low/mid-degree arena grows in absolute count -- degree-stratified reporting is a permanent requirement, not a today-only patch. Make-or-break property = reusable relation OPERATORS vs per-entity MEMORIZATION (GraIL/NBFNet architectural argument); brain literature (grid-cell modular reuse, TEM structure/content factorization, CLS consolidation) says the current flat per-entity fit is the wrong shape to scale gracefully. Cheapest next test: rerun the already-built grounding_learned_sr_heldout_reasoning_v1 held-out-ENTITY split harness on the current rotation/additive fit codes -- P=0.15-0.20 it passes, deflated hard because a structurally similar mechanism already FULL HARD_FAILed this exact test.
plain_language: We asked whether our relational-reasoning approach would keep working as we feed it much bigger knowledge graphs, or hit a wall. Answer: the plumbing (memory/compute) scales fine, but the current result is a partial win with an unresolved red flag (it correlates too much with plain popularity), and a simpler method currently beats the fancier one on its own home turf. The bigger risk as graphs grow is that a few super-popular hub facts will make up a growing share of the total, so we must keep measuring fairness separately for rare vs. famous facts forever. The real make-or-break question is whether the system learns reusable RULES (which would work on brand-new facts) or just memorizes a bigger lookup table -- we already have one failed test of this on a related mechanism, and the cheapest next step is re-running that exact test on todays result before spending compute on a bigger experiment.

summary: storage_is_the_map: brain-scale storage-architecture drill (TEM/successor-representation/CA3 unify storage+inference; HolE/VSA precedent confirms structure-content factorization is real and already present in KGStore; HRR-linear vs resonator-quadratic vs Hopfield-exponential capacity laws mapped; CLS/replay consolidation mechanism matches existing continual.py/hippocampal_encoder.py primitives) + concrete integration path: promote KGStore bind op from bipolar to complex64 phase-rotation (FHRR=RotatE native), refine phases via existing replay/consolidation cycle instead of standalone torch fit, remote-runnable Cell A(parity)/B(relation-pattern lift)/C(consolidation wiring) test pre-registered with HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL thresholds; explicitly scoped OFF the separately-proven held-out inductive-inference wall.
plain_language: Studied how brains store huge amounts of knowledge without a separate reasoning system bolted on top -- the brain uses ONE representation for both remembering and inferring, and reuses a fixed relational scaffold across many facts instead of rebuilding it each time. Our substrate KG store already does the reuse trick (proven, CERT 585) but our new rotation-based reasoning math currently lives in a disconnected side-table instead of being part of the actual store. Proposed a concrete way to fold it in natively and refine it during the same overnight-style consolidation process we already have, with a pre-registered pass/fail test ready to ship remotely.

summary: kg_degree_community_diagnostic: 3-way lit scan (degree/topology vs link-prediction difficulty, TEM factorized-operator graph prerequisites, brain semantic-network community structure) + pre-registered remote-runnable diagnostic (power-law/Gini/max-mean-ratio/clustering/modularity/per-relation-cardinality/core-periphery-localization/fair-stratum-vs-degree-cutoff curve) on the actual 12-core CSKG test graph (N=25752, 29 relations). Key new facts: (1) Aiyappa et al ICML2025 shows standard link-prediction eval protocol is ITSELF implicitly degree-biased -- backdoor_r=0.31 gate failure may be partly a measurement artifact, cheaply checkable via degree-corrected negative sampling, independent of graph shape; (2) CSKG explicitly design-disclaims schema cleanliness (own paper: blurring object/class/action distinctions) -- literature (Krompass/Baier/Tresp type-constrained KGE) says this is direct evidence against an easy win for a shared relation operator; (3) TransH/RotatE cardinality-heterogeneity critique predicts SYNONYM/IS_A relations will show worst structural purity in pure graph stats with zero training, giving an independent triangulation path against the already-found trained-model functional-form gap; (4) brain semantic networks (Steyvers-Tenenbaum, Borge-Holthoefer-Arenas) show established modularity that schema theory and TEM explicitly exploit -- brain literature does not license schema-agnostic factorization either.
plain_language: Studied what specific measurements of our knowledge graph shape (how lopsided popularity is, whether it has consistent neighborhoods) would tell us about beating the popularity baseline and about building a reusable-rulebook reasoning system. Found a very recent finding that the standard way the field checks did-you-beat-popularity is itself quietly biased toward popularity, meaning part of our own worrying signal might be a measurement-ruler problem, not just a real graph problem -- cheap to check. Designed six specific graph calculations (all pure counting, no training, runnable on a normal computer) with pre-registered pass/fail bars, reusing data we already have on disk.

plain_language: Designed the concrete fix for a knowledge-graph reasoner that currently memorizes a private vector per concept and therefore cannot handle brand-new concepts it never saw before. The fix: represent any concept (new or old) as a quick on-the-fly combination of how it connects to a small fixed set of well-known landmark concepts, reusing math the system already knows how to do -- no retraining needed for new concepts. This mirrors how a brain instantly maps a brand-new room using a fixed toolkit of spatial cells rather than learning a whole new map from scratch. We designed a cheap, pre-registered test for this, but it is explicitly queued to run AFTER the current in-flight test (checking whether the existing simpler approach already fails on brand-new concepts) finishes -- that test has not landed a clean verdict yet.

summary: inductive_map_builder_best_in_class_magnitude_levers: calibrated proven ANCHOR_COMPOSE result (held-out MRR 0.1282, Hits@10 0.278, CSKG-12core N=25752, support_frac=0.50, zero-training) against inductive-KGE literature -- correct comparison class is commonsense-KG trained-encoder methods (InductivE/ConceptNet, MRR ~0.18-0.21, Hits@10 ~0.29-0.50), NOT curated-ontology benchmarks (WN18RR/FB15k-237, MRR 0.37-0.73) which use cleaner relation semantics; we already sit at 60-95pct of the correct target band with zero training. Flagged a protocol trap (50-sampled-neg vs full-entity-ranking inflate Hits@10 by ~2x; ours matches the harder full-ranking family). Ranked 6 levers to close remainder: top-ranked is sequential/iterative SIC-peel of the support bundle (brain: theta-gamma sequential slotting + predictive-coding error correction; field: VSA resonator sequential-decode 8x component-recovery precedent, arXiv:2412.00354) and hard-negative scorer refit (KGE lit +0.02-0.04 MRR convergent across 3 papers) as the two cheapest/best-evidenced next cells; multi-hop expansion has the single largest quantified field number but is explicitly GATED by the proven GrapHD SNR~5log(D/d) capacity-tracks-local-degree law (bigger bundles trade SNR against dimension at fixed D).
plain_language: We now have a proven zero-training way for our knowledge system to instantly describe brand-new concepts, but its raw accuracy score is objectively modest. This drill checked that score against the outside world: it turns out we already land close to the bottom of the right comparison band (other systems handling messy real-world common-sense graphs), not embarrassingly behind -- and a much higher-scoring benchmark family out there is actually testing an easier, cleaner kind of graph, so comparing against it would be unfair. We then ranked concrete next fixes, led by a brain-inspired one (check-and-recheck a noisy memory trace instead of reading it once) and a proven training tweak (make the underlying scorer pickier), both cheap to test next.

plain_language: We looked for the NEXT wave of upgrades (beyond the two already shipping) for our brand-new-concept-description system, with a hard rule that any upgrade must be buildable using only the systems own native math toolkit, not a bolted-on trained neural network. The most important finding: we checked the actual measured numbers for the worst-off concepts (ones we have almost no information about) and found they currently score WORSE than random guessing -- not just weak, genuinely broken -- because several candidate upgrades (double-checking the guess, weighting evidence better) cannot help when there is no evidence at all to work with. Reading the real code turned up a concrete fix specifically for this worst case: the system currently throws away facts pointing FROM a new concept, only using facts pointing TO it, even though it already has a trained mechanism (built for another reason) that can read facts in reverse for free. This is the one upgrade that can plausibly rescue the worst-off new concepts specifically, and it costs nothing new to try.

plain_language: We checked whether our from-scratch, no-training memory mechanism could ever be upgraded to match the ceiling of a more expensive, gradient-trained version, without turning it into a trained neural network. Four independent research angles all pointed at the same answer: the bottleneck is HOW the system writes new facts into memory (a simple one-pass addition rule), not how big the memory is or what format facts are stored in. There is a decades-old, purely arithmetic upgrade to that writing rule (no training loop needed) that plausibly closes most of the gap, and it is cheap to test directly. If it does not work, we already have a brain-inspired backup idea built and just not turned on yet.

summary: deployable_representational_capacity_levers_relational_map_builder: RNS/CRT multi-module residue coding (grid-cell analog) identified as leading deployable ceiling lever -- capacity=product-of-moduli, cost=sum-of-moduli, sub-quadratic vs monolithic n_dim increase; ranked 5 levers total (SBC+block-factorizer decode, resonator iterative decode, Kronecker clean-up, DG/cerebellar sparse front-end); P_deflated=0.35 top lever
plain_language: We asked whether there is a cheaper way to raise our knowledge-memory system capacity ceiling than just making the underlying vectors much bigger (which works but gets expensive fast, cost growing with the square of size). The brain answers this with grid cells: several small cheap clocks running at different speeds combine to represent huge ranges cheaply, because the range multiplies while the cost only adds. That exact idea already exists as a published vector-symbolic-math recipe we could adapt, not something we would invent from scratch. Next step is one cheap, reused test to see if it transfers to our specific knowledge-graph task.

summary: Grounding-foundation build plan: reconciled 5 prior grounding notes (Harnad/Barsalou theory, MGS/NSM/CSKG data-source spec, percolation reachability audit, verifier-not-geometry architecture) with 3 new lit-scan fills (Barsalou PSS mechanism specifics, measured-numeric physical-property source scan, VSA fractional-power-encoding wiring mechanics incl. newly-surfaced bundling-degradation risk arXiv:2412.00488). Recommends periodic-table cross-channel grounding cell as FIRST buildable step (small, real measured atomic data, FPE-wired, lawful oracle, A-vs-A+B ablation) ahead of the broader MGS/NSM Shell-0 ingest.
plain_language: We researched how to give the substrate real grounded knowledge (measured facts, not just word-relationships) and found that most of the theory and data-source homework was already done this week. This drill filled the three remaining gaps: the exact brain-science mechanism for grounded-vs-floating concepts, what real measured-data sources exist for everyday physical properties (mass, density, nutrition) without borrowing an LLM, and the specific math for encoding a number like density into the substrate's native vector format. Recommendation: build a small periodic-table test first (real atomic properties, a lawful check against reality) before scaling up to everyday concepts, because it is the cheapest way to prove the whole mechanism works.

summary: drillB_bio_grounding: non-neural biology lens (chemotaxis/two-component signaling, morphogen positional-information + immune self-non-self, evolutionary/cybernetic teleosemantics) converges on ONE minimal grounding loop across all 4 literatures -- physically-coupled sensor + comparator (fast-vs-slow-reference | value-vs-threshold | candidate-vs-independent-recheck) + irreversible asymmetric consequence. Kinetic proofreading (Hopfield 1974/Ninio 1975) is the most load-bearing new transfer: a checkpoint two-stage-commit write-rule (query exogenous attribute twice independently, discard on disagreement rather than average) for the already-designed periodic-table/numeric-core grounding cells, currently missing any discard mechanism. Secondary: chemotaxis fast-vs-slow-reference (methylation-adaptation) suggests surprise-weighted active-query-selection as an untried alternative to uniform-random sampling in the already-landed exog-predictive-anchor decorrelation cell (3rd independent mechanism now plateaued at corr~0.38-0.39). Ashby Law of Requisite Variety flagged as a computable sizing-bound candidate for exogenous-referent channel richness (theory-only, not yet operationalized).
plain_language: We looked at how living things without any brain -- bacteria, developing embryos, the immune system, evolution itself -- build reliable internal information about the real world, to see if biology has a cheaper trick for grounding than what we already found in the brain-and-cognition literature. All four biological cases turned out to use the exact same three-part trick: a sensor thats directly physically triggered by the real thing (not a symbol standing in for it), a simple compare-to-a-reference step, and a real, non-reversible cost for being wrong (a wasted resource, a discarded molecule, or death, not just a small penalty). The most useful new idea: cells achieve very high accuracy from a weak, noisy signal by checking it twice independently and throwing away disagreements rather than averaging them -- a cheap, concrete upgrade we can add to our already-designed real-data grounding test before it even ships.

summary: drillA wildcard cross-domain (coding-theory/linguistics-econ/number-theory/graph-spectral): 4-field convergence confirms residue/CRT label-encoding is Shannon/Kolmogorov-doomed (closure, not implementation flaw) -- exploitable structure never lives in the arbitrary label, only in (a) the measurement/codebook operator (RIP, expander spectral gap, Welch-bound, sparse-superposition+AMP), (b) external usage-frequency (Zipf/Huffman/water-filling), or (c) the relation/co-occurrence graph (Laplacian eigenmaps, NetMF-equivalent spectral factorization). Top unconsidered avenue: two-layer hybrid codec (frequency-driven variable budget alloc over a usage-graph spectral basis, JL/expander random backstop for isolated entities), P_deflated=0.28-0.30. Cheap CPU decisive test proposed (Gini + Laplacian spectral-energy check on existing 190k-edge KG graph, no new experiment needed) with pre-registered HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL thresholds.
plain_language: We asked four totally unrelated fields (coding theory, linguistics/economics, number theory, graph math) the same question: since our entity labels are arbitrary and carry no compressible structure, where can cheap extra capacity come from? All four gave the same answer independently: never from the label itself (this is now a proven dead end, confirmed by hard theorems, not just our failed attempt) -- only from how often something is used, how it relates to other things, or clever properties of the shared code-space design. This gives us two concrete, cheap-to-test next ideas that do not require expensive brute-force high dimension, plus a same-day CPU-only test to check if our data even has the right shape for them before we build anything.

summary: drillB_neuro_grounding_mechanism: forward-model/prediction-error loop identified as the minimal brain mechanism turning a floating symbol into a grounded one (cerebellar grip-force forward models -- heaviness perception derived from predicted-vs-actual load mismatch, not raw sensing); already-designed periodic-table Phase-1 grounding cell structurally IS this mechanism, add residual-binding + precision-weighting + boundary-vector-cell drift-recalibration as 3 cheap amendments; abstract-concept reachability requirement independently corroborated by corpus-linguistics finding (abstract words co-occur mostly with other abstract words); CMT metaphor-priming evidence deflated by non-replication (Williams-Bargh warmth priming failed multi-lab replication). P_deflated=0.30-0.45 per component, 0.38 overall
plain_language: We asked neuroscience: what actually makes a word like heavy mean real heaviness instead of just pointing at other words? The brain answer is concrete: when you lift something, your cerebellum predicts how hard it will feel before you feel it, and what you consciously perceive as heaviness is the MISMATCH between that prediction and the real feedback, not a raw sensor reading. This is good news for our substrate because the first grounding test we already planned (a periodic table cell that predicts an unmeasured chemical property from known neighbors and checks it against the true value) already works this exact way -- we just found three cheap, brain-justified upgrades to make before running it: store the prediction error itself as part of the representation, weight different measurements by how reliable they are, and periodically double-check inferred values against real ones the way the brain resets its internal compass using landmarks. We also found independent evidence, from real language data, that abstract words (like justice or truth) tend to only connect to OTHER abstract words -- confirming a check we already planned to run is genuinely necessary, not optional.

summary: drillA_bio_capacity_structure: non-neural biology lens (DNA/genomic coding, protein domain-shuffling, immune V(D)J combinatorial repertoire, morphogenetic TF combinatorial codes) on cheap-capacity + exploitable-structure for arbitrary structureless entity labels, after grid-cell/RNS-CRT (neural lens) failed to transfer. Leading lever: V(D)J-style combinatorial segment-library construction + clonal-selection population-based retrieval (Perelson and Oster 1979 shape-space theory) -- impose combinatorial structure at CONSTRUCTION time via a small typed-segment library instead of mining structure out of an already-opaque atom, retrieve via existing resonator/SIC-peel decode reframed as population/threshold matching (not hard CRT decode), directly avoiding the hard-decision fragility that independently killed the thalamic-router RC2 CRT attempt. Secondary levers: cis-regulatory AND/OR combinatorial logic (Istrail and Davidson) for relation-level composition, protein domain-shuffling for typed-attribute entity construction. Protein-folding funnel and morphogen-gradient positional info explicitly ruled OUT for arbitrary-label transfer (both require continuous/metric structure that does not exist for arbitrary labels) -- reported honestly rather than force-fit. P_deflated=0.35 leading lever.
plain_language: We asked biology a harder version of last cycles capacity question: forget the brains spatial position-coding trick (needs a natural continuous range our arbitrary entity names do not have) -- how does biology build huge, cheap, structured spaces out of things that are ALREADY just arbitrary labels with nothing special about them? The clear answer: the immune system. It builds a nearly incomprehensible number of distinct antibody shapes from a small parts catalog (pick one gene fragment from each of three shelves, splice them together, add a little random variation at the seam), and none of those fragments need any inherent order to work -- unlike the brains trick, this works on plain arbitrary labels, which is exactly our situation. And when the body needs to recognize a threat, it does not do one fragile precise lookup -- it lets many close-enough candidates compete and refine, a forgiving strategy that avoids the exact brittle failure we already hit with an earlier strict-decode attempt. We designed one cheap, reusable test with a clear pass or fail line to check whether this transfers to our knowledge-graph memory.

summary: drillA_quantum_capacity_structure: quantum-information lens (amplitude encoding, tensor-network/MPS compression, quantum associative memory, stabilizer/holographic QEC) mapped to classical VSA realizability. 5/6 mechanisms confirm no-free-lunch for arbitrary structureless entity codes (triangulated w/ area-law entanglement failure mode + dequantization complexity lower bounds arXiv:2402.15686), extending Harlow-OAQEC closure with an independent Holevo channel-capacity no-go. Top classically-realizable lever: dense/modern associative memory with super-quadratic interaction energy function (Krotov-Hopfield 2016, Demircigil et al 2017) -- exponential capacity via readout nonlinearity, requires zero code-level structure, already flagged fruit-bearing in field advisor. Secondary lever: LDPC/expander-code redundancy wrapper (payload-agnostic, mature, fully classical). Independently converges same-day with wildcard-lens drill (coding-theory/linguistics/graph-spectral) on same negative result via different formal machinery.
plain_language: We asked whether ideas from quantum physics (like packing huge amounts of information into a few quantum bits) could give our memory system a cheap capacity boost. The honest answer across five of six mechanisms checked: no -- those tricks only work when the data being stored has hidden patterns to exploit, and our system deliberately uses arbitrary, patternless labels, so there is nothing for any of these tricks (quantum or classical) to grab onto. This closes off an entire family of compression ideas for good. But the search also found one genuinely useful, fully classical, no-quantum-hardware-needed idea that does not need any hidden pattern: a smarter memory-readout rule (borrowed from well-established brain-inspired associative-memory math) that can store exponentially more retrievable facts just by changing how memories are recalled, not how they are stored. That is now the top candidate for a cheap experiment.

summary: drillA_neuro_capacity_structure: RNS/CRT residue lever failed as expected (arbitrary labels have no numeric substructure); neuro lit-scan finds (1) dense/modern associative memory (higher-order readout sharpening) raises capacity for genuinely random content with no structure needed, (2) structure is always a SEPARATE learned relational scaffold (schema/TEM/SR) bound to arbitrary content, never derived from the item identity -- corrects the grid-cell analogy RNS/CRT mis-modeled, (3) JL-lemma optimality + Shannon floor confirm no compression trick exists for arbitrary content. Heavily deflated the schema-congruent lever given adjacency to already-HF grounding_learned_sr_heldout_reasoning_v1.
plain_language: We asked how the brain gets huge memory capacity cheaply, and where structure ever comes from for things that start out totally arbitrary. Found a cheap, structure-free capacity trick (sharper matching instead of compressing the item) plus a mechanistic explanation for why our earlier grid-cell-inspired idea used the wrong analogy -- the brain never derives structure from an item itself, it learns a separate map from how many things relate to each other and only then attaches it to a new item.

summary: neurosymbolic/logical-inference drill: 3-way lit-scan (brain rule-cells+TEM, differentiable rule induction Neural-LP/DRUM/AnyBURL/GraIL, prob-logic/path-ranking LTN/DeepProbLog/MLN/PSL/PRA). Field verdict: pick at most 2 of {inductive, glass-box, cheap-at-scale}. Substrate-specific: rule APPLICATION already CG (PP-196 forward-chain perfect recall, PP-252 defeasible NAF 100pct) but rule INDUCTION (learning confidence-weighted Horn rules from data, tested for held-out-entity generalization) is untested -- a genuinely new mechanism axis vs the 3 embedding-family negatives already on record. Top candidate: AnyBURL-style statistical rule mining + apply via proven forward-chaining with oracle (exact-dict) grounding, deliberately isolating rule-induction from the already-closed learned-router SNR wall. Cheap CPU-only test reuses grounding_learned_sr_heldout_reasoning_v1 exact split + shuffle control.
plain_language: We studied rule-based (neuro-symbolic) reasoning methods as an alternative to the embedding-based approaches that have failed 3 times to let the system infer facts about entities it has never seen before. The appeal: a learned RULE (like "if X works for Y and Y is part of Z, then X might work for Z") applies to ANY entity automatically, unlike a trained per-entity code. The literature says these rule methods genuinely avoid needing a trained code per entity, but no method gets speed, inductive generalization, and human-readability all at once -- you always give up one. The good news specific to us: we already proved the system can APPLY logical rules correctly (forward-chaining, default-with-exception reasoning) at perfect accuracy -- what is untested is whether we can LEARN good rules from our own data and have them generalize to new entities. We proposed a cheap, CPU-only test for exactly that, reusing an existing evaluation setup.

summary: training_recipe_improvement_theories: our additive KG map fit already implements self-adversarial CE + N3 + reciprocal (RotatE/N3 lit-precedent, already applied); 4-way lit-scan (hyperparam-tuning / negative-sampling / curriculum-ensembling-init / loss-label-smoothing) ranks structural spectral-Laplacian init warm-start as top lever (deflated +3-15% relative MRR, reuses same Laplacian-eigenmap primitive already scoped in same-day wildcard capacity drill), snapshot-ensembling ranked 2nd but blocked on checkpoint module being durability-only (1 snapshot retained, infra prereq not recipe change), full hyperparam re-tuning sweep ranked 3rd (well-precedented +8-10 MRR pts in transductive lit but priced as Phase-2 sweep not single swap). Ruled out: independent multi-seed ensembling (5-7x compute, dominated), GAN negative samplers (proven worse than self-adversarial already in use), InfoNCE/contrastive redesign (architecture-confounded, out of scope for architecture-fixed drill). Cheap decisive test + HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL pre-registered with scrambled-init must-fail control.
plain_language: We asked the literature: without touching how our knowledge-graph memory is structured, can we just train it better? We already use several of the field-best training tricks (a self-adversarial hard-example weighting scheme and a shrinkage regularizer). The single biggest remaining lever we found is surprisingly simple: how we RANDOMLY seed the starting point before training matters a lot -- swapping a plain random start for a start derived from the shape of the knowledge graph itself (which we can compute cheaply, reusing math we already scoped for a different idea two days ago) is reported in the literature to give a real, if modest once we discount for our specific harder setup, accuracy boost with basically zero extra cost. We also found a second good lever (averaging snapshots taken during training, like the brain consolidates memories during replay) but it needs a small plumbing fix first before we can use it. We wrote a precise, fail-able test with a built-in trap (a scrambled-control version) so we will know for certain whether the improvement is real structure or just a lucky numbers coincidence.

summary: drill_hopfield_multihop_fidelity_envelope: envelope-push on VET-confirmed negative (dense/modern-Hopfield super-quadratic readout lifts fidelity but not retrieval at single-hop, vanishes at scale). Brain-first + field + generic-math lit-scan finds two DIRECT formal theorems (Ross-Bagnell DAgger quadratic-in-horizon imitation-learning bound; Richardson-Urbanke LDPC density-evolution iteration-depth threshold) establishing that per-step error SHAPE (fidelity vs identification) stops being irrelevant once chain length nears 1/epsilon_pairwise -- but ZERO direct paper isolates dense-Hopfield specifically winning a real multi-hop benchmark over pairwise. CA3 single-vs-multi-step recall asymmetry (Rolls 2013, Pfeiffer and Foster 2013 Nature) is well-evidenced brain-side support. Proposed a zero-new-compute arithmetic gate (compute our own epsilon_pairwise from existing Stage-4 metrics, compare to 1/epsilon) to decide BEFORE spending any Stage-5 DENSE_HOPFIELD_CLEANUP compute whether 2-3 hop chains can even reach the crossover regime; amends the already-designed reader_decisive_multihop_win_engineering Stage-5 cell to measure retrieval/rank accuracy alongside raw fidelity (the original design only measured fidelity, not the retrieval conversion the single-hop negative was actually about).
plain_language: We already found that a fancier memory-readout trick makes reconstructed memories sharper but does not help pick the RIGHT memory out of a crowd -- so it did not help our single-step task. We asked: could that sharper trick still matter for CHAINS of 2-3 reasoning steps, where a fuzzy answer in step 1 poisons step 2? Two solid, independent branches of math (one from robot-imitation-learning theory, one from error-correcting-code theory) say yes, that CAN happen, but only once the chain gets long enough relative to how often a single step already gets it wrong -- and we have not yet checked whether our chains are long enough to hit that point. Good news: checking that is free, just arithmetic on data we already have, so we can settle whether to bother building the fancier version before spending any real compute on it.

summary: composition-operator+rule-structure drill: additive geometry CONFIRMED (brain TEM analog + closed-form OOKB algebra both independently favor it over bilinear RESCAL/TuckER); top new lever = AMIE-style rule mining used as a GATE on which 2-hop terms enter the existing ANCHOR_COMPOSE bundle, targeting measured d1/d2_3 degree-starved buckets; P_deflated=0.35
plain_language: We scoured the wider research world for a fundamentally different way to combine known facts about entities to predict facts about brand-new ones (beyond our current simple averaging approach). The brain evidence and a clean math proof both say our current additive approach is already the right family -- no need to switch. The one genuinely new, cheap idea found: mine simple logical rules (like a spell-checker for facts) from what we already know, and use those rules only as a filter deciding which extra 2-hop clues are trustworthy enough to add in for entities with very little known about them. This targets exactly the weakest, most under-served entities we already measured.

summary: drill_graph_structure_inductive_transfer_envelope: code-verified correction to the graph-spectral-entity-codes negative -- the compose (inductive, no-fold-in) arm was already tested (LAP_COMPOSE) and landed a scramble-verified REAL but sub-threshold lift (0.0099 vs RAND_COMPOSE 0.0040, needs 0.010; MIDDLE_BAND not HARD-FAIL), and only the transductively-WORST codebook family (LAP) was ever tried inductively -- PPMI (11x better transductively) and SR (5x better, the direct successor-representation brain analog) were never composed. Brain lit (Dayan 1993 SR Bellman recursion; Whittington et al 2020 TEM structure/content split) and graph-theory lit (Nystrom out-of-sample extension, Levin et al arXiv:1802.06307) independently converge on the SAME fix: weight the neighbor-aggregation by eigenvalue/transition-similarity, do not flatten it (current code uses a flat unweighted mean). Near-zero-cost cell proposed: reuse the shipped compose_score/compose_neighbor_codes functions verbatim, swap codebook to SR/PPMI, add Nystrom-style weighting; same seeds/thresholds/scramble-control discipline. P_deflated=0.30 (SR arm) to 0.42 (best-of-three, capped at 0.50 novel-synthesis ceiling).
plain_language: We asked whether the way the brain reuses a learned mental map for brand-new places (successor representation / grid cells) is the fix for a math result that only worked when we let the map peek at the answer. Turned out we had already tried a fair, no-peeking version and it was NOT a clean failure -- it genuinely used the right neighbors, just fell a little short of our pass bar. We found the exact reason: we only tested the weakest of three map-building flavors, and we averaged neighbor information in the dumbest possible way. Both brain science and separate graph math independently point to the same fix (weight neighbors by strength/importance, do not flatten), and we can test it almost for free using code that already works.

summary: reframe_true_bottleneck: zero-new-compute degree-stratified re-read of already-landed exp_anchor_compose_scaling_ladder_cskg_v3 metrics.json shows the aggregate ~0.13 MRR / 0.05 Hits@1 is a MIXTURE, not a monolithic representation wall -- mid/high-support-degree buckets (d2_3 through d8plus) already sit at 60-133% of their own supervised-code oracle ceiling across all 3 landed scaling rungs (zero headroom for more representation capacity), while the entire deficit concentrates in cold (0 support edges, scores BELOW random at 0.08x, same-day reciprocal-edge fix gives real but partial 370x lift, verdict flagged BROKEN_TEST_CONTROL_BEATS_POP) and d1 (1 support edge, only 15-18% of its own oracle -- genuine, real headroom). External lit-scan cross-validates: TransH category-split Hits@10 (87.6 vs 28.7 for 1-N vs N-1 queries) is a direct precedent for structural degree/ambiguity-driven score gaps; brain lit-scan finds regime-dependent bottlenecks (cortical WM-binding-limited vs hippocampal retrieval-limited vs task-underdetermination, converging with this substrate own prior PFC-hippocampal goal-disambiguation finding from 2026-07-09). This explains why 8+ same-day representation-capacity drills came up empty: they targeted the aggregate number, dominated by a population that was never representation-limited. Pre-registered next cheap tests: (1) decoder-budget sweep scoped ONLY to d1 bucket (existing aggregate budget sweep already ran and found STRICT_DEAD but on the wrong, saturated population), (2) data-coverage graph-path check on cold/d1 to distinguish fixable-representation vs ingest-more-knowledge (cross-mechanism analogy to the already-confirmed SR-routing ingest conclusion, explicitly NOT assumed transferred).
plain_language: We stopped asking whether our knowledge-reasoning system needs a bigger or smarter internal representation, and instead checked whether the low overall test score was even coming from one place. Using data we already had on disk (no new experiments), we split the score by how much the system already knew about each held-out item. Turns out: for items with a decent number of known facts, the system is already performing about as well as a version that got to cheat and see the answer during training -- there is nothing left to gain there. The entire shortfall is concentrated in items with almost no known facts. That reframes the whole days worth of make-the-codes-better research as having targeted a population that was never actually broken -- which is exactly why it kept coming up empty. Next cheap checks will tell us whether the true fix for the remaining broken bucket is a smarter algorithm or simply feeding the system more real facts.
