summary: schema_fit_derivability_signal_upgrade: current ingest-gate schema_fit proxy (0.5*(reach_pct[h]+reach_pct[t]), a per-node aggregate percentile) is structurally NOT pair-specific -- both brain lit (CA3 attractor convergence, Gentner structure-mapping systematicity, Kemp-Tenenbaum Bayesian structural-form inference) and network-science lit (Katz/Resource-Allocation/personalized-PageRank beat plain reachability+degree baselines, Lu and Zhou 2011 survey) converge on pair-specific MULTI-PATH aggregation as the fix. Concrete design: Tier A = cheap pairwise Resource-Allocation index (near-zero build, reuses existing adjacency); Tier B = pairwise SR/personalized-PageRank resolvent score M[t,h] reusing the ALREADY-LANDED, self-test-passed SRColumnSolver class built for a different task (autonomous path-routing) -- zero new machinery, one new call site. Separate free finding: the reported 0.761/0.836 headline is partly a small-sample artifact of unweighted 3-seed averaging (one seed has only 8 test-eligible facts, giving a degenerate 1.0 AUC); the most-trustworthy single estimate (largest seed, N=83) is 0.642-0.745, materially below the headline -- recommend a zero-cost pooled/n-weighted recompute BEFORE any new signal build.
sub_agents: lit-scan:sonnet x2 (brain schema-congruency mechanism, network-science pairwise link-prediction indices)
plain_language: The piece of our foundation-builder that decides whether a new fact fits our existing knowledge (schema-fit) currently just checks how generally well-connected each of the two things is on its own -- it never actually checks how the two specific things relate to each other. Both real-brain research (how the hippocampus completes patterns, how analogy-making brains compare relational structure) and internet-search/network-science research point to the same fix: measure the SPECIFIC connection between the two things, counting all the ways they link up, not just how well-connected each one is in general. We found the exact machinery to do this already built and tested elsewhere in the project for a different job -- reusing it here needs no new construction, just pointing it at a new question. We also found the current headline number is partly inflated by a very small sample in one of three test batches, so a free re-check of the existing numbers should happen before any new build.

summary: consolidation_gate_signal_mechanism_and_integration: landed ingest_gate_combination_rule_race_v1 FULL result (schemafit_alone AUC=0.836 vs brain-multiplicative=0.530 vs flat=0.542) is NOT a refutation of the 3-signal theory -- it is a diagnosed implementation error. Brain lit (distributional dopamine RPE, OFC cognitive-map state, CA3-pattern-completion-vs-CA1-mismatch, Bayesian-surprise=KL(posterior||prior)) converges: surprise must be measured against a LOCAL/structured predictor, not the additive_maps global corpus-wide rank -- our raw_PE is schema-blind by construction, so multiplying it into schema_fit added noise not signal. Non-redundancy re-derived per signal (surprise=deviation-magnitude vs a rich predictor; schema-fit=pairwise/relational structural-routing, CA3 attractor-basin + Gentner/Kemp-Tenenbaum, NOT node-generic; recurrence=temporal-reliability via synaptic-tagging-and-capture, most dangerous failure mode is one-off-noise that is both surprising AND schema-congruent). Integration verdict: branch/route (CLS anatomical separation + Tse near-step transition), NOT a sum/gate -- confirmed literature gap on the parametric discriminating experiment. Proposed cheap decisive test: add a local_surprise arm (rank restricted to the k=2-hop reachable set schema_fit already scans) to the SAME race arena, zero new acquisition.
plain_language: The recent experiment that tested being exactly like the brain (a multiplication of surprise and fit-to-existing-knowledge) came back negative -- multiplying in our surprise signal made things worse, not better. New research explains why: our surprise signal checks a fact against the WHOLE knowledge base at once, but real brains check surprise against a narrow, locally-relevant prediction (like recognizing something is wrong about a specific nearby detail, not a vague sense that something in the world is off). That mismatch, not the three-signal idea itself, is the likely bug. We also nailed down why the brain keeps all three signals separate (surprise=how wrong, fit=where does it belong, repetition=is it real not noise) and found the strongest evidence points to the three signals working as a branching decision path, not a single blended score. A cheap, no-new-data test is proposed to confirm the fix.

summary: multisource_memory_assimilation_arena: characterized why brain surprise (temporal/predictive, CA1 comparator + MMN local/global) / schema-fit (structural mPFC/SLIMM associative-overlap) / recurrence (source-independence-weighted evidence accumulation, truth-discovery copying-detection) are 3 independent axes in real multi-source environments but collapse to 1 axis on a single static KG (one generative process = all 3 signals collinear); delivered concrete circularity-free multi-source claim-stream arena spec (sources w/ hidden reliability+dependence graph, pre-built schema disjoint from claim stream, temporal arrival, ground truth independent of all 3 signals, stratified factorial eval, copying stress-test) with HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL thresholds and a cheap pre-substrate simulation test. P_deflated=0.45.
plain_language: We studied how the brain keeps its three memory-gatekeeping signals (is this surprising, does it fit what I already know, has it been independently confirmed) genuinely separate in the real world, and found our current test setup accidentally makes two of those signals near-copies of each other because it only has one static knowledge graph to compute them from. We designed a fix: a test arena with multiple information sources of different trustworthiness, some independent and some copies of each other, arriving over time, so the three signals can actually be told apart and tested honestly.

summary: surprise_decomposition_unexpectedness_vs_importance: deep drill on whether the ingest-gate consolidation surprise signal is one axis or two. Finding: strongly separable (P=0.65 deflated) -- Bayesian surprise KL(P(M|D)||P(M)) [Itti-Baldi] is a belief-change quantity, distinct from a salience/value/stakes quantity computed by dedicated dopamine sub-populations (Matsumoto-Hikosaka unsigned-salience neurons), amygdala-noradrenergic arousal tagging (McGaugh), and geometric threat/looming detectors (LGMD, superior colliculus) that carry zero probability content. Combination law (additive vs multiplicative) is NOT settled in the literature -- same shape of confirmed-gap as the parallel omnibus drills schema-fit x surprise combination gap, now found a second independent time one level up. Value-of-information/expected-free-energy/learning-progress formalism (Schmidhuber compression-progress) gives the correct fix for the raw-surprise white-noise pathology and surfaces a candidate 4th ingest-gate signal (downstream-reach/hub-centrality, a no-external-stakes-required value-of-information proxy) distinct from the omnibus schema_fit signal -- flagged as an addendum with its own cheap decisive test, not a redesign.
plain_language: We asked whether surprise (the thing that flags a memory as worth keeping) is really one thing or secretly two things: how unexpected something is, versus how much it actually matters. Real brain science says it is genuinely two things, computed by separate machinery -- there are literally different brain cells that fire for how important something is (good or bad, does not matter which) versus cells that fire for whether it was better or worse than expected, and a rock falling toward your head is detected by a totally different geometric threat-detector, not by a probability calculation. But how those two signals should be combined is not settled in any published study -- same open question we hit yesterday from a different angle -- so that combination remains ours to test, not borrow. We also found the correct mathematical fix for why pure randomness should not count as memorable (an idea called learning-progress), and it points to a new, promising 4th signal our memory-gate does not have yet: how much a new fact would matter to everything else it connects to, which needs no stakes or reward system at all to compute.

summary: threshold_calibration_gate_boundary: lit-scan across SDT/DDM/BCM/consolidation/normative-decision-theory on how biology calibrates a fast-vs-slow route threshold. Verdict: ADAPTIVE via 3 mechanistically distinct knobs (SDT/DDM leaky-recency criterion update per Norton et al 2017; STN-hyperdirect conflict-triggered threshold raise per Frank et al; schema-gated consolidation-rate per Tse et al 2007/2011), NOT one unified mechanism. BCM sliding-threshold (Abraham 2001) is real homeostasis but flagged as likely wrong donor mechanism for route-selection (synapse-level, not routing-level) -- gap. Normative Bayes-cost derivation (Bogacz 2006) of the consolidation-route transition rate specifically was never found in the literature -- actionable novel-synthesis gap, capped P=0.50.
plain_language: Researched how brains decide when to switch from a fast decision route to a slow, careful one, and whether that switch-point is fixed or adjusts itself. Finding: it adjusts, but via three different biological knobs (recent-trial-history learning, conflict-triggered caution, and schema-familiarity) that nobody in the literature has combined into one rule -- which is exactly the same kind of gap our ingest-gate design left open, and now has concrete brain-inspired candidates to fill it with.

summary: multisource-arena-real-corpora: mapped real external data landscape for the synthetic claim-stream arena de-risk path; top pick = Weather dataset (Dong/Berti-Equille/Hu/Srivastava VLDB 2010) which uniquely ships a labeled gold+silver copying/dependence graph alongside real conflicting claims + ground truth; full truth-discovery benchmark hub (Book/Stock/Flight/Restaurant/Population, all live at lunadong.com) plus Snorkel/WRENCH source-correlation modeling as a candidate method; reliability-tier contrast now empirically confirmed across instrument-measured (CODATA/Gaia) vs expert-curated (MeSH/ICD) vs LLM-generated (Kish n_eff ~2.2/9 effective independent judges, TruthfulQA shared-misconception structure) tiers.
plain_language: We looked for real-world datasets that could later replace our synthetic test-arena with genuine multi-source data (some sources reliable, some copying each other, some conflicting). Good news: an academic dataset from 2010 (weather forecasts from 18 real websites) already comes with a hand-labeled answer key for exactly which sources copy which others -- a free, ready-to-use pilot. We also confirmed with hard numbers that AI-generated content really does behave like the copying problem we were worried about (multiple AI models asked the same question behave like only 2 truly independent opinions out of 9, not 9).

summary: combination_rule_menu_and_route_calibration: Lisman-Grace confluence node has NO stated combination arithmetic (confirmed 4x today); wherever neuromodulation lit commits to an equation it is multiplicative gain (Cohen/Servan-Schreiber, Aston-Jones/Cohen, Yu-Dayan, Doya), STC tag-capture is binary AND at synapse scale but graded in population aggregate; route boundary is adaptive via 3 distinct mechanisms (SDT/DDM leaky-EWMA criterion, STN conflict-raise, Neyman-Pearson tau*=Cfp/(Cfp+Cfn) normative form) never connected to consolidation timing in the literature; delivered 5-form swappable combination-rule menu (branch/route, Bayesian precision-fusion, additive-logistic, multiplicative-gate, 2-accumulator race) with functional forms, weight-setting method, and discriminating predictions, ready to race in the memory-assimilation arena gate module once built.
plain_language: We researched how the brain actually combines its three memory-filing signals (surprise, does-it-fit-a-known-pattern, has-it-been-confirmed-before) into a keep-or-discard decision, and how it sets the boundary between fast filing and slow careful filing. No biology paper spells out the exact math for this, so we built a menu of 5 concrete candidate formulas (a branching decision tree, a Bayesian-style weighted blend, a simple learned weighted sum, a multiply-together gate, and a race between two competing evidence-accumulators) each with a clear test that tells them apart, ready to race once the multi-source test environment is built.

summary: CLS-route/STC-hold negative re-diagnosed as WRONG-CURRENCY not same-limitation: MMOR1995 CLS + Frey-Morris STC literature both ground the mechanisms benefit as continual-learning interference-avoidance/capacity-economy/retention-at-later-test, never single-trial accuracy-at-encoding. Single-shot i.i.d. accuracy race structurally cannot exercise the mechanism. Corrected test regime = sequential multi-item ingestion with confirmed-forgetting positive control, measuring early-item retention loss vs N/overlap (scaling signature required for HARD-PASS). P_deflated=0.45.
plain_language: We asked: did the brain-based fast/slow memory-route mechanism fail for a real reason, or did we test it wrong? Answer: we tested it wrong. In real brains, this fast/slow split and the memory-tagging hold-window exist to stop new learning from overwriting old learning when you learn many things over time (like a filing system that prevents your new notes from erasing your old ones) -- they were never meant to make one single decision more accurate. Our test only checked one single decision, so of course it tied. The right next test is to teach the system many overlapping things in sequence and check whether old knowledge survives better with the route than without it.

summary: full4signal_realdata_capability_test: scoped the real-data corpus for the ingest gates 4-signal (surprise/schema-fit/recurrence/importance) capability test. Top pick = Wikidata edit-history/vandalism-detection corpus (WDVC/WDVD, 82.68M revisions, 198147 labeled vandalism) + constraint-violation study -- all 4 signals native (literal reference-count field for recurrence, literal constraint-violation flags for an independent schema-fit ground truth, trainable link-prediction rank for surprise, literal degree/sitelinks for importance) plus a real temporal arrival stream, closing a gap the prior corroboration-only survey left open. Companion corpus = Hetionet/Rephetio/repoDB, which supplies the strongest published content-wall control found: a naive degree/frequency baseline hits AUROC 97.9% in-sample then COLLAPSES to 54.1% out-of-sample while the full structural model holds 85.5% -- and Wikidata separately supplies an already-published, already-quantified degree-bias number (310.7x naive bias ratio, debiased only to 11.9x by the fields own fix). Pre-registered HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL requires beating the ALREADY-DEBIASED SOTA baseline (not just naive degree), AUPRC not just AUROC, and a genuine temporal/external holdout, not a random split.
plain_language: We scoped which real-world dataset could give the memory-filing gate (the 4-signal system that decides whether a new fact is worth keeping) an honest real-world test, not just another synthetic practice run. Best answer: Wikipedia's sister project Wikidata already has everything we need in one place -- a public record of every edit including which ones were vandalism, a citation-count field on every fact, and known structure -- so it doubles as a real vandalism-detection test. Crucially, other researchers already measured the exact trap we keep worrying about: a lazy shortcut (just flag edits from anonymous users) looks 310 times more suspicious than it should, and even the best published fix only gets that down to 12 times, not to zero. So our gate has to beat that already-fixed version, not the lazy shortcut, to count as a real win. We also found a second dataset (a drug-database network) with the cleanest evidence yet that a simple shortcut can look like it works great on the data you trained on and then collapse to useless on new data -- exactly the trap our test has to guard against.

summary: biology-beyond-neocortex ingest-gate drill: immune system contributes a candidate NEW danger/context gate axis (orthogonal to schema-fit/surprise/recurrence); swarm/quorum biology (honeybee cross-inhibition quorum-on-independent-scouts) independently converges on the same independent-source-corroboration fix the truth-discovery literature already derived; population genetics (Hsp90 evolutionary capacitance) suggests a genuine third buffered/dormant tier distinct from provisional and foundationalized; brain-efficiency-frontier premise only partially supported (~8x gap from theoretical optimum in best direct measurement; replay/CLS interference-avoidance is substrate-general per McCloskey and Cohen 1989, so an exact-write substrate cannot assume it skips consolidation for that reason, though it can skip the protein-synthesis-slowness tax).
plain_language: We asked whether biology beyond just the brain has better ideas for our knowledge-admission gate. Turns out: the immune system offers a genuinely new signal (does this arrive with real-world consequences, not just does it fit or repeat), swarm behavior like bee colonies independently confirms our fix for telling real corroboration from copied information, and evolution suggests a useful third holding-tier for information. Separately, we checked whether the brain is really near-maximum-efficient (a premise we had been assuming) and found it is only partly true — some brain workarounds are avoidable on our exact digital system, but the core anti-interference mechanism (replay/consolidation) is not avoidable just because we can write exactly; it is a general problem any distributed system faces.

summary: consolidation currency (accuracy vs metabolic-cost/capacity): CLS rationale is pure accuracy/interference-avoidance with zero capacity framing (verified, McClelland 1995/2013, McCloskey&Cohen 1989) -- its home-field advantage requires >=2 competing/overlapping items, absent from the single-stream hold-vs-flat-accumulate test, so the null there is a regime-scope finding not a general refutation. STC (Frey&Morris 1997/Redondo&Morris 2011) founding rationale is specificity/accuracy with capacity-competition (Fonseca 2004) secondary. Active-forgetting/SHY literature explicitly bundles generalization-accuracy and capacity, not separable. Trajectory-coding claim upgraded to rigorous proof-shaped support (White/Lee/Sompolinsky 2004 linear memory-capacity bound; Dambre 2012 memory-nonlinearity tradeoff): flat linear accumulation is structurally blind to order/sequence info a nonlinear hold-trajectory can carry, but only in a task that needs order discrimination -- the tested task did not. Proposed cheap decisive test: rerun on (1) two competing sequential streams (interference axis, tests CLS) and (2) a capped consolidation-write budget (capacity axis, tests STC/SHY).
plain_language: We asked: does the brain hold onto memories carefully (instead of just adding up evidence) to be MORE ACCURATE, or to SAVE ENERGY/SPACE? Answer: it is neither cleanly -- one brain mechanism (hippocampus-to-cortex transfer) is purely about accuracy (stopping new memories from overwriting old ones), and that specific benefit only shows up when there are multiple competing memories at once, which our test did not have -- so our finding that the fancy machinery adds nothing is correct but narrow, not a general verdict. The other two brain mechanisms (protein-budget gating, sleep-based downscaling) are about accuracy and energy-savings tangled together in the actual science, not two separate things we can weigh apart. We also found strong evidence that a different technique -- letting memory strength rise-and-fall over time rather than just adding up -- can carry information about the ORDER events happened in, which flat addition genuinely cannot; our test never asked an order question, so that advantage was never on the table either.

summary: developmental_curriculum_permissive_to_selective_gate_schedule: brain builds foundation on a SCHEDULE not a uniform gate -- core-knowledge/Piaget confirm concrete-before-abstract macro-order (Piaget stages themselves superseded); Elman/Newport starting-small is MORE contested than assumed (Rohde-Plaut 1999/2003 direct failed replication, Brooks 2019 systematic review sides less-is-less); Quinian bootstrapping (Carey) shows exact-integer concept acquisition structurally REQUIRES admitting a placeholder structure before a strict schema-fit gate could ever pass -- strict-from-start gating would block bootstrap formation; critical-period biology (Hensch GABA/PV open, PNN/Otx2/Lynx1 close, all reversible via chABC/fluoxetine) confirms permissive-early/selective-late is real AND live-verified citations (Chang and Merzenich 2003, Toyoizumi et al 2013 SNR theory) show closure is SIGNAL-DETECTION-gated not noise-accumulation-gated -- a system fed pure noise stays plastic rather than prematurely locking in. Builder implication: replace fixed 3-signal gate thresholds (schema-fit/surprise/recurrence) with an SNR-gated stringency schedule keyed to the substrates own measured signal-extraction success rate, reversible and region-scoped per Petanjek-2011-style hierarchical staggering. Cheap test designed reusing existing additive_map.score_all + reachability_audit.py, zero new scoring mechanism.
plain_language: We asked whether the brain builds its knowledge foundation in a fixed uniform way, or on a developmental schedule (permissive when young, selective/protective once mature). Literature confirms the schedule is real, and -- crucially -- shows the brain tightens its filter specifically once it has found real signal to protect, not just because time has passed or noise has piled up; a brain fed only noise stays permissive rather than prematurely locking in garbage. This directly suggests our foundation-builder should start permissive (accept broadly, nothing to protect yet) and tighten its gate only as it detects its own successful pattern-extraction rising, rather than using one fixed strictness setting from day one.

summary: ingest-gate Wikidata-vandalism negative: task-mismatch confirmed (editor-behavior vs claim-validity), not a bound; frequency-dominance on familiar claims is brain-consistent (illusory-truth effect, Fazio knowledge-neglect); gate advantage theoretically confined to NOVEL claims where frequency=0 by construction; fair test exists (VitaminC / Symmetric-FEVER frequency-matched splits) but untested; HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL thresholds registered.
plain_language: We asked whether the gate genuinely fails at fact-checking, or whether we tested it on the wrong job (spotting bad editors, not spotting false facts). Answer: wrong job -- and human psychology backs this up: people also rely on familiarity/repetition to judge truth (this is well-documented, not a flaw), and only fall back on structural reasoning for claims they have never seen before. Real datasets exist to test the gate on that narrower, fairer case; we have not run that test yet.

summary: curriculum/prerequisite real-dataset survey: no single public dataset ships BOTH validated prerequisite order AND attached facts; TQA (real textbook content, implicit linear order, zero access friction) is cheapest pilot for the ingestion-order test; Junyi Academy (837-exercise, 1131-pair expert-labeled prerequisite DAG, no content) is best-confirmed real order structure; MOOCCube claims both but unverified live (TLS host failure). P_deflated=0.35 that real data materially strengthens the order test over synthetic.
plain_language: Surveyed real-world datasets of school-style facts organized in a foundational-to-advanced learning order, to test whether feeding our system knowledge in the right order (like a curriculum) beats feeding it in random order. Found: no single dataset gives both a validated order AND real content for free — the closest zero-friction option is a public middle-school science textbook QA dataset (TQA), with a second-stage option (Junyi Academy) giving a more rigorously validated concept-dependency map but no attached facts.

summary: brain capacity-efficient language mechanisms -> VSA/HDC capacity-fix menu: sparse combinatorial coding (Willshaw 0.69 bits/synapse, superposition-catastrophe cliff), hierarchical chunk-and-pass (PFC-BG adaptive chunking, HRR recursive cleanup), structure/content factorization (grid-cell remapping/TEM, resonator networks F=3-4 factor sweet spot + quadratic-N capacity), phase/positional multiplexing (theta phase precession, FHRR/SSP fractional binding). 4-mode capacity-fix menu keyed to probe failure type (vocab/recursion-depth/sentence-length/compositional-generalization), each with HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL thresholds. Key caveat: disentangled/factorized reps alone are empirically insufficient for compositional generalization (arXiv 2501.18797) -- pair with training-curriculum signal (MLC). ~45 live-verified citations across 4 parallel Sonnet lit-scans.
plain_language: We looked at HOW the brain fits huge language capability into a finite number of neurons, so we have brain-tested fixes ready when our reading-comprehension probe hits a capacity wall. The brain uses four tricks together: sparse coding (combinatorially cheap addressing), chunking things into hierarchical units, splitting structure from content (like a map grid vs. the specific places on it), and phase-timed positional codes. Each trick has a known VSA/HDC analog and a known breaking point, so depending on WHERE our probe walls out we now have a specific, pre-tested fix to try first.

summary: early_reader_language_acquisition_curriculum: scoped graded early-reader vocab+grammar corpora (Dolch/Fry/CEFR-J/Simple-Wikipedia/CHILDES/Kuperman-AoA/Wordbank-CDI) + built a from-zero curriculum ladder (Rung0 statistics-only Saffran-segmentation on Bernstein-Ratner -> Rung1 Dolch PreK+K 92-word SVO-present -> Rung2 morphology -> Rung3 agreement/tense gated by Processability-Theory implicational hierarchy -> Rung4 clause-embedding). Tolerance Principle (e<=N/ln(N)) proposed as quantitative rung-mastery gate formula. Oxford Reading Tree/Reading A-Z/Lexile confirmed proprietary (do not budget). Smallest starting corpus = 92 Dolch PreK+K words + SVO templates.
plain_language: We scoped out real, free, kid-reading-level datasets (sight-word lists, CHILDES child-speech recordings, Simple Wikipedia, vocabulary-by-age lists) and built a concrete step-by-step lesson plan for teaching our system English from absolute zero, the way a child actually learns: first just recognizing word boundaries in speech, then ~92 of the simplest sight words in simple sentences, then grammar added piece by piece in the order kids and language learners actually acquire it. We identified the cheapest possible starting point (92 public-domain sight words) and flagged which popular reading programs (Oxford Reading Tree, Reading A-Z, Lexile) are locked behind paywalls and should not be relied on.

summary: word grounding + lexicon structure-content unification: 3-lane lit-scan (symbol grounding/hub-spoke, child word-learning, TPR/HRR/SPA binding) converges on role-filler binding with foundation-concept fillers (not random phasors) as the correct glass-box architecture to unify the proven syntactic scaffold with the foundation content; word-form is a lexical SPOKE feeding the same hub as other grounded attributes (not a privileged channel); relational-only grounding is literature-OPEN not refuted (Cangelosi/Riga grounding-transfer + Taddeo/Floridi structural grounding legitimize a small grounded-kernel-plus-relations path for a bodyless substrate); the lexicon-learning UPDATE RULE itself is the one genuine gap in all 3 literatures (no published pointer-to-meaning attachment mechanism) -- built glass-box from 4 converging child-language mechanisms (cross-situational co-occurrence, mutual exclusivity, syntactic bootstrapping, fast-mapping) as an inspectable lookup table. Composite P_deflated=0.36.
plain_language: Researched how the brain connects words to meaning (symbol grounding, the ATL semantic hub, child word-learning) and how AI architectures bind structure to content (tensor-product/holographic representations). Found that our syntax-only language module and our separate knowledge-foundation work can be unified with one mechanism: treat each word as a pointer into a foundation concept, then the same binding operation that already proved it can parse sentences will also retrieve real facts. Proposed the smallest possible test of this (about 10 words) with a companion hand-off file for exp_dev to pick up.

summary: grounding-cell VSA unbind geometry risk: no published VSA/HRR capacity theorem covers correlated/learned codebooks (all i.i.d.-only); generic matched-filter/correlated-Hopfield theory + this substrate own prior anisotropy-drill negative result (whitening HARD_FAIL on sibling dense-KV mechanism) predict real concept-filler geometry degrades FHRR unbind; 3-diagnostic pre-flight (coherence-excess-over-Welch, effective-rank/PR, degree-cosine-corr) + oracle-lexicon isolation test proposed to attribute HARD-FAIL to geometry vs lexicon-learning-rule; fix-menu ranked with sparse-expansion pattern-separator (reuse of already chain-grade-validated substrate primitive) as highest-expected-value, whitening flagged low-value per substrate prior.
plain_language: We checked whether the shape of the knowledge-foundation own concept vectors (which are not perfectly spread-out/random, unlike the ideal test vectors used so far) will break the language-modules bind/unbind mechanism when real vectors are swapped in. The math literature has no direct answer (its an open gap), but closely related theory plus a directly analogous experiment already run on this substrate (which failed when we tried the obvious fix, whitening) both suggest this is a real risk, not just a theoretical worry. We wrote a cheap 3-part diagnostic and a decisive test so the next experiment can tell instantly whether a failure is caused by this geometry problem or by something else, plus a ranked list of fixes to try, cheapest first.

summary: curriculum-order CoDEx null brain-check: KST surmise-relation degeneracy + Piaget figurative-vs-operative + interleaving-needs-structure literature converge (stitched synthesis, P=0.50 capped) on order-sensitivity scaling with dependency density. On-disk diagnostic (density-vs-tree, hierarchical-edge-fraction) computed directly from CoDEx-S/M train triples confirms CoDEx is a flat dense web (11-16x tree density, 0.18-0.26% hierarchical edges) -- corpus-mismatch, not refutation. AL-CPL (live-verified, 4 domains, author-validated strict partial order, 2.5-6x tree density, 100% prerequisite-typed edges) identified as the ship-ready re-test corpus; harness port is a data-source swap only, no new architecture.
plain_language: We checked whether the missing curriculum-order effect on real Wikipedia-style facts was a real failure or just the wrong test material. Turns out real cognitive-science theory (how kids actually learn skill hierarchies vs random facts) predicts order should only matter when facts build on each other -- and we measured directly that our real-data test used a flat, unstructured fact set with almost no dependency structure. We found a better real dataset (university course prerequisite graphs) that actually has the right structure, ready to re-test.

summary: brain effective-N + sparse-vs-dense-N cost-circumvention: sparsity buys real combinatorial capacity (Willshaw/Tsodyks-Feigelman/Amari, textbook) via sparse KEYS/PATTERNS not sparse VALUES (this substrate already HARD-FAILED naive value-sparsification, ratio 0.40-0.94); residual costs are real and non-vanishing (O(M*N) brute-force search relocated not removed, log(N) compressed-sensing floor, decode complexity O(D_i*sqrt(D_o)) for structured block-sparse). No neuroscience validation found for Kanerva N~10^4 as a measured population dimensionality -- it is anatomy-inspired, not measured; brain converges on a region-specific SPARSITY REGIME not a fixed operating N. Cheap decisive test proposed: retarget the already-HARD-PASS blocklocal-K sparse resonator (K4=1.00,K8=1.00 factor recall) as a bundling/associative-capacity code, sweep N prime=1024/4096/16384 at near-optimal fixed k, compare vs dense N=1024 baseline.
plain_language: Researched whether a sparse high-dimensional code can give big-N memory capacity without big-N cost, as the USER suspected. Answer: partially yes, but not free -- the brain gets its capacity boost from sparse PATTERNS (which units fire), not from sparse VALUES, and this project already tested the wrong version and it failed. The right version (already built and proven on this substrate) has never been tested at the capacity question this asks; a cheap test to check that is proposed.

summary: working_memory_integration_upper_limit: brain WM = Cowan embedded-processes (~4-chunk focus nested in activated LTM) + Baddeley episodic buffer + chunking/expertise-templates (Gobet) + Ericsson-Kintsch long-term-WM + center-embedding depth-2-3 wall (Christiansen-Chater chunk-and-pass, not a true stack) + Kintsch situation-model/gist discourse comprehension + CLS regional dimensionality specialization (sparse DG vs dense cortex vs tiny PFC buffer, translated via EC). KEY CORRECTION: substrate N/16-32 bundle crosstalk cliff (measured on disk) is NOT the ~4-chunk-focus analog -- it is the raw passive-store analog; the resonator F=3-4 factorization sweet spot (prior note) is the correct Cowan-4-chunk-focus analog. Design: hierarchical chunk nesting (depth target 2-3, brain-matched) + decoupled dimensionality per subsystem (chunk-N vs sentence-N via a fixed EC-style projection, cost ~O(Na x Nb) per swap, substrate precedent in Spoke3 DG-expansion design) + exact external paging (Frontier-2, beats brain because brains own cortical disk is lossy). Upper limit is per-subsystem not one number: buffer-crosstalk (N/16-32), chunk-decode fidelity (F=3-4), nesting depth (~2-3), paging bandwidth (throughput not capacity), store capacity (unbounded if exact-record). Recommended first cell: hierarchical_chunk_crossN_projection extending exp_nativelang_svo_vsa_probe_v1 with a fixed cross-dimensionality projection at the clause/sentence interface. Reconciled with prior CLS-route wrong-currency finding (route != dimensionality-specialization, independently falsifiable). 32 external citations + 3 internal cross-thread notes verified across 5 parallel Sonnet lit-scans.
plain_language: We studied how the human brain manages to hold a whole conversation in mind despite only being able to actively juggle about 4 things at once, and used that to design working memory for our substrate. The brain uses a small active focus (about 4 items) nested inside a much bigger but passive pool, packs information into compressed chunks (like an expert chess player sees whole patterns instead of individual pieces), and uses different memory formats in different brain regions (sparse fast hippocampus, dense slow cortex, tiny working-memory buffer) connected by dedicated translator circuits. We found our own system already has two matching numbers measured on disk, but they answer different questions and we corrected a mapping mistake before it became load-bearing. We designed a way to nest smaller chunks (like a clause) inside bigger ones (like a sentence) using different-sized number-spaces for each, mirroring how the brain translates between its own regions, plus a way to page exact, lossless memories in and out of the small working buffer (something the brain cannot do because its own memory storage is inherently lossy). We recommend one concrete, cheap next experiment that tests both ideas at once using code we already have.

summary: learned_noise_robust_addressing_page_routing: hippocampal memory indexing theory (Teyler-DiScenna/Rudy) + place/grid cells (CRT-style modular generalization, Fiete-Burak-Brookings) + TEM structure-content factorization (Whittington-Behrens 2020) + DG pattern separation (Marr, O-Reilly-McClelland) + CA3 pattern completion (Treves-Rolls, formally = modern Hopfield/attention per Ramsauer 2020) converge: brain solves noise-robust + generalizing addressing via a TWO-STAGE architecture (fixed DG-style expand+sparsify router = LSH-equivalent, generalizes for free; CA3-style resonator completion = noise-robust for already-known content), NOT one mechanism -- separation and completion are provably antagonistic on one substrate (O-Reilly-McClelland 1994), forcing the division of labor. Both existing exp_wm_paging_* cells hand-build an EXACT dict page-table with zero learning/noise-tolerance at the ROUTING step (only value-decode is noise-robust) -- this is the untested gap. Substrate already has certified primitives for both stages (Spoke3 fixed-expansion projection, block-local-K sparse resonator for DG-analog; FHRR bind/unbind+cleanup resonator for CA3-analog) but has never paired them into a router. Directly-relevant prior negative respected: DG-separator-prewrite composed with dense-KV Tikhonov cleanup HARD-FAILED (geometry worked, recall got worse) -- flagged as a pairing-mismatch risk, not assumed to transfer, and the recommended cell is an ablation ladder built to catch a repeat early. First cell recommended: exp_addressing_learned_noise_robust_page_router_v1 (fixed expand+sparsify DG-analog router + resonator CA3-analog completer vs hand-built-exact/sparsify-only/flat controls; sweep noisy-cue + novel-content query conditions). P_deflated=0.38.
plain_language: We asked: can our substrate LEARN how to find the right memory page from a fuzzy or partial hint, the way the brain does, instead of relying on a perfect hand-built lookup table? The brain solves this with two separate steps working together, not one clever trick: one brain region (dentate gyrus) spreads out and sparsifies any input -- including things it has never seen -- into a well-separated address, and a second region (CA3) uses an attractor-like settling process to recover the full memory even from a noisy or partial cue. Research showed these two steps fight each other if combined in one mechanism, which is why the brain keeps them separate. We already have working substrate building blocks for both steps, just never wired together as an address-finder; we designed the cheapest test to check whether pairing them actually works, while explicitly guarding against a past failure where a similar-looking fix made things worse instead of better.

summary: consolidation function inventory: schema-driven consolidation splits into fast write-time integration (COVERED by existing ingest-gate) vs reorganization of already-consolidated old memories (GAP, confirmed real, separable from the already-closed interference-avoidance question); recommended targeted-exact-reindex cell to test whether staleness causes measurable error and whether exact addressing makes reorg cheaper than the brain-forced costly reconsolidation route
plain_language: We asked whether rejecting brain-style memory consolidation was a mistake. Answer: consolidation actually does 5 different jobs in the brain, and we already correctly rejected one (avoiding memory overwrite, which our exact-storage design does not need) while separately already building another (fast filing of new schema-fitting facts). But one job -- going back and correcting an OLD stored fact when new information recontextualizes it (like realizing a whale is a mammal, not a fish) -- is a genuine, real gap nobody has tested yet. We proposed a cheap experiment to check whether this actually causes wrong answers in practice, and whether our exact-addressing could fix it more cheaply than the brain can.

summary: importance/downstream-reach correct-function drill: retrieval-time relevance (not active-reading acquisition-order, which already HARD_FAILED and is now literature-explained via the BatchBALD/coreset redundancy anti-pattern) is the load-bearing role for an unbounded-exact-store substrate, per convergent brain evidence (value-driven attentional capture, priority maps, Mattar and Daw Gain x Need retrieval utility) and classical-IR precedent (PageRank/HITS as retrieval-relevance signals, distinct from crawl-order per Olston and Najork). Recommended cell reuses 100pct existing machinery from the HARD_FAIL cell (importance_btwn_orth vs held-out test-query-count, degree-orthogonalized) at near-zero new compute.
plain_language: We figured out WHERE importance/downstream-reach actually helps: not deciding what to learn first (that already failed a test), but deciding what to surface first when answering a question -- like how the brain prioritizes recalling important memories over deciding what to memorize in the first place. Proposed a nearly-free next test to confirm it, reusing data we already have.

summary: glass_box_reading_robust_parsing_ceiling: biology (Frazier Minimal-Attachment/Late-Closure + Lewis-Vasishth cue-based retrieval + surprisal-via-PCFG + MacWhinney cue-validity thematic roles + Ferreira good-enough processing) converges with classical Open-IE toolkit (ClausIE clause-typing beats ReVerb on passive/relative-clause via dependency roles; CALM coordination pre-split is precision-POSITIVE unlike in-line CC handling; RELNOUN for nominals; Hearst patterns narrow to taxonomic is-a; OpenIE6 explicitly disqualified as neural-core) on a specific glass-box architecture recipe. Narrow-neural-syntax-parser carve-out is literature-supported via closed-output-space argument (17 POS tags/37 UD relations, cannot emit new fact content) though the exact hallucination-immunity claim is this note own synthesis not a direct citation -- flagged honestly. Confirmed literature GAP: no study measures OIE/SRL precision-recall directly on native graded/simple prose. Coreference is the one failure mode that does NOT shrink with simplification (may worsen, since simplified prose substitutes pronouns for long NPs) and is unaddressed by every technique reviewed. Cheap decisive test: triage exp_read_grow_foundation_endtoend_v1 own logged misses against the literature failure taxonomy (coordination/relative-clause/passive/nominalization/coreference/parse-error) -- HARD-PASS >=60% match means roadmap is actionable, HARD-FAIL <30% means the current positional-SVO parser itself is the priority fix. Deflated coverage-ceiling estimate: fully-classical ~70-85% precision/~50-70% recall on graded prose (P=0.35, extrapolated not measured); narrow-neural-parser-for-structure-only adds +5-15 relative points (P=0.45). Pre-registered good-enough glass-box reading definition delivered.
plain_language: We researched how the human brain manages to understand messy real sentences without a giant memorized language model -- turns out it uses a handful of cheap, general-purpose tricks (default guesses about sentence structure, a fuzzy memory-search for connecting far-apart words, and settling for good-enough understanding rather than perfect understanding) rather than one big learned system. We matched this against the best rule-based (non-AI) fact-extraction tools used in computational linguistics and found a concrete recipe for our own no-LLM reading pipeline, plus an honest admission that nobody has ever measured how well these rule-based tools work on genuinely simple text (a real gap in outside research). We identified that our current reading pipeline is missing a real grammar-parsing step (it currently just reads word order), that one specific upgrade (splitting sentences with and before extracting facts) has real evidence of being a pure win with no downside, and that understanding pronouns (he, she, it) is a permanent weak spot that does not get easier even with simpler writing -- something we need to plan for, not something that will resolve itself.

summary: grid_cell_crt_multimodulus_addressing_verdict: drilled grid-cell/CRT multi-modulus addressing as a v2 lever for the learned page router. Verdict: DEFER, not hypothetical -- this substrate already built+ran a hard-decision non-redundant CRT-residue router (RC2, exp_multihop_router_crt_residue_addressed_v1) and it LOST to naive baseline (route 0.415 vs 0.503, e2e 0.147 vs 0.237, delta=-0.088), exactly matching classical RNS/CRT theory (independent per-modulus hard decode is fragile-by-construction) and grid-cell biology (robustness needs BOTH redundant moduli (RRNS) AND soft/joint decode -- RC2 had neither). Current page router degrades gracefully via CA3-analog attractor search; its one gap (correlated keys) already has a cheaper non-CRT lever in flight (decorrelation front-end, partial recovery). CRT proven strong only in exact/noiseless algebraic regime (800x, 143x), not noisy routing. Concrete revisit trigger + pre-registered RRNS+soft-decode cell spec filed for if/when the decorrelation lever plateaus AND a range/capacity gap (not robustness gap) remains.
plain_language: Researched whether a brain-inspired multi-part addressing scheme (like how grid cells in the brain use combinations of repeating patterns to encode huge ranges of positions) would help our memory-paging system route to the right stored page. Finding: we already tried the direct version of this on a related problem and it lost to a simpler approach, for the same reason the brain never does it the simple way (the brain always pairs this trick with built-in redundancy and soft/fuzzy decoding, not a rigid formula) -- so we are deferring, not abandoning it, with a specific trigger for when to revisit with the corrected (redundant, soft-decode) design.

summary: coreference resolver (Hobbs/Centering): closes local-antecedent coref gap via a discourse-memory shim + recency/subject-role ranking + number-agreement filter, P=0.45 deflated; found the current parser has no cross-sentence state at all (the real prerequisite) and the current coref test rows are mis-specified (isolated sentences, not local-antecedent pairs); register-specific weakness flagged: closed animal-noun lexicon has no gender cue so number is the only hard filter; world-knowledge/genuine-tie coref confirmed permanent correct-abstain residual (P=0.55).
plain_language: Researched whether a classical rule-based algorithm (no AI language model) can teach the reading pipeline to figure out what a pronoun like "it" or "they" refers to. Found the human brain and a 1978 computer-science algorithm both solve this the same simple way: remember the last couple of sentences, then pick the most recent matching noun. The real fix needed first is giving the reading pipeline a short memory of recent sentences (it currently reads one sentence at a time with no memory at all) -- once that exists, the resolution rule itself is small and cheap. Genuinely confusing cases (two equally-likely candidates) should still be correctly skipped rather than guessed at, which protects the no-hallucination guarantee.

summary: new-relation (verb) glass-box grounding: three-tier split verdict (not flat fundamental-limit) -- Tier-1 identity (achievable via DORA-style repeated structural comparison widening arg-type-only coherence to symmetry/order + co-occurrence signature), Tier-2 class (achievable via Gentner structure-mapping/systematicity alignment to known relations), Tier-3 fine-grained idiosyncratic meaning (FUNDAMENTAL LIMIT, matches brain own root-meaning/idiosyncratic-component ceiling per Pinker/Levin, needs external anchor the substrate lacks -- P=0.90). Recommended cell extends exp_read_grow_openvocab_fastmap_v1 relation track with a same-arg-type structurally-distinct distractor (Tier-1 fix + required arg-type-only negative control) + systematicity class-labeling battery (Tier-2). P_deflated=0.38 composite.
plain_language: Studied how children learn new verbs (much harder than nouns, since a relation has no single thing you can point at) and mapped the findings onto our new-relation-grounding gap. Good news: two real, buildable upgrades exist (telling two new relations apart, and roughly classifying what kind of relation one is) using the same comparison tricks kids use. Bad news, confirmed by the science rather than assumed: pinning down a new relations EXACT meaning needs real-world context our system does not have -- this is a genuine wall, not a bug to fix, same as it is for kids without enough context.

plain_language: Studied how children move from known-word reading to genuinely new text, and what old-school (no-AI) text-parsing tools can actually achieve. Result: our existing high-precision parser design is already the right shape — the honest engineering ceiling for rule-based extraction favors precision over recall, matching what we already built. Named a concrete, free, fully-inspectable toolchain for the next step, and confirmed that resolving pronouns referring to earlier context (without world knowledge) is a real, permanent limit — not something to keep chasing.

plain_language: A prior experiment measured whether a brain-inspired 'pattern separation' step (like the dentate gyrus in the hippocampus) can rescue a fast sparse-memory trick that breaks when stored items are realistically correlated. The quick test came back with an inconclusive number because its search hit an artificial ceiling before finding the real answer at one of the two check points. I measured (using the experiment's own real code, not a guess) that the MORE IMPORTANT check point -- the worst-case correlated case -- was actually already finding a real, non-ceiling answer even before any change; I doubled the search room anyway for a comfortable safety margin. The other, less important check point will still hit its ceiling even after doubling, but that's expected and already handled honestly by the experiment's own logic (a ceiling-hit there only makes the true answer look smaller than it really is, and it already clearly clears the bar). Chasing a literal non-ceiling answer there would cost many extra hours of computer time for a question that's already answered. Handed off to the orchestrator to actually launch the full run on the remote computer.

plain_language: Last time (v2), two made-up relations (vorbs and dringles) genuinely fooled our smarter same-relation check -- they are different words for different things, but they looked structurally identical because the sentences around them never gave the check anything to tell them apart with. The open question was whether that's a permanent blind spot (the check can never tell them apart no matter what) or just a data-poverty problem (give it more surrounding context and it would sort them out). This test kept the two confusing relations exactly as-is and only added more surrounding sentences (about other, unrelated animal pairs) using a neutral, non-cherry-picked rule for what to add and in what order -- so it wasn't rigged toward either answer. The result: even a modest amount of extra surrounding context was enough for the SAME mechanism to correctly tell the two relations apart, and it stayed correct as more context kept being added. So this was a data-poverty problem, not a permanent limitation -- the fix already works, it just needed a richer corpus to have something to work with.

plain_language: RUNG 2 tested unknown NOUNS (animal/food/place words the parser had never seen); this rung tests unknown VERBS instead -- taking away the safety net that let RUNG 2 always recognize a known action-word. We confirmed the tagger really does sometimes misread an unfamiliar verb as a noun (the exact failure mode the previous audit predicted would now matter), and this costs us about 12% of sentences -- the parser correctly gives up on those rather than guessing wrong. Crucially, every fact it DID extract was still completely correct (0 wrong facts out of 127) -- so the cost of the newly-exposed weak spot is missed sentences, not wrong answers, and we can point to exactly why: the parser is built to require a verb before it tries to guess who did what to whom, so a misread verb just causes a clean pass rather than a bad guess. We also confirmed the backup spelling-pattern trick (recognizing -ing/-ed/-s endings) genuinely helps sometimes, rescuing a few of those misreads.

plain_language: Rungs 2 and 3 each tested ONE kind of unknown word at a time (unknown nouns, then unknown verbs) on sentences that were otherwise easy (one clause, no coordinated actions). This rung removes both trainer wheels at once: unknown nouns AND unknown verbs together, PLUS the harder sentence shapes we had been avoiding, especially two actions joined by "and" ("The X does this and does that"). The previous test predicted this would finally make the parser produce wrong answers, not just honest shrugs -- and it does, but only in that one specific sentence shape. Every other hard case we threw at it (two subjects joined by "and", relative clauses like "the X that does Y", passive sentences) stayed completely clean even with fully unfamiliar words. Within the coordinated-action sentences, we found and precisely pinned down why: the classical tagger sometimes misreads the first action as a plain object noun instead of a verb, and when that happens the parser can accidentally splice the wrong noun into the wrong role. Overall, across a 216-sentence test, correct answers stayed the overwhelming majority (90.6% of everything extracted was right, and we recovered 69.7% of the total facts present) -- both numbers land above the honest ceiling the classical-NLP literature sets for this kind of task, supporting the idea that easy, simple-sentence-style text should do better than general news text. The old parser alone (no unknown-word handling) never got a single fact right on this test -- it either honestly gave up or, on two sentence types, confidently stated a wrong fact.

summary: classical Open-IE / glass-box parsing frontier: hand-built SVO grammar HARD_FAILed on real prose (58.6% unhandled, precision 0.18) because it spuriously fires on unhandled constructions instead of abstaining. Brain-check: good-enough parsing (Ferreira) shows humans do the SAME thing -- commit to confident, plausibility-driven WRONG parses on noncanonical constructions, not graceful abstain; P600/regressions are post-hoc difficulty signals, never a pre-commit gate. But human syntax IS one broad-coverage generalizing parser, not per-construction hand rules, and verb/relation vocabulary is open-class and unbounded (fast-mapping, syntactic/semantic bootstrapping, no closed ceiling) -- so hand-building constructions one at a time and using a small closed relation list are both implementation gaps, not fundamental walls. Classical non-neural Open-IE (ReVerb/OLLIE/ClausIE on MaltParser/Charniak/Stanford-classic backends) confirmed genuinely non-neural + glass-box-legal, reaches CaRB F1 0.41-0.45 (ClausIE best, because its 7-clause-type grammar directly covers the copular/adjunct constructions our toy grammar buckets as other), capped partly by real-prose parser accuracy itself (80-84% F1 on web treebank). Recommendation: adopt classical clause-typology toolchain for coverage + open relation vocab, AND add a strict full-slot-match abstain gate (substrate-native precision lever, not a brain-copied mechanism -- the brain does not do this by default) as a cheap complementary fix.
plain_language: Our rule-based sentence-reading pipeline (no AI model, just hand-written grammar rules) failed badly on real web text -- it guessed wrong on 82% of the sentences it tried to parse instead of admitting it did not understand them. We checked how humans handle sentences they cannot fully parse: turns out humans also confidently guess wrong rather than gracefully giving up, so that part is not a bug unique to us. But the research also shows two real fixes: (1) swap our hand-written mini-grammar for a fuller, still fully-transparent (no AI) classical parsing toolchain that already covers far more sentence types, and (2) add a strict yes/no check so the system says nothing rather than guessing wrong when a sentence does not clearly match a known pattern -- something exact-check systems like ours can do better than brains can. Also confirmed: our tiny list of allowed relationship-words is an easy fix, not a deep limitation -- kids learn new verbs by the thousands with no ceiling, so we should too.

report: experiments/exp_read_grow_realprose_abstain_gate_rung5b_v1.py (pre-reg embedded in module docstring; no separate preregs/ file)
plain_language: Rung 5 found that our rule-based sentence reader, when let loose on real web text, gets things wrong far more often than it admits defeat -- only 18% of its guesses were correct. We checked how humans handle sentences they cannot fully parse and found humans do the same thing (confidently guess wrong rather than shrug), so this cell tried a fix humans do NOT do: a strict pass/fail check that only lets the reader commit to an answer when the sentence structure is FULLY and unambiguously one of the patterns it knows -- otherwise it says nothing. We built two such checks: one that refuses to treat an -ing/-ed word as the main action unless it is clearly attached to a helper word like "is" or "was" (catches sentences where a side-phrase gets mistaken for the main clause), and one that refuses to commit if there is a leftover, unaccounted-for action word later in the sentence (catches sentences like "the manager believes the plan will succeed", where the naive reader wrongly grabs "the plan" as the thing believed instead of noticing a whole second clause is attached). Both checks measurably worked: wrong-answer rate on sentences the classifier already knew had no derivable fact dropped by over a third, and correctness among the answers it did give jumped 60% relative (18%->29%). Crucially, it did this WITHOUT wiping out the good answers -- 4 out of the 5 correct answers the old version found survived the new stricter check, and the reader still attempted something on 12 of 210 sentences rather than going silent on all of them. But the jump from 18% to 29% correct still falls well short of the roughly 60% correctness bar that would put it in the range of published rule-based systems doing this same job -- so this is an honest partial win, not a fix: the strict-check idea clearly helps and does not just work by refusing to answer anything, but real prose still has more wrong-guess patterns (at least one more, a specific kind of embedded description clause, was found and explicitly flagged rather than hidden) that this cell did not address.

plain_language: We asked: does the simple no-AI text-reading pipeline that already failed badly on general web text (weblogs/reviews/emails, only 18% correct) do better once we restrict to genuinely SHORT, SINGLE-IDEA sentences -- the kind an early reader actually sees, as opposed to the messy general internet? We could not fetch a real early-reader storybook corpus in one session, so we took the closest honest shortcut: filter the SAME web-text corpus down to only the sentences that are objectively simple by their grammar (short, one clause, one main verb) BEFORE looking at how the reader does on them -- so we are not cherry-picking sentences it happens to get right. That filter worked as intended: within this simple slice, plain single-subject-verb-object sentences jumped from a quarter of the text to well over half, and the two hardest sentence types (multi-part sentences, sentences with a which/that clause) dropped out entirely by design. So the TEXT really did get simpler. But the reader is STILL wrong more often than right (38% correct among sentences it attempted, and even among only the plain simple sentences it is right just 55% of the time -- short of the 60% bar we set for calling it a genuine win). Looking closely at the actual mistakes, they are not really about sentence complexity anymore -- they are things like getting confused by irregular verb spellings (turning has into the nonsense word ha) and picking the wrong word out of a two-word name (reading Santa Claus and reporting Claus as clau, or reading customer service and picking customer instead of service). So the honest finding is: simplifying the SENTENCE STRUCTURE helped, exactly as predicted, but it uncovered a SECOND, previously-hidden problem (word-form and multi-word-name handling) that a real early-reader corpus would very likely still trigger too, since early-reader text still has ordinary irregular verbs and names. This is a genuine, useful negative result -- it tells us where to fix next, not that the whole idea failed.

All 4 named bugs live-verified fixed on general nonce constructions + 2 real Rung-6 false-positive rows, not memorized patches.

COREF_UNRESOLVED (1st/2nd-person pronoun subjects) remains the dominant unfixed coverage bottleneck, explicitly out of the VET named scope.

plain_language: Rung 6 found that our rule-based text reader, once we gave it genuinely short single-idea sentences, still got most of its guesses wrong (38% correct) -- but a close look at the actual mistakes showed the sentence-complexity problem was basically solved; the remaining errors were three small, specific, fixable glitches: (1) it mangled irregular verb spellings ("has" became the nonsense word "ha"), (2) it picked the wrong half of a two-word name or phrase (reading "Santa Claus" and reporting "Claus" mangled to "clau"; reading "customer service" and picking "customer" instead of the more important word "service"), and (3) it had never been taught to recognize COMMANDS ("Sit down.", "Look at the cat.") at all -- worse, it would sometimes mistake the word "Please" at the start of a command for the subject of the sentence, guessing nonsense. This cell fixed all three: taught it to check a small existing dictionary of irregular verbs BEFORE guessing at spelling; taught it a simple rule for picking the more important word out of a two-word phrase (first word for names like Santa Claus, last word for descriptive phrases like customer service); and taught it to recognize commands and correctly figure out that the reader is being told to do something to WHOM ("you", the implicit listener) and WHAT. After all three fixes, its accuracy on attempted sentences jumped from under 4-in-10 correct to almost 2-in-3 correct, clearing the bar we set in advance for calling this pipeline genuinely good at simple sentences. We verified each fix with brand-new test sentences the reader had never seen (not just the exact sentences that were broken before), so this is a real, general improvement, not a cheat. One thing we did NOT fix (on purpose, out of scope): the reader still cannot handle sentences that start with "I", "you", or "we" without more context -- that remains the single biggest source of missed sentences, flagged honestly for a future round. Also, since this text is still ordinary internet writing (just simple in sentence-structure), not an actual childrens book, the next real test is trying this on genuine early-reader material.

summary: exp_read_grow_realprose_simple_register_rung8_coref_1st2nd_person_v1 (RUNG 8) FULL landed HARD_FAIL per pre-registered bands (claim, VET-pending): resolves 1st/2nd-person subject pronouns (I/we/you) DIRECTLY instead of abstaining COREF_UNRESOLVED, on the SAME simple-register UD-EWT slice Rung 7 measured (n=300, seeds=[7,13,19]). Coverage recovers materially: 0.130->0.307 (+0.177 absolute, +136% relative, n_attempted 39->92), confirming the Rung-7 VET dominant-coverage-bottleneck framing was correct and the fix is NOT inert. Overall GATED precision DROPS 0.643->0.526, below the 0.55 HARD-FAIL floor. MECHANISM-LEVEL LOCALIZATION: the coref-fix itself makes ZERO referent-assignment errors (subject-role-correct-rate=47/47=1.000 on every newly-covered row with any gold); every whole-triple error traces to 4 SEPARATE pre-existing downstream bugs (irregular-plural-noun lemma restoration, brand/product compound-noun head-selection, OOV verb spelling-restoration, do-support negation parsing) that these sentences never reached before because COREF_UNRESOLVED gated them out upstream. Zero-hallucination guardrail PRESERVED: 0 of 32 genuine 3rd-person COREF_UNRESOLVED rows newly fire; hand-built 3rd-person nonce battery + fix-disabled positive control both pass.

plain_language: Rung 7 left one big gap flagged: our rule-based text reader was throwing away EVERY sentence that starts with I, we, or you, treating them the same as genuinely ambiguous pronouns like he or she or it (which really can refer to someone from an earlier sentence we cannot see). But I/we/you are NOT ambiguous -- I is always the speaker, we is always the speaker-group, you is always whoever is being addressed -- no detective work needed. So this cell taught the reader that one simple rule: if the sentence starts with I/we/you, just use that word directly as the subject instead of giving up. The coverage win was real and large -- the reader now attempts nearly a third of simple sentences instead of only an eighth (roughly 1-in-8 to nearly 1-in-3). But the sentences it newly reads exposed FOUR separate, previously-invisible weaknesses in other parts of the reader that had simply never been exercised before (because these sentences always got thrown out before reaching them): it does not know irregular plural spellings (turns teeth into tooth would be correct but it left it as teeth), it sometimes picks the wrong half of a two-word product/brand name (reading HTC Evo and reporting HTC instead of Evo), it mangles some ordinary verb spellings when restoring them to their base form (need becomes the nonsense ne), and it does not understand contracted negation (dont, wont) at all, latching onto the wrong verb. Crucially, we double-checked and the SPEAKER/ADDRESSEE identification itself was PERFECT -- every single one of the 47 newly-read sentences correctly identified who I/we/you referred to; all of the wrongness came from those four separate, older problems getting exposed for the first time, not from any mistake in this cells own fix. Because the overall correctness score dropped below the safety floor we set in advance, this honestly counts as a step backward on the strict scorecard even though the underlying idea worked exactly as intended and the reader never once wrongly guessed who someone else (he/she/it/they) was -- that safety rule held perfectly. The four newly-found problems are now the clear next-round shopping list.

summary: glassbox reading synthesis: ranked 5 barriers to achievable glass-box real-prose reading (foundation-size, WM, prediction, lexicon, core-syntax) using 2 new lit-scans + 5 prior same-week notes; core-syntax/construction coverage is empirically confirmed #1 (today HARD_FAIL was pure grammar-coverage failure, not WM/foundation/prediction), lexicon-meaning-attachment #2, prediction #3, WM #4, foundation-size #5 -- directly refutes just-foundation-and/or-WM premise
plain_language: Studied what actually blocks the substrate from reading normal sentences without an LLM. Ranked five candidate blockers using cognitive-science literature plus a real test result from today. Surprising finding: the size of the knowledge base and the working-memory limit -- the two things suspected to be the bottleneck -- are actually the LEAST important. The real problem is missing grammar rules (the hand-built parser does not recognize enough sentence types) and a missing recipe for attaching word meanings, both of which are known, buildable fixes.

summary: exp_read_grow_realprose_simple_register_rung9_downstream_bugs_v1 (RUNG 9) FULL landed HARD_PASS per pre-registered bands (claim, VET-pending): fixes the 4 downstream bugs Rung 8's coref-coverage-expansion localized (irregular-plural-noun lemma restoration; brand/product compound-noun head-selection; OOV verb spelling-restoration; do-support negation parsing) on the SAME simple-register UD-EWT slice (n=300, seeds=[7,13,19]). GATED precision_on_attempted rose 0.526 (Rung-8 reproduced exactly, n_attempted=92/n_correct=50) -> 0.747 (FIXED_ALL, n_attempted=92/n_correct=71), clearing the 0.60 milestone bar WHILE coverage_sentence_rate stayed unchanged at 0.307 (the 4 fixes correct already-attempted rows; they do not change what gets attempted). This is the FIRST high-coverage-high-precision landing in the Rung 5-9 arc. Per-bug contribution (independent single-bug arms, purely additive, sums exactly to the +21 total gain): plural +6 correct, brand/compound-head +7, verb-OOV-lemma +5, do-support +3. All 4 fixes verified GENERAL via novel nonce cases (distinct words/names from the literal Rung-8 error rows) -- not memorized patches. Zero-hallucination guardrail PRESERVED (0/32 3rd-person breaks). DECISIVE TAIL-LENGTH DIAGNOSTIC: the milestone WAS reached this round (short-tail outcome on the precision gate), but a residual-error classification of the 26 still-wrong rows shows the onion-peeling pattern is NOT fully closed -- 14 rows are a NAMED NEW pattern (BARE_ADJUNCT_OVEREXTRACTION: bare temporal/locative NPs after intransitive verbs mistaken for direct objects, e.g. 'i flew here last night.' emits a spurious object), 6 are a second NAMED NEW pattern (MODAL_OR_FUNCTION_WORD_MISTAGGED_AS_MATRIX_VERB: reduced-modal 'better' in 'I better pass on the Comets game.' mistagged VBP and picked as the main verb by the classical tagger), and 6 are honestly unclassified. Neither new pattern is one of the 4 just-fixed bugs -- both were ALREADY visible in Rung 8's own sample before this cell ran, not introduced by this cell's fixes.

plain_language: Rung 8 found that teaching our rule-based text reader to understand 'I'/'we'/'you' as subjects (instead of giving up on them) massively increased how many sentences it would even attempt, but also dragged its accuracy down below a safety floor -- because those newly-attempted sentences exposed four separate, older, previously-invisible weak spots in other parts of the reader (irregular plural spelling, picking the wrong half of a two-word brand name, mangled verb-spelling restoration, and not understanding contracted negation like 'don't'/'won't'). This session fixed all four as GENERAL rules (verified on brand-new test sentences, not just the ones that broke before) and re-measured. The result is the best outcome so far in this multi-week series: accuracy on attempted sentences jumped from about 1-in-2 correct to about 3-in-4 correct, clearing the bar we set in advance, WITHOUT losing any of the coverage gained (still attempting about a third of simple sentences) and without breaking the safety rule that stops the reader from guessing who 'he'/'she'/'it'/'they' refers to. But we did not stop at the headline number -- we specifically checked what's STILL wrong on the sentences the reader gets right most of the time now, and found two NEW, previously-unnoticed weak spots already sitting in the data: it sometimes mistakes a leftover bystander detail (like 'last night' or 'here') for the actual object of the sentence when there isn't one, and it occasionally confuses a casual spoken-style word like 'better' (as in 'I better go') for the sentence's main action verb. Neither of these was one of the four things we fixed this time -- they were quietly there all along, just outnumbered by bigger problems until now. So the honest picture is: we reached the goal we set for this round, but the same pattern that has repeated every round so far (fix a batch of bugs, and the newly-clean data reveals the next smaller batch) has not stopped -- it just didn't block us from clearing the bar this time. That is useful, concrete evidence for deciding whether to keep hand-fixing bugs one round at a time versus switching to an off-the-shelf grammar toolkit for the remaining, smaller issues.

summary: hard-rule-vs-predictive parsing barrier: bio (surprisal theory, parallel constraint-satisfaction) + ML history (PCFG/CRF/supertagging glass-box, 88-92pct F1 vs ~55pct hard structural heuristics) + classical ambiguity-explosion (Church and Patil Catalan-number PP-attachment, Hindle and Rooth 55->80pct via lexical stats) all confirm hard-rule-vs-graded-probability is a real, distinct axis from rule-coverage. Cross-checked against OWN Rung 5-8 read->grow error data: most observed failures (Rungs 6-7) were coverage/morphology bugs fixed by MORE hard rules exactly as predicted, but Rung 5b declared one residual (reduced-relative-clause-on-subject, e.g. horse-raced-past-barn-fell) that NO hard rule can catch -- literally Jurafsky 1996 82:1/6.4-bit calculation, requiring a graded frequency scorer. Compound-noun head selection (Rung 8: HTC Evo / customer service) is a second such case. Glass-box probabilistic scoring (named frequency counts, log-odds -- same primitive as the existing surprise-gate KL(post||prior) quantity) is achievable and cheap; proposed cheap decisive test = 2 narrow frequency scorers targeting exactly these 2 named VET residuals, NOT a general PCFG rebuild.
plain_language: We asked whether our rule-based sentence reader keeps failing because it uses rigid yes/no rules instead of the kind of graded guessing humans and modern statistical parsers do. The science says yes, this is a real and different problem from just missing rules -- but when we checked our OWN test data, most of our actual mistakes so far were fixable by adding more precise rules (irregular verbs, name-vs-phrase word order), not by graded guessing. There is exactly one confirmed case where graded guessing is truly needed: a classic tricky sentence type (like the horse raced past the barn fell) that no fixed rule can resolve, plus a related word-order guessing case. We proposed a small, cheap, fully-inspectable fix (frequency-based scoring, no AI model) targeting just those two known trouble spots rather than rebuilding the whole reader.

summary: lexicon_richness_subcategorization_barrier: 3-lane lit-scan (psycholinguistic lexicalist-parsing, lexicalized-statistical-parsing, lexicalized-grammar-formalisms) confirms subcat/selectional lexicon richness is a real, distinct, bounded barrier from foundation/world-fact size -- VerbNet/FrameNet/PropBank/WordNet already exist as free symbolic non-LLM resources (integration problem, not generation problem like the foundation build). Klein & Manning 2003 caution: historical lexicalization-accuracy gains partly conflate lexicon richness with grammar/category-granularity refinement -- our own build must test both levers with a 3-arm design, not assume lexicon alone explains gains. P_deflated=0.38-0.45 per prediction, composite 0.40.
plain_language: We studied whether real-sentence (not toy-sentence) parsing needs each word to carry rich grammatical information (which sentence patterns a verb allows, what kinds of things can fill its roles) -- like a human dictionary entry does -- and whether that is a different, cheaper problem than general world-knowledge. Answer: yes to both. Free, ready-made linguistic dictionaries (VerbNet, FrameNet, PropBank, WordNet) already contain exactly this information for thousands of verbs, so building this piece is mostly plugging in existing resources, not the expensive fact-generation work the general-knowledge foundation needs. One caution from the research literature: past parsing systems sometimes gave credit to a richer dictionary when the real fix was better sentence-structure rules, so our test plan checks both separately instead of assuming.

summary: WM-barrier-for-glassbox-parsing: bounded-capacity buffer framing is NOT the mechanism (Just&Carpenter single-resource theory contested, not consensus; weak correlation with ONLINE parsing specifically). Real lever = (1) incremental structural memory of open dependencies (a dependency-parser stack), which the current positional-SVO parser lacks and the already-recommended ClausIE-style upgrade already supplies -- same lever as 07-16 finding, confirmed independently via Dyer-et-al-Stack-LSTM vs Chen-Manning feedforward same-task comparison (93.1 vs 91.8 UAS English); (2) content-addressable interference-aware retrieval (Lewis and Vasishth) for long-distance argument resolution, a genuinely NEW mechanism not yet actioned. Chart-parsing full memoization confirmed pure efficiency device, not accuracy lever. Human ~2-3-deep center-embedding capacity bound should NOT be copied (limitation not capability) per two-frontiers doctrine.
plain_language: We asked: is the reason our rule-based sentence reader struggles a missing WORKING-MEMORY mechanism (holding partial understanding while reading a sentence), the way psychologists describe it in humans? Answer: partly, but not the way the hypothesis framed it -- the human WORKING-MEMORY-CAPACITY story is actually contested science, not settled fact. What the research does confirm as real and useful: our reader needs a way to track which parts of a sentence are still incomplete as it reads (like a dependency parser already gives you), which is the SAME fix we already identified yesterday, now confirmed from a second angle. It also surfaces one genuinely new idea: when a sentence refers back to something far away with multiple possible matches, we need a smarter matching rule (not just nearest-word), which is new and worth testing cheaply before building.

summary: discourse state-of-mind: characterized the situation-model/working-memory overlay (Kintsch CI, Zwaan event-indexing, Gernsbacher structure-building, Centering Theory Cb/Cf, McElree direct-access focus, EST event-boundaries) and mapped it to a 4-tier glass-box architecture (Tier0 single Cb pointer / Tier1 F=3-4 Cf resonator / Tier2 N-16-32 situation-model bundle / Tier3 exact-record foundation) that is the connective tissue between the already-scoped WM-focus note and coreference-resolver note, not a new subsystem; load-bearing new finding: Event Segmentation Theory boundary-detection is a prediction-error spike mechanistically identical to the already-VET-d ingest-gate unexpectedness axis, giving that signal a second role (discourse consolidation trigger)
plain_language: Studied how humans keep track of what a story or conversation is currently about while reading or talking -- a small mental spotlight on one thing, a slightly bigger shortlist of recently-mentioned things, a larger working picture of the scene, and a permanent memory store, each updated as new sentences arrive. Found this maps cleanly onto architecture pieces already designed this week (the working-memory-focus design and the pronoun-resolver design) -- it is the glue between them, not a new thing to build from scratch. Also found that the machine already built to decide what facts are worth remembering permanently can double as the trigger for when to save the current scene into permanent memory, because both jobs use the same kind of surprise signal.

summary: exp_read_discourse_state_of_mind_wsm_coupling_v1: first build of a minimal glass-box discourse state-of-mind (Tier0 Cb pointer + reused Tier1 Cf resolver + reduced Tier2 active-event slot), assembled from the coref resolver + parser (no new subsystem), plus the decisive coupling test (does discourse state improve per-sentence extraction on genuinely discourse-dependent sentences vs an isolated-per-sentence baseline).
