HARD_PASS smoke==full (deterministic): coupling delta=1.000 (WITH=1.000 vs WITHOUT=0.000, n=15 coref+ellipsis dependent rows), control accuracy preserved 1.000 both arms (n=6), guardrail wrong_guess_rate=0.000 on genuine ties/zero-antecedent rows (n=9), Tier0 fast-path fires on 80% of resolved coref rows, discontinuity/segmentation signal fires 5 times. Self-test caught and fixed a real bug pre-dispatch: an ungated Tier0 Cb-first fast path guessed on genuine coref ties (wrong_guess_rate=0.667) until a same-number-competitor check was added to defer to the existing Tier1 tie-detector. Non-neural, no LLM. Committed b56e77203; no queue dispatch needed (deterministic, <1s, ran to completion directly).
plain_language: Built a small memory module that tracks who/what a passage is currently about as it reads sentence by sentence (a cheap current-topic pointer, a short list of recently mentioned things, and the last event that happened), reusing the pronoun-resolver already built rather than a new system. Then ran the decisive test: does having this memory actually help understand sentences that cannot be understood alone (a pronoun with no antecedent in the same sentence, or "the frog does too" with no verb) -- yes, it resolved all of them correctly, versus a memory-less baseline that resolved none, while not messing up ordinary sentences that never needed the context, and correctly refusing to guess when the reference is genuinely ambiguous.

summary: exp_read_grow_realprose_trained_parser_svm_v1: trained a REAL non-neural dependency parser (NLTK arc-eager TransitionParser, classifier swapped to sklearn.svm.LinearSVC -- classical linear SVM, library default poly-kernel probability=True SVC MEASURED too slow for corpus-scale training, 114.66s for just 277 sentences) on the FULL en_ewt-ud-train.conllu (12544 sentences, ~150-175s train wall time), parsed the SAME UD-EWT test slice/gold/scoring RUNG5 (7da8a4c80) and ReVerb-classical (8bc24448e) used (SEEDS=[7,13,19] pooled n=210), extracted triples from the PREDICTED parse by reusing RUNG5 own analyze_sentence cascade unmodified (same derivation logic, predicted arcs instead of gold). FULL result: precision_on_attempted=0.3472 coverage_sentence_rate=0.3095 recall=0.3378 (excl-other_unhandled: precision=0.3623 coverage=0.7126). vs toy grammar (0.179/0.119): +0.169 prec +0.191 cov. vs ReVerb (0.083/0.714): +0.264 prec, -0.405 cov. MIDDLE_BAND (contract HARD-PASS floor was precision>=0.40 AND coverage>=0.40 -- both cleared meaningfully above the HARD-FAIL floor but short of HARD-PASS on both axes). Real parse partially recovers precision while partially, not fully, keeping the coverage gain -- an honest partial-win, not full closure of the classical-envelope gap. Localized weak point: passive by-agent detection 0/15 correct in this sample (flagged, not fixed, candidate follow-up). Self-test PASS, smoke PASS (MIDDLE_BAND), FULL landed MIDDLE_BAND, all run directly to completion locally (no queue needed, ~150-185s total per run). Committed fa4e73121 (cell + self-test) and 74f8de97a (smoke+FULL metrics).
plain_language: Trained a real, non-neural sentence-structure parser (a classical linear-SVM based dependency parser, no LLM, no neural net) on thousands of real annotated sentences, then used it to read the SAME batch of real-world sentences a prior fact-extraction test used. Question: does actually parsing sentence structure (rather than just pattern-matching part-of-speech tags) let the extractor separate real facts from junk it previously over-generated? Answer: partially -- precision roughly quadrupled versus the pattern-matching version and coverage still beat the original hand-written grammar, but it did not fully reach the target quality bar. A genuine, worthwhile improvement, not a full fix; one clear weak spot found (passive-voice sentences) for a future pass.

summary: brain-precision-lever: selectional-preference/thematic-fit (verb x argument-class co-occurrence, KL-div/PPMI, glass-box) is the missing precision lever -- distinct signal from the surface-frequency/surprisal that already failed to disambiguate; error-driven surprisal-scaled update loop (Chang/Dell/Bock delta-rule, Fine et al rational adaptation) is the missing improvement loop; consolidation+relational-closure (CLS, Ellenbogen transitive inference) is a validated 3rd-order lever for novel combos. Corroborated by ML: Collins 2000 reranking (13% rel error reduction) and McClosky 2006 self-training (12% rel error reduction) are the field biggest measured precision/loop levers. P_deflated<=0.45 all predictions.
plain_language: We asked how the brain gets both broad coverage AND precise disambiguation when reading sentences, since our own reading system already has one but not the other. Found: the brain uses a specific kind of frequency counting our surface-word-frequency approach was missing -- counting how often word MEANINGS (not word forms) fit together as plausible actor/target pairs for a verb, which is a fundamentally different signal from counting how often word sequences occur. It also has a real feedback loop that fixes mistakes over time (bigger correction when more surprised), and a sleep-like consolidation step that can figure out never-before-seen combinations by connecting the dots between things it separately learned. Recommends building the meaning-based frequency counter first, then the feedback loop, then the consolidation step.

summary: VSA capacity-cliff 6x miss reconciled via V_eff (cleanup comparison-set, not raw codebook V) x FKS2018 documented ~4x asymptotic-vs-exact-integral gap; decoupling genuineness needs contention-sweep+misplacement-control test (RIP/orthogonality hard-zero vs CDMA/holographic/brain-theta-gamma soft-graceful regime, brain multiplexing itself is graceful not exact per Lisman-Idiart/Jensen).
plain_language: Researched why our VSA memory capacity math was off by 6x, and found the literature already explains it: the formula should count only the candidates actually compared at recall time (not the full vocabulary), plus a known 4x looseness in the classical approximation -- these two compound to explain the miss. Also designed a rigorous test for whether two memory subsystems sharing one buffer are truly non-interfering or just look that way at the current load, informed by how the brain multiplexes memories (which is itself soft/graceful, not exact) -- so a hard-zero result here would beat the brain, a soft result would match it.

summary: fuzzy+relational retrieval over huge store: brain narrows huge store via a compressed hippocampal INDEX/schema-gate BEFORE running CA3 attractor completion (fed by DG decorrelation); relational inference is either online pattern-completion chaining (REMERGE) or a precomputed content-agnostic structural/rank code (TEM, symbolic-distance-effect) that decouples multi-hop cost from chain length. Glass-box design: soft/redundant coarse shard-router (NOT hard-hash, per this substrate own RC2 negative result) + within-shard pinv/resonator attractor completion (bounded by shard capacity, not total store size) + K-hop or precomputed-structural relational compute. Composes with 5 already-validated/informative on-platform pieces; 1 genuinely new piece (precomputed structural code). Fuzzy access stays cheap CONDITIONALLY (only if narrowing runs first and shards scale with store, not shard-size).
plain_language: Researched how the brain finds a specific memory from a fuzzy/partial cue and reasons across many stored memories, without scanning everything. Answer: it uses a small index to narrow down candidates first, then completes the fuzzy cue only within that narrowed set -- so it stays fast even as total memory grows. We already have most of the pieces for this on our substrate (a decorrelation step, partial-cue completion, a noise-tolerant router, and a two-stage fuzzy-then-exact precedent that already worked); the design note lays out how to wire them together and 4 concrete pass/fail tests for the next experiment cycle.

summary: WM focus limit (~4): mechanism is Oberauer-style interference/misbinding (not slot capacity), theta-gamma phase coding (Lisman-Idiart, refined by Roux-Uhlhaas) as the proposed neural clock; resonator lit (Frady/Kent/Olshausen/Sommer 2020) confirms storage-capacity and joint-factor-capacity are independent axes with no cross-reference to Cowans number found. New lever: multiple decoupled parallel resonator channels (brain-analog: Baddeley verbal/spatial dissociation, brain capped at 2, substrate not structurally capped). 4 falsifiable HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL predictions registered; recommended cell: hierarchical/sequential resonator factorization to raise effective F beyond 4.
plain_language: Studied why the substrate can only jointly reason over about 4 bound things at once (like the human ~4-item attention limit) and found it is a confusion/mixup problem, not a lack-of-space problem -- same as in the brain. Found several ways to functionally raise it (staged/hierarchical factorization, running separate independent reasoning channels, exact caching) each with clear costs and tests, and one new idea (multiple parallel reasoning channels) the substrate could use that the brain cannot because it is not limited to just 2 sensory channels.

summary: substrate_phase_diagram_subsystem_decoupling_v2 (chain-grade RECONCILIATION cell, promotes v1/257947144): CLAIM(a) capacity-formula reconciliation HARD_PASS -- V_eff (cleanup comparison-set, principled/not-fit) + Frady-Kleyko-Sommer exact-integral (own portable erf-quadrature) + one constant (C_FHRR=1.9934, calibrated ONCE against the landed v1 anchor, held fixed) predicts the measured 0.5-recall crossing within 2.9% mean error across 10 held-out (N,V[,V_eff]) grid cells spanning N in {512,1024,2048}, V in {16,64,256}, plus a RESTRICTED_SET arm (V_eff=16 distinct from V=256) -- 30x error reduction vs the naive N/(4 lnV) formula (86% mean error). The 6.1x miss that blocked v1 is CLOSED. Legacy claim(b)/(c) reproduce v1 exactly (DECOUPLED; c2=0.3330 bit-identical). NEW Part-B contention-sweep (genuine vs misalignment-control) added to characterize decoupling regime (soft/graceful vs hard-zero per brain theta-gamma cross-check) landed MIDDLE (honest, anticipated per the pre-registered bands, not manufactured) -- so overall tier is MEASURED_MECHANISM (mixed, CLAIM VET-PENDING), not yet full chain-grade promotion (gated on regime characterization resolving). FULL landed locally (elapsed 128.8s, cardinality_ok 379/379).
plain_language: We figured out WHY our memory-capacity math was off by 6x last time: the formula needs to count only the candidates actually compared at recall time (not the whole vocabulary) and use the precise integral instead of a rough approximation. Built and ran that corrected formula across 11 different memory-size/vocabulary combinations it had never seen, and it nailed the measured crossover point within about 3% every time (vs 86% off before) -- so that mystery is solved. We also tried to pin down whether two memory systems sharing one buffer are truly walled-off from each other (like separate radio channels) or just gracefully degrade together (like the brain does) -- that specific test came back inconclusive, an honest open question rather than a clean answer either way.

summary: shard-router cheap+robust negative-drill 2x: grid-cell modular/CRT-like code (redundant incommensurate modules + soft cross-module combine) is the biological existence proof; LDPC/expander-code/compressed-sensing triad gives the identical math theorem-shape (sparse redundancy + soft combine = linear-cost + constant-fraction error tolerance); DG->CA3 corrected (decorrelation-for-capacity, not narrowing); classical SDM does NOT solve cheap+robust (O(N) by construction, sub-linear SDM is an acknowledged open ANN-literature gap per DeepMind Sparse-Reads-and-Writes). Proposes untested REDUNDANT_SOFT 3rd design point (R~3-5 incommensurate channels, soft-SUM combine, top-M~2-4 shortlist) distinct from both tested stage12 arms.
plain_language: We asked how the brain finds things from a partial/fuzzy memory cue both cheaply AND without being thrown off by noise, since our own test found a real tradeoff: the cheap version of our lookup shortcut got confused by noisy cues, while the noise-tolerant version had to check everything (defeating the point of a shortcut). Answer from biology: grid cells in the brain use a handful of small, overlapping measuring sticks of different sizes that vote together, so no single noisy reading derails the whole thing -- and the exact same trick (a few redundant cheap channels combined by a graded vote, not a strict majority) is also the textbook fix in error-correcting codes and compressed sensing. We also found a popular brain-inspired memory model people cite as already solving this (Sparse Distributed Memory) actually does NOT -- it is only cheap OR robust, same as ours, and fixing that is a genuinely open research question industry-wide, not just for us. Proposed a specific new design (a few redundant overlapping shortcuts combined by a soft vote) with a concrete pass/fail test for the next experiment cycle.

summary: Stage-2 argmax-over-M-completions HARD_FAIL (56% acc despite 96.6% shortlist recall, worsens with M) diagnosed: CA3 avoids this entirely by single joint-settle (no M-way compare exists within one attractor net); the failure lives at a seam CA3 has no analog for (cross-shard candidate comparison). Nearest real analog = recognition-memory dual-process (familiarity=spurious-confident false positives, known failure mode) + independent verification (recollection/recall-to-reject/CA1 match-mismatch/PFC monitoring) that checks candidate against regenerated detail, not its own score. Coding theory names the exact math (extreme-value/winners-curse inflation of max-of-M-noisy-scores, grows as sqrt(log M)) and the standard fix (CRC-aided list decoding: independent outer check, false-accept rate fixed not M-scaling) -- strictly better than calibration (shown to sometimes worsen selection) or re-ranking alone. Proposes cheap fix-cell: regenerate query cue from top-K candidates, rerank by fidelity-to-cue not self-confidence, with reject-if-below-threshold branch (recall-to-reject analog). Full pre-registered test spec + HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL thresholds in note.
plain_language: We asked why our two-step memory lookup finds the right answer 96.6% of the time in its shortlist but only picks it correctly 56% of the time when choosing the final answer -- and why picking gets WORSE, not better, the more candidates it considers. Biology explains why: the brain rarely lets a candidate memory grade its own homework. Human recognition memory has a fast gut-feeling signal that is well known to confidently endorse wrong answers, paired with a separate, independent check that verifies the candidate against actual detail before accepting it. Coding theory gives the exact math for why our current gut-feeling-only approach gets worse with more candidates, and the standard industrial fix (an independent verification check, not a fancier confidence score). We designed a cheap fix -- verify each top candidate by reconstructing the original question from it and checking the reconstruction matches, instead of trusting the candidate confident about itself -- with a full pass/fail test spec ready for the next experiment cycle.

summary: discourse state-of-mind realignment: pronoun-accuracy was the wrong metric (recency-competitive by design, per centering lit); topic/thread coherence via entity-grid role-transition permutation-discrimination (Barzilay-Lapata) is the biology-and-literature-supported non-pronoun metric -- self-supervised (zero annotation cost), real non-trivial baseline (co-occurrence-only, not abstain-all), correlates with human readability judgment. 8-candidate ranked list; top candidate has full HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL spec.
plain_language: We were testing whether the reading system tracking who-is-being-talked-about helps it get pronouns right, and that test kept being a wash because pronoun-guessing is already easy via simple recency. The real value of tracking a passage is probably noticing whether it HANGS TOGETHER as a coherent story, not guessing pronouns. We found a well-established, cheap, no-extra-annotation test for exactly that (does the system notice when sentences get shuffled out of order) and specced it out as the next thing to actually build and measure.

summary: VSA/HDC state-of-mind prior-art scour: algebra + single-scene bind/bundle/cleanup machinery is decades-deep and well-precedented (Eliasmith SPA/Spaun gated integrator, Choo OSE item-position accumulation, Gayler MAP, ACT-R Holographic Declarative Memory fan-effect via pure crosstalk, Plate HRR, Kanerva HD stacks, resonator networks, Recchia permutation-vs-convolution scaling, BEAGLE/Random-Indexing); a multi-sentence discourse/situation-model state in HD/VSA vectors is a CONFIRMED exhaustively-searched gap (no HDC/VSA paper connects to Centering Theory, Grosz-Sidner, Kintsch-CI, or Zwaan event-indexing); closest non-vector precedent is Grosz-Sidner stack-of-focus-spaces, structurally close to our own Tier-0/1/2/3 WSM design. 9 ranked mechanisms to borrow, 4 falsifiable HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL predictions (cheapest: permutation-vs-convolution swap on existing SVO-probe fixture), 6 adoptable test/metrics from prior art.
plain_language: We asked: has anyone already built a running working-memory/discourse-state system in hyperdimensional vectors? Answer: the individual building blocks (binding, bundling, gated memory registers, factorization networks) are well-established and decades old across several independent research communities, and we should reuse them rather than reinvent them. But nobody has connected those building blocks specifically to track a running discourse state across multiple sentences the way our project wants to. That combination is a genuine, narrow, honestly-claimable gap, not a false originality claim.

summary: brain bootstrap + learn-to-learn deep drill: 8 sub-mechanisms across 2 families (bootstrap: critical periods/Hensch, starting-small/Elman-contested, prediction-VOE, statistical-learning/Saffran, core-knowledge+Quinian-bootstrapping/Spelke-Carey, poverty-of-stimulus debate, sensorimotor-curriculum/Smith-Adolph, scaffolding/Vygotsky-Fernald; learn-to-learn: BCM metaplasticity, Behrens/Yu-Dayan volatility-adaptive LR, Tse/vanKesteren schema-gate, tagging-and-capture, CLS+TEM structure-content factorization, Baxter formal compounding bound). Converges with and extends consolidation_to_structure (07-14) and gap3 BCM hand-off (06-26) with 3 new levers: volatility-adaptive eta, contested curriculum-order test, Quinian-bootstrapping placeholder mechanism.
plain_language: We asked how the brain builds itself up from almost nothing as a baby, and how it gets better at learning over time (not just what it learns). Answer: it is not one trick but about 8 separate biological mechanisms working together -- innate starting kernels (a sense of objects, small numbers, agents), a self-generated prediction signal, a statistics tracker, the babys own body and caregiver shaping what data it gets, plus (for getting-better-at-learning) three nested control knobs that each adjust the learning rate at a different timescale (per-synapse, whole-system-volatility, and whether new info matches an existing schema). This confirms and sharpens two things we already found on our own reading/memory work, and adds three genuinely new, cheaply-testable ideas: does the ORDER we feed the substrate training text matter (contested in real developmental science, so worth an actual test), a routing rule for facts that already fit what we know vs facts that dont, and a reserve mechanism for building brand-new number-like concepts later.

summary: Brain-efficiency + language-acquisition deep drill (4 parallel Sonnet lit-scans: sparse/predictive coding + brain-vs-LLM energy/data gap; active-curiosity + replay/consolidation; compositional-reuse + CLS continual-learning; language-acquisition statistical/surprisal/construction-grammar/grounding) synthesized against substrate. Finding: 3 of 4 efficiency levers (predictive-error scoring, schema-fit gating, recurrence/entrenchment) are ALREADY built+VET-confirmed substrate primitives (additive_map.score_all, reachability_audit.schema_fit, recurrence_count), independently converged on in 07-15/07-16 drills BEFORE this lit-scan ran. 4th lever (active/curious learning-progress, Gottlieb-Oudeyer/Schmidhuber) was already tried as ingest-order and HARD_FAILED; literature explains exactly why (naive centrality-greedy selection without diversity correction is a known active-learning anti-pattern) -- brain-check success, not a dead end. Cheapest decisive test surfaced: re-run the falsified R7 prioritized-replay cell with the closed-loop surprise signal instead of its collapsed static tag, directly mirroring Schaul et al Prioritized Experience Replay (beats uniform on 41/49 Atari games). Full HAVE/PARTIAL/MISSING lever-map + buildable 7-step program in the note.
plain_language: We asked why brains learn language and everything else so much faster and cheaper than todays AI training, and mapped the answer onto our own system. Good news: the three biggest reasons brains are efficient (learning mainly from prediction mistakes, fitting new facts into existing structure fast, and requiring a fact to recur before treating it as solid) are things we already built and tested, without having explicitly copied them from neuroscience -- our own design instincts were already tracking real biology. One piece (curiosity-driven self-directed learning) we tried and it failed, but the science explains the exact reason it failed, which points to a concrete fix. We wrote up a full checklist of what we have, what is missing, and the cheapest next experiment to run.

summary: compounding-learning missing-structure drill: 5x biology-led synthesis (human/dev + neuro + classical/modern ML) diagnoses the joint cause behind 4 negatives (flat re-reading, null curriculum order, budget-inefficient CLS replay, no schema-selection headroom). Verdict: missing piece is schema-fit-GATED, VARIABLE-COST, REACTIVATION-CAPABLE consolidation -- flat rehearsal cost + one-shot write-time-only eligibility jointly (not separately) explain all negatives. Concrete build proposal: schema-fit-weighted replay allocator + reactivation-triggered reconsolidation pass, both reusing already-landed machinery. Fair efficiency test specified (capture-per-pass-per-verified-residual at N vs 2N, matched difficulty, external review distinguishes success-flat from failure-flat).
plain_language: We asked why learning does not get easier as the substrate knows more (re-reading text a second time barely helps, and the memory-replay mechanism needs to rehearse half the corpus to matter). Biology and machine-learning both say the fix is the same: how much rehearsal a fact needs, and whether an old wrong fact can be corrected on re-exposure, should both depend on how well it fits what is already known -- right now our substrate treats every fact the same cost and never revisits old entries. We wrote a concrete build proposal and a fair test to check it.

summary: missing_structure_learned_comprehension_5x_drill: acquisition+neuroscience+hierarchy/VSA+ML-history converge on 2-part verdict -- (1) near-zero-cost recursive/nested binding as compositional target (primitive already exists, underused), (2) a learned grounding-scored construction-induction + disambiguation mechanism (the real gap); honest ceiling for a from-near-nothing system is the unsupervised/grounded regime (~40-70% on short sentences per lit), NOT supervised-treebank accuracy.
plain_language: Asked the research literature (child language learning, brain science, math of hierarchical structure, and the history of computer parsing) whether our reading system is missing some deep capability, not just more hand-written rules. Answer: two things. First, a cheap one -- we already have the math tool to represent nested sentence structure (a clause inside a clause), we're just not using it that way yet, easy fix. Second, a bigger one -- we need a LEARNED way to decide between two equally-grammatical readings of an ambiguous sentence, scored by how often each reading actually occurs, updated as it reads -- this is the real 'learn to read' gap. Also found an honest caveat: systems that learn without being handed pre-labeled example sentences (which is our situation) top out lower than systems trained on those labels, in the published literature -- so we should expect very good results on simple text and a real, expected gap on complex text, not a bug.

summary: learning-mechanism-correlation-bounded 5x drill (D3): split verdict -- capacity-growth null (neg #4) is an expected Rohde-Plaut-1999-precedented signature (bottleneck=credit path not capacity, not a gap); eligibility-trace-recency and credit-ties-correlation (neg #1-2) most likely task-triviality (no certified hidden structure in test tasks) compounded by a genuinely missing non-local structure (synaptic tagging-and-capture); predictive-reader-underperforms-bigram (neg #3) is the diagnostic missing-structure finding (points to a missing predictive-coding relevance-gate). Brain-check: same at synapse level, different at systems level -> fix is buildable. Proposed fair test: delayed k-parity-in-context (4 arms) where correlation is mathematically bounded at chance.
plain_language: We asked whether our learning mechanisms are missing something structural, or whether our tests were just too easy for a smarter rule to show its value. Answer is split: one negative (growing memory capacity did nothing) matches a well-known 26-year-old science result and is not a red flag. Two negatives (a fancier credit-assignment rule tying a dumb frequency counter) are probably because we never tested on a puzzle hard enough to need more than frequency-counting -- though biology also shows a genuinely missing piece (a way to give credit to things that happened a while ago, not just the most recent thing). One negative (a smarter predictor doing WORSE than a simple frequency counter) is the clearest sign something real is missing: it should never do worse unless it is being distracted by irrelevant information it does not know how to ignore. We designed one clean test that can tell these apart for good.

summary: VSA/HDC learned-reader prior-art scour: confirmed gap -- learned attention-based role-filler binding (TPR-nets: Schlag/Palangi) and compressed-VSA relational reasoning at scale (PSI, HolE/ComplEx, resonator nets) are two disjoint literatures never combined for natural-language text; PSI proves VSA multi-hop reasoning over text-derived triples works but extraction is hand-built (SemRep); HolE proves circular-correlation binding is learnable via gradient descent but only over pre-curated KGs, never raw text. Closest single system: Palangi/Smolensky learned grammatically-interpretable TPR-QA.
plain_language: We searched the published literature to see if anyone has already built a system that LEARNS (rather than hand-codes) how to read sentences into structured vector representations for reasoning. Answer: no single system does this, but all the pieces exist separately -- one research lineage learns how to bind roles and fillers together (but uses a different, more expensive math representation and only tested on synthetic puzzle stories), another lineage reasons well over text-derived relationships using the efficient vector representation we use (but only after a hand-built rule pipeline extracts the relationships first). Combining them into one learned system is a real, confirmed opportunity, not something we would be reinventing.

summary: Prior-art scour: text -> structured relational meaning (AMR, DRT/DRS+UD/UDS, denotation/grounded weak-supervision + NMN + compositional generalization, neural-OpenIE + Frame Semantics update). 4 parallel Sonnet lit-scans synthesized. Verdict: representation target (AMR/PropBank/DRS-style graphs) and full-treebank-supervised parsing are mature/solved -- adopt, do not reinvent. Denotation/weak/grounded supervision is mature but only proven at closed-domain (GeoQuery) or narrow-world (navigation) scope. Fully-unsupervised structure induction has a stable 30-40 F1 gap vs supervised parsing after a decade of architecture work -- not a shortcut. The one open mainstream finding: SCAN/COGS show systematic/compositional generalization fails under flat seq2seq regardless of supervision, fixed only by architectural compositionality (AM-parser ~98 vs flat 16-35 on COGS) -- this is where native VSA compositional binding has a plausible, UNPROVEN edge, specifically at the text-to-role-assignment encoder stage (not yet tested anywhere, including by us). Cross-validates independently against the 07-18 thematic-roles biology drill (same encoder-is-the-gap conclusion via a different method).
plain_language: We asked whether the mainstream science of turning sentences into structured meaning (who-did-what-to-whom, plus nested facts) is already a solved problem we can just adopt, or whether there is something genuinely new about our approach. Answer: the target format (what a fact-graph should look like) is fully solved, so we should copy that, not reinvent it. Training a reader the normal way (with tens of thousands of hand-labeled example sentences) is also solved, but that is not our situation. Training a reader with only a light checkable signal (like whether it can answer a question correctly) is a real, working approach in the science, but it has only been proven on small, narrow topics, not general open text. And training a reader with literally no supervision at all is a proven dead end that ten years of research has not fixed. The one genuinely open scientific question we found: normal AI readers fail badly at applying what they learned to new combinations they have not seen before (a well documented failure), and the known fix is building the combination-logic directly into the architecture rather than just training more. Our own vector-binding math does exactly that kind of built-in combination logic, so that is our one credible claim to something new -- but it is unproven at the specific step (matching words to their roles in a sentence) where we would need it to work, so we designed a cheap test to check it rather than assume it.

summary: neurosymbolic/glass-box read-to-reason prior-art scour (4 parallel Sonnet lanes: KB-construction NELL/DeepDive/Snorkel/KnowledgeVault/UniversalSchema/OpenIE; neurosymbolic reading-QA NTP/DrKIT/DeepProbLog/LNN/NS-CL; cognitive architectures Soar/ACT-R/Sigma/Leabra/Spaun; VSA-binding bridging TPR-RNN/TP-N2F/NVSA/HRR-parsing/SCAN-COGS). Verdict: no published system unifies learned-read + fixed-algebra VSA-binding + glass-box multi-hop reasoning over text. NVSA (IBM, fixed VSA algebra + learned front-end + glass-box reasoning) is the closest structural analog but is vision-only (RAVEN matrices), never extended to text. NS-CL (vision, CLEVR) is the closest architectural TEMPLATE (learned perception/parse -> program -> glass-box executor). DrKIT closest on learned+text-grounded+multihop but not glass-box at evidence level. Convergent with 07-13 rule-mining drill and 07-17 VSA-discourse-state scour: the VSA/HDC literature stops at single-proposition binding, never extended to either running discourse state OR read-then-reason pipelines. Concrete pointer: port NVSA pattern to text via NS-CL three-stage skeleton -- offered as input to director cross-synthesis with 3 sibling scours, not a pre-registered anchor.
plain_language: We asked: has anyone already built what we are building -- a system that reads text, turns it into a structured vector-based memory, and reasons over it step-by-step in a way a human can fully audit, with no hidden black-box AI making the call? We searched 4 different research traditions (systems that build knowledge bases from text, AI-plus-logic hybrid systems, brain-inspired cognitive models, and vector-based symbol systems). Answer: no single system does all of it. The closest single piece is an IBM system that combines learned perception with a fully transparent vector-math reasoning step -- but it has only ever been used on visual puzzle-solving, never on text. That gives us a concrete, well-proven pattern to adapt rather than invent from scratch, and confirms the gap we are trying to fill is real and still open, not something we would be redoing.

summary: Prior-art scour: incremental comprehension-loop models (Kintsch CI 1988 + van Dijk macro-rules 1978, Landscape Model+LSA, Rabovsky Sentence Gestalt 2018, Franklin/Gershman SEM 2020, Hale/Levy surprisal) + grounded language learning models (Steels naming games/FCG, Frank-Goodman-Tenenbaum + Yu-Ballard cross-situational, Artzi-Zettlemoyer 2013 weak-supervised CCG, Chen/Mooney sportscasting EM, Cangelosi grounding-transfer, BabyAI/Hermann RL agents, Chang ECG construction-grammar induction). Verdict: the compress-and-carry loop IS essentially Kintsch CI re-implemented -- credit not novel; grounded relation-learning is PARTIALLY solved (Artzi-tier validation-driven relation learning is real precedent, adopt) with a confirmed literature gap (KB-distant-supervision, Mintz 2009, never searched) flagged as next drill. Two cheap code audits specified (settling-vs-single-pass; boundary-trigger; grounding-signal) with HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL thresholds.
plain_language: We searched the science literature to see if anyone has already built (1) a computer model that reads a bit at a time, builds an understanding, compresses it to the gist, and carries that forward to make the next bit easier to read, and (2) a computer model that learns what words and relationships mean from real-world grounded experience rather than just text. Good news and a reality check: both of these are real, decades-old research programs with working (if small-scale) demonstrations, so we should credit and build on them rather than claim to have invented the idea. The reading-loop concept matches a 1978-1988 psychology model almost exactly. The grounding side is trickier: learning simple word meanings this way is well studied, but learning RELATIONSHIPS between things (not just object names) from weak evidence is much rarer in the literature, and one especially relevant technique (learning facts from text checked against an existing knowledge base) was not covered in this pass and is queued as the next thing to look up. We also wrote two cheap yes/no checks to see if our current build already matches the best published mechanisms or is still behind them.

summary: BRAIN-DRILL 5x compositional role-binding: conjunctive-coding wins binding-problem lane (synchrony critiqued/weak); SPA/VSA circular-convolution IS the tensor-product/outer-product binding operation; TEM (Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine) supplies the ranked mechanism -- learned content-blind structural code g bound to content x via outer-product, transferring zero-shot to novel content -- well-evidenced for spatial/conceptual/social domains, explicitly UNTESTED for language role-binding (honest gap, not already claimed). Design: learned role/construction-position encoder g (never sees filler) + native FHRR bind + Gentner-style progressive-alignment training (comparison across varied fillers-in-role is the developmental abstraction mechanism, not frozen after childhood). Brain-check: SHRUTI ~10-binding cap, tensor blowup, and VSA superposition noise are THREE independent derivations of the SAME simultaneous-binding capacity wall -- same-limit-ACCEPT, design around small enumerable role-inventories (2-4/frame). Fair COGS-style held-out role-filler-combination test specified vs flat baseline.
plain_language: We asked: the brain clearly manages to use a familiar word in a brand-new grammatical role it has never seen that word in before (like using "glass" as the tool that broke something, having only ever seen "glass" as the thing that gets broken) -- how does it do that, and can we build our reading system the same way? We found the brain likely does this by keeping a completely separate, reusable "slot" code (which role a word is playing) from the "content" code (which word it is), then combining them with a binding operation -- and this reusable-slot mechanism is best documented in a brain system (the hippocampus and its grid-cell partner) that normally handles map-like knowledge of physical space and abstract concepts, not language specifically. That is an honest, still-open question: nobody has yet shown this exact brain trick working for sentence roles, so we get to test it, not just assume it. We also found that our vector-math binding operation is mathematically the same kind of operation the brain uses for this, which is a real advantage if it works. And there is a shared, brain-and-math limit on how many things you can bind together at once before they blur -- both biology and our substrate hit that same wall, so we designed around it (small numbers of roles per sentence) instead of fighting it. We designed one clean, fair test that can prove or disprove the whole idea.

summary: coherence/schema-fit gate 5x brain-drill: N400/predictive-coding graded score + P600-style structural flag + Kintsch CI bounded settling, ranked over a fixed-centroid baseline; found an ALREADY-CODED first-draft gate (exp_role_filler_factorization_reader_coupled_cg_v1.py schema_fit_gate, real_reader_gated arm) never dispatched -- cheapest next action. Proposes upgrading it: condition score on the current situation-model (not a static slot centroid), add a discrete taxonomic/structural-incoherence flag, and add a third DEFERRED state (not silent accept/reject) for ambiguous cases, mirroring the reconsolidation shape from the sibling memory-consolidation drill. Brain-check: settling-to-wrong-answer is a real shared bound (garden-path lingering misparse) -- accept; good-enough/Moses-illusion ~40-50% miss rate is a brain FAILURE mode -- fix is substrate-native always-on verification, not brain-imitation.
plain_language: Studied how the brain decides a sentence interpretation makes sense vs is wrong, to design a filter that catches bad automatic text-reading extractions before they get stored. Found we already wrote a first-draft version of this filter in code but never ran it -- running it is now the cheapest next step. The brain research suggests two upgrades: judge each new fact against the CURRENT understanding of the passage (not a fixed reference point), and add a third option of "not sure yet, revisit later" instead of forcing an immediate accept-or-reject.

summary: learned argument-structure parser (5x brain-drill): ranked mechanism = LEARNED CUE-COMPETITION PARSING (Competition Model, language/construction-specific learned cue weights) scaffolded by usage-based CONSTRUCTION ABSTRACTION (Tomasello/Goldberg, generalization unit) + PREEMPTION/ENTRENCHMENT retreat (Ambridge, fixes coherent-but-wrong FPs without treebank) + a genuine PREDICTION-ERROR learning signal (Fitz and Chang 2019 literal error-propagation account of N400/P600). Designed a concrete glass-box Learned Cue-Competition Parser (LCCP, Steps 1-6) composing with existing candidate-generator + dependency-stack WM + coherence gate; FAIR Arm A/B/C can-fail test with held-out verb x construction split for compositional generalization. P_deflated=0.35-0.45 (novel-synthesis capped). Brain-check: coherent-but-wrong is a shared human limitation too (garden-path lingering, Moses illusion) -- honest fallback if coherence-only feedback proves insufficient is a substrate-native always-on document-scope consistency check.
plain_language: Researched how children learn to correctly figure out who-did-what-to-whom in a sentence, since our reader currently makes grammatically-plausible-but-wrong mistakes that a coherence check cannot catch. Found the brain uses a layered learning system (not one trick), and designed a matching glass-box parser that learns from whether its guesses make sense (not from labeled training data), which should fix these subtle wrong-but-plausible errors and generalize to new word combinations it has not seen before.

summary: Compress-and-carry situation-model-guided comprehension loop: wires WSM Tier2/3 into LCCP Step2/3 as a document-coherence feature (constraint-based-lexicalist immediate-integration design, not late rerank), macrorule-compressed + LTWM-cue carry checkpointed at PE-detected discontinuity (MAP vs SHIFT). Fulfills LCCP note contingent anchor 3 directly. Honest gap: no human-lit precedent for within-document compounding curve in either direction -- Prediction 2 is a genuinely novel test. P_deflated=0.32 (composes 3 already-capped novel-synthesis notes: WSM 0.40, coherence-gate 0.50, LCCP 0.35-0.45).
plain_language: Studied how human readers use a running mental model of a story to catch parsing mistakes that look fine sentence-by-sentence but contradict the wider story, and to get better at reading as they go. Designed the matching piece for our reader: a compressed, carried situation-model feature that re-scores candidate sentence-parses against what the document has established so far, with a bounded compress-and-checkpoint step so it does not grow forever. Flagged honestly that no direct evidence exists (human or otherwise) for whether this actually gets better over the course of one document -- that is a genuinely new test, not a known result.

summary: NP-head candidate generation brain-drill: two non-redundant hard gates (structural-position + graded grounding/entity-hood) needed to fix the break-0.50 LCCP candidate-gen bottleneck; fields/table-class errors are position failures, regular-class errors are entity-hood failures; single-gate fix cannot close residual; grounding gate must be graded not hard (metonymy brittleness risk per Katz-Fodor -> Resnik history)
plain_language: Studied how the brain finds the correct noun for who-did-what-to-whom, and found our parser is failing in two DIFFERENT ways at once: sometimes it picks the right kind of word in the wrong sentence position (like table), sometimes it picks the wrong kind of word entirely (like an adjective, regular). Both need separate fixes layered together; a single fix will not be enough, and the fix must stay flexible or it will break on figurative language.

summary: Argument/adjunct distinction brain-drill (5x): came-home/stood-there mis-licensed as PATIENT since selectional coherence is orthogonal to subcategorization (semantic gate cannot catch it). Linguistic-theory literature itself treats arg/adjunct as gradient not binary (Przepiorkowski, Toivonen) with a documented DERIVED-ARGUMENT middle category (Needham & Toivonen 2011) formalizing exactly this case (VerbNet Destination role, PropBank AM-DIR vs ARG4 hedge). Ranked mechanism: gradient verb-frame-specificity gating (verb-diversity entropy, mirrors PropBank ARG-N vs AM-* design, computationally validated by Korhonen/Villavicencio/Kim et al 2019) + construction-level frame-TYPE membership (Friederici & Frisch 2000 ERP dissociation: frame-TYPE violation = P600-only, frame-NUMBER violation = N400+P600 biphasic) + explicit DEFERRED middle state instead of forced binary. Designed Role-Eligibility Cascade (REC): Signal 0 cheap categorial prior (bare locative/temporal/manner adverbials excluded from PATIENT candidacy by default) + Signal 1 learned verb-diversity entropy + Signal 2 construction frame-type membership. Sits as a third, non-redundant layer alongside todays GHC (wrong-token) and LCCP (wrong-candidate-scored) drills: this one fixes wrong-ROLE-ELIGIBILITY. FAIR Arm A/B/C/D test vs the ~23-case came-home residual on existing LCCP/GHC gold; cheapest first build = Signal 0 alone (category prior), P=0.45. P_deflated=0.35-0.45 overall (novel-synthesis capped). Brain-check: field diagnostics themselves conflict on binary arg/adjunct (same-limit, accept, design three-way not binary); corpus-sparsity for entropy estimates is a real separately-tested bound (Prediction 4), not necessarily an REC defect if it fails.
plain_language: We asked: how does the brain know that came HOME does not mean home is what got hit or moved (a patient/object), the way came home is not the same kind of thing as hit the ball, since our reader currently confuses the two. We found that even professional linguists do not have one clean test for this -- it is genuinely a matter of degree, with a well-known in-between case (home after came/went) that linguists call a derived argument, neither a true object nor a true throwaway modifier. We also found the brain checks two separate things: whether a word FITS the kind of slot a verb expects, and whether the NUMBER of slots is right, as two different brain signals. We designed a three-part filter for our reader that starts cheap (exclude location/time/manner-type words from ever being treated as the object) and adds a smarter, learned layer only if the cheap part leaves gaps, with a built-in in-between answer for the genuinely ambiguous cases rather than forcing a wrong yes/no.

summary: cross_document_compounding_consolidation_viability: 3-lit-scan synthesis (Documents Model / knowledge-threshold / self-training-decorrelation theory) gives a 3-condition gate for cross-doc compounding via consolidation (schema-fit-correctness x confidence-decorrelation x knowledge-threshold), directly explains why CCL failed and predicts naive coherence-gate reuse as a consolidation filter risks the SAME systematic-error failure one level up; designed a cheap zero-compute pre-check (confidence-correctness correlation on existing eval data) plus a 3-arm cross-doc FAIR test (no-carry / irrelevant-consolidation / relevant-consolidation) reusing CCLs own arm-A order-effect-control lesson.
plain_language: Looked at how humans get better at reading as they read more (the "rich get richer" effect) and found it only works if the knowledge being carried forward is actually correct and reliably filtered -- wrong prior knowledge measurably makes comprehension WORSE, not just unhelpful. Our reading system already has one documented case (the CCL experiment) where its own confidence signal was systematically wrong in a correlated way, which is exactly the failure pattern the machine-learning literature warns about for self-training. Before building a bigger cross-document memory system, there is now a cheap, free check to run first on data we already have, to see if that same trap is waiting at the next step.

summary: reading-pedagogy craft lit-scan: 5 lit-scan lanes (strategy-instruction pedagogy, how-to-read-well craft, reading-science synthesis, early-childhood pedagogy, images/grounding) converge on our coherence-gate + compress-and-carry loop (triple-cross-validated); surface 4 new candidate levers (curriculum-ordering by knowledge-dependency, self-generated question-difficulty ladder, document-level preview pass, feedback-scored compression objective) plus a real dictionary-grounding gap for concrete vocabulary (future vision-track strengthener, not actionable now). P_deflated 0.25-0.55 per lever, novel-synthesis cap 0.50 respected.
plain_language: Read the human literature on how reading comprehension is taught (classroom strategies, expert how-to-read-well advice, early-childhood reading pedagogy, and how pictures help kids learn words) to see if it suggests improvements to our reading system. Good news: it independently confirms two things we already built (the coherence-check gate and the summarize-predict-clarify comprehension loop) are the right design. It also surfaces four concrete new ideas worth considering (ordering what text we read next by what background knowledge it needs, having the system quiz itself about what it reads, previewing a document structure before reading it linearly, and giving the summarization step a scored feedback signal) plus confirms that our dictionary-based word-grounding has a real, literature-documented gap for concrete nouns specifically -- which strengthens (but does not yet trigger) the case for eventually adding an image-based grounding channel.

summary: Open-licensed modern graded-reader corpus scan: Bloom Library (sil-ai/bloom-lm HF dataset) ranks #1 -- bulk-ready plain text, per-item CC license, but translation-artifact risk UNCONFIRMED (needs origin-language check before staging). StoryWeaver/African-Storybook/GDL all real but weaker bulk-access or higher translation risk (African Storybook = highest). Post-McGuffey PD readers (Elson/Beacon/Baldwin/Aldine/Winston) verified PD-US, thin on Gutenberg (1-3 vols/series), Aldine has the least-archaic register but none deliver contemporary vocabulary. Newsela/CommonLit/ReadWorks/ReadingA-Z/F&P/UniteForLiteracy/ICDL confirmed copyrighted or access-restricted, ruled OUT. Recommendation: acquire Bloom CC-subset pilot now (near-zero cost, <1 day, HF dataset already exists) but DEFER larger acquisition (StoryWeaver scraping, PD-reader OCR) -- reader is mechanism-bottlenecked (0.557, structural-works/semantic-fails) not corpus-bottlenecked; full generalization test premature until parser improves.
plain_language: Looked for a modern, freely-licensed set of easy-reader storybooks to add alongside our old public-domain McGuffey readers, so the parser sees current-day vocabulary and we can test whether it generalizes beyond one 1870s textbook series. Found a good bulk-downloadable candidate (Bloom Library, via a ready-made research dataset) but flagged that it and its sibling platforms (StoryWeaver, African Storybook) often contain text translated from other languages, which could look like non-native English and confuse a clean grammar-precision test -- that risk needs a direct check before we rely on it. Older public-domain readers from the early 1900s (Elson, Beacon, Baldwin, Aldine) are real and zero-risk but still nearly as old-fashioned as McGuffey, so they do not solve the vocabulary goal. Recommendation: grab the modern candidate now since it is nearly free to do, but hold off on the bigger sourcing effort since the parser itself, not the text supply, is the current bottleneck.

summary: argument/adjunct + subcat brain-drill: verb-specific subcat-frame-frequency (retrieved at-verb, not post-hoc) + directional-PP-as-non-patient diagnostic (Levin/Rappaport-Hovav) are the missing LCCP features for the come/sit/stand/walk spurious-patient residual (0.557 precision, 92 FPs); Villavicencio 2002 nails these exact verbs at n=3 scale w/ curated selectional hierarchy; but brain pays real IFG/RT cost for this class and PropBank/FrameNet gold standards disagree on ground truth for a slice of these -- honest ceiling is NOT zero-FP.
plain_language: Drilled why the reader still mis-reads sentences like "he came home" (treating "home" as who got acted-upon, which is wrong). Human psycholinguistics shows people resolve this using a per-verb memory of what that verb usually takes as a complement, checked immediately, plus a grammatical rule that a following direction-phrase after a motion verb signals a location not a victim. We do not yet have either as an explicit feature in the learned-parser design from earlier today. Proposed adding both as a small patch, not a rebuild. Caveat: even expert human-built dictionaries (PropBank vs FrameNet) disagree on some of these exact sentence types, so a chunk of the errors may be genuinely ambiguous, not fixable to zero.

summary: mcguffey_source_apparatus: mined RAW McGuffey Primer/1st/2nd/3rd/4th readers (not secondary lit) for embedded teaching apparatus (vocab lists, definitions, comprehension questions, review cadence); confirmed cleaning pipeline strips it from 2nd-4th graded corpus (kept in grade1); reframed per USER mid-task as method FOR THE TEACHER (Director), not substrate-facing signal. Concrete pacing numbers: ~6 new words/lesson (Primer stated), ~1.7-2.2x vocab-type growth per grade. Apparatus escalation is non-monotonic: exhaustive pre-teach word-lists (Primer-2nd) -> gap (3rd, transcription caveat) -> selective definitions+comprehension-Qs (4th). Fourth Reader comprehension-Q apparatus (43 blocks) assessed as narrow eval-triangulation resource (~25-35% clean argument-structure, no answer key), not a training signal.
plain_language: Read the actual old McGuffey textbooks (not summaries about them) to see what teaching tricks the original authors built in -- word lists before each lesson, definitions, review schedules, and comprehension questions. Found real, usable ideas for how I (the Director) should pace and check the substrates learning, and confirmed our own data-cleaning step was silently deleting most of this apparatus from three of the five books. No changes to the substrate itself yet -- this is planning input.

summary: directional-marker distributional de-confound brain-drill: buildable de-confound for the atom-29349 shared-detector circularity (compute a candidate directional/closed-class set from an INDEPENDENT distributional fingerprint -- frequency+length+closed-neighbor-set+post-verb positional-slot statistics -- seeded from a small credited exemplar set and distributionally expanded, then feed that INDUCED set into both teacher and feature instead of the identical hand list) BUT full elimination of any seed is not an honest target: Redington-Chater 1998 explicitly finds function words HARDER not easier for zero-seed distributional clustering, and no paper found induces a fine directional/path subclass with zero seed. The reason maps onto a real asymmetry: humans bootstrap the fine category by binding a PERCEPTUAL path/goal channel (Pulverman/Golinkoff/Lakusta-Landau/Mandler/Talmy, prelinguistic, independent of syntax) to a frequency/prosodic channel (Shi/Werker/Cutler) that a text-only substrate structurally lacks the first half of. Ranked verdict: Rank-1 de-confound buildable (P=0.38 deflated) for the SPECIFIC shared-detector circularity; Rank-2 honest given-floor (P=0.65) that a small credited seed remains legitimate, brain-analogous, not a hand-rules violation. Falsifiable HARD-PASS/HARD-FAIL predictions + a fair can-fail test (scrambled-seed must-fail control + re-run the syntactic-frame teacher test on the induced set) specified.
plain_language: Drilled whether the substrate could learn to spot direction-words (home, up, into, away...) by itself from reading, instead of us handing it a pre-made list -- the exact gap the adversarial check found in last nights learning result. Answer: partially yes. We can build a version that spots directional words using their own statistical fingerprint (common, short, appear right after motion verbs) seeded from just a handful of examples, which genuinely removes the specific circularity the check caught. But we cannot get the full human trick from text alone: children learn the fine category partly by watching real physical motion happen while hearing the words, which text does not give us. So a small seed list is a fair, human-like starting point, not a cheat -- the honest claim becomes learns the rule from a self-built detector, not learns everything from absolute zero. Designed a fair test with a must-fail control to check this rather than just assuming it works.

summary: FORK-C (compounding + end-to-end-in-substrate) brain-drill: binding operator has NO learned-acquisition precedent anywhere in brain-model literature (VSA/HRR/SPA all treat bind algebra as given, only content is learned) -> deprioritize reader-forms-HD-natively, route all learning to selection/scoring/consolidation policy (matches Stage-1 bridge already being zero-training). Zacks EST + hippocampal-boundary/indexing/Mattar-Daw replay independently reinforce (7th convergent lit) the PE-triggered MAP/SHIFT + LTWM-cue design from sibling notes. First buildable component sequenced: Step0=redundancy-decorrelation check (near-zero-cost, gates cross-doc consolidation) then Step1=structured within-doc FHRR role/event carry (CCL non-closed variant, reuses CCL harness, exercises 2 VSA-envelope GAPS). P_deflated=0.30.
plain_language: Studied how the brain builds a running mental model while reading and files it away for later, to design the substrate C build. Key finding: no brain-science evidence exists for LEARNING the core binding mechanism itself (only its content) -- so we should keep our already-working, zero-training binding operation fixed and put all the learning into deciding what to keep/trust/store. Also found the boundary-detection and memory-filing mechanisms line up with what we already designed. Names two concrete, cheap next builds in priority order.

summary: coref/entity-tracking brain-drill: mechanism (cue-based cleanup-memory retrieval) is a strong native fit; accuracy ceiling (65-89%%, worse intersentential) is a genuine brain-shared same-limit; prior HARD_FAIL explained by BOTH upstream candidate-gen bug (partly fixed) AND ungated application in the honest-ceiling-limited regime -- fix is a margin-gated, local-window (intrasentential) coref that abstains under low confidence, feeding both precision and the fork-C entity-carry lever. P_deflated=0.40.
plain_language: Looked at how humans resolve pronouns (he/she/it) to figure out if we can safely add that ability to the reader. Good news: the underlying memory mechanism (cue-matching retrieval) matches our own associative-memory building block well. Bad news: even humans and the best rule-based computer systems only get pronoun resolution right 65-89%% of the time (worse for pronouns pointing back several sentences) -- so it will never be perfect, in a brain or in our substrate. The fix is to only resolve a pronoun when confident and skip it otherwise, starting with the easy same-sentence cases, rather than forcing every pronoun to a guess (which is what broke things last time).

summary: animacy-vs-worldknowledge residual brain-drill: distributional animacy is a cheap, discrete, glass-box feature (architecturally kin to gender/number agreement, not to the failed selectional-coherence-cosine) that should resolve most of the named they->inanimate coref harm; full commonsense world-knowledge (ConceptNet/ATOMIC/COMET-class) is a categorically larger multi-year investment and is NOT a substitute; parser argument-structure residual stays owned by subcat-frame+directional-PP, not animacy. P_deflated=0.45.
plain_language: We asked whether a cheap animacy feature (person vs thing) can fix the reader errors where "they" gets wrongly linked to flowers/huts instead of people. Answer: yes for that specific error, cheaply and without a big knowledge-base investment -- animacy is fast and categorical in the brain too, unlike the fuzzy semantic-similarity signals that already failed this session. But animacy cannot substitute for full common-sense world knowledge, which is a much bigger, separate investment (would need something like ConceptNet). The other hard parser error (verb-object confusion) is not fixed by animacy -- that already has its own separate fix.

summary: mental-simulation scene as VERIFIER/error-signal: attribute-scene (WordNet supersense + VerbNet selectional features) buildable non-perceptually (P=0.45); scene-coherence-as-self-supervised-training-signal is theoretically grounded (predictive coding double-duty, N400-as-implicit-learning-signal analog) but unprecedented in combination (P=0.35); key ML finding = trainability needs CONTRAST across rival candidate parses (not gradedness/discreteness), diagnosing why prior cosine (no contrast) and animacy (pre-filter, no contrast) both failed to train; first buildable = Scene-Coherence Verifier scored contrastively on rival LCCP candidates for build/huts-vs-build/stream class, design-gated 3-prediction can-fail
plain_language: Studied whether humans imagining a simple mental picture of a sentence is really a built-in checker: does it just pick the right meaning, or can it also teach the reading system to get better on its own, with no answer key? Found this idea is well supported in brain science in principle (the same brain signal that tells you something read wrong also nudges learning) but has never been directly tested in this exact combination. Designed a concrete, cheap, no-camera-needed component to test it, plus honest pass/fail bars.

summary: prior-art drill: picturing sentences as scenes (brain+ML landscape). WordsEye/SPICE/AbstractScenes/Tenenbaum-PLoT ranked as glass-box-adoptable prior art extending the SCV; Dreamer/World-Models gives an independent double-duty precedent; WinoVis/LaViSA give a credited NEGATIVE result (pixel/generative scene-check near-chance to weak-partial for linguistic disambiguation specifically) validating the SCV discrete-attribute-lookup design choice over any pixel route.
plain_language: Researched how psychology and AI literature handle the idea that people picture a sentence as a scene to understand it. Found the idea is well established in psychology (not new), and in AI the closest matches are WordsEye and a rule-based scene-graph parser (both fully inspectable, adoptable for our project) plus a striking negative result: when other researchers actually tried rendering an image to disambiguate a sentence, it barely beat random guessing. That negative result supports our choice to keep using a simple type-checking scene rather than trying to generate pictures.

summary: integrated graded-experiential reader viability + corpus precondition: escapes SCV post-hoc null closure (P=0.45 deflated) on general per-step-vs-global-scalar credit-assignment argument (RL credit-assignment + SSL-collapse literatures both support per-step > post-hoc); concrete architecture = McRae/Spivey-Knowlton CIM normalized-recurrence (verified 3-equation weighted-sum-plus-feedback) for use-time integration + per-step delta-rule for learning (CIM itself fits weights offline, does not demonstrate online learning -- thats the novel piece here). Corpus precondition resolves as a SCOPE SPLIT: learning NEW distributional thematic-fit values is corpus-gated (Resnik needed 1M words + WordNet-class smoothing even then; Erk/Padao/Baroni-Lenci need 100M-1B+; 99k words is ~10x below the smallest precedent) but learning only the small cue-INTEGRATION weights on top of the already-built WordNet/VerbNet categorical scaffold is buildable now, same scale as existing LCCP cue-weight vector. Recommendation: build now, narrowly scoped, with mandatory firing-rate diagnostic to distinguish sparse-event coverage gap from mechanism null (the same ambiguity may be hiding inside the SCVs own 0.000-delta result).
plain_language: Studied whether a smarter version of the failed picture-checker idea (one that blends the picture-check INTO reading word-by-word, instead of checking after the fact) would actually learn anything, and whether we have enough reading material (99 thousand words) to teach it. Found: yes, blending it in word-by-word IS a genuinely different and more promising design (well-supported by both brain science and general machine-learning theory on why after-the-fact checks fail to teach anything) -- but only if we scope it correctly. We should NOT try to teach the substrate brand-new word-meaning statistics from only 99 thousand words (real research shows that needs at least a million, more realistically hundreds of millions); we SHOULD reuse the categories we already built (WordNet/VerbNet) as ready-made scaffolding and only teach the substrate how much to trust each existing clue relative to the others, which is a much smaller learning problem that fits our data. Recommend building this narrowly-scoped version now, with a built-in check for whether it is actually learning or just never getting triggered.

summary: structural residual (case-b build-huts vs build-by-stream) is dominantly constructional (preposition-class), not world-knowledge; carry-forward discourse context does not resolve unique-referent role-assignment ambiguity (same wall); factorization core validated as shared binding formalism not literal shared circuit; next build = small preposition-class feature on existing symbolic front-end, must-fail via scramble control, before further learned-reader investment
plain_language: We brain-drilled the last hard reading-parser bug (mixing up a thing-you-built with a place-you-built-it-near, e.g. build HUTS vs build BY THE STREAM). Turns out this specific bug is mostly a grammar-marking problem (which preposition is used), not a world-knowledge problem -- so a small, cheap fix to the existing rule-based parser should help, and we should try that before building the bigger learned reading system. We also checked whether remembering earlier sentences would fix this bug: the science says no, that trick helps with a different kind of confusion (which THING a pronoun refers to), not this one. So we scoped the next cheap build correctly instead of over-investing in the big rebuild too early.

summary: incomplete_kg_reasoning_substrate_edge_or_extraction_pivot: NO genuine edge for glass-box VSA on real incomplete-KG link prediction/conjunctive-query answering, confirmed both externally (arXiv 2606.24948 HRR/FHRR gets RotatE-parity single-hop MRR 0.35 on FB15k-237 but collapses to chance at 2-hop composition; BetaE 3i>2i shows conjunction gain is answer-set-shrinkage generic math not learned) and via this project own already-landed in-house history (native Hebbian VSA KGStore oracle ceiling MRR 0.0231 vs SGD-trained additive-map ANCHOR_COMPOSE 0.1282 on real CSKG, a 5.5x gap; crux_engine_fb15k237_vsa_gt_v1 pure-VSA attempt HARD_FAILed on real FB15k-237). Brain: novel relational inference (unlike CA3 pattern completion) IS learned/experience-dependent (hippocampal-lesion transitive-inference studies) but brain solves it via slow neocortical statistical-regularity extraction -- the biological analog of training an embedding -- and no known local/Hebbian-class rule closes the gap to gradient training. Verdict: path (A) incomplete-KG-reasoning chain-grade is CLOSED (neural-embedding turf); path (B) extraction/grounding is the only genuine remaining chain-grade thread, confirming rather than contradicting the current session pivot.
plain_language: Checked whether our transparent/glass-box style of reasoning has any real advantage on the specific job of guessing missing facts in incomplete knowledge graphs (the kind of task modern neural embedding models like RotatE/ComplEx are built for). Answer: no. Outside research shows glass-box symbolic-vector approaches match neural methods only on the easiest single-step guesses and collapse to random guessing on anything requiring two or more chained steps. More decisively, we already ran this exact comparison ourselves months ago on real data and got the same answer: our pure transparent-memory version scored 5.5x worse than a version that used ordinary gradient training, and a from-scratch attempt on a standard benchmark repeatedly failed. Brain science backs this up too: guessing a genuinely new fact (as opposed to recalling something you already learned) is a skill that improves with experience, and the brain builds it the slow statistical way, similar to how neural networks train, not through any quick transparent shortcut. Bottom line: this is not a fight worth picking; the real opportunity stays where we already refocused, on getting correct facts INTO the system by reading, not on guessing facts it was never told.

summary: Platform maturity audit (5x drill): capacity MATURE (m<=24 robust, brain-matched); discourse/WM buffer SETTLED (two-layer, already built); cleanup/attractor memory IMMATURE (measured hard step-function sigma2.0->3.0 vs brain graded attractor completion, cheap fix available); encoding PARTIALLY mature (structure/content split validated, content not yet similarity-structured); MOST LOAD-BEARING MISSING element = error-driven/predictive-coding correction loop around the extractor (does not exist in any form; independently explains both construction-determined chain-grade attempts and the closed glass-box extraction ceiling at 0.41-0.46 < 0.70 floor). Build order pre-registered: (1) cleanup swap [cheap], (2) correction loop [crux], (3) similarity-structured content vectors.
sub_agents: research:sonnet x4 lit-scan (WM-capacity, CA3-cleanup, encoding-similarity, missing-elements)
plain_language: We asked: is the substrate biologically mature enough yet for real chain-grade reasoning, or is something basic missing? Answer: capacity and short-term memory are already brain-sufficient and settled. But two things are behind the brain: our memory cleanup only works if the cue is nearly exact (the brain can reconstruct a memory from a partial, messy cue -- ours cannot yet, though a cheap fix exists and is already tested). More importantly, the substrate has no way to learn from its own mistakes and repair its understanding over time -- today its reading rules are hand-built and static, with no feedback loop, which explains why every reasoning test so far has either been rigged to succeed by construction or capped by a frozen, already-proven-insufficient extractor. Recommended build order: fix the cheap memory issue first, then build the missing self-correction loop (the hard, central piece), then give the substrate word-meanings that are similar-to-each-other in the right way (not just random codes).

summary: deep brain drill (5x, given session failures): geometry-learning is a hybrid (scaffolded attractor manifold + learned predictive binding, TEM/SR), grounding demoted to sufficient-not-necessary for a trainable error signal (strongest N400-as-error models are amodal); single unifying mechanism explaining all 3 failures = contrastive predictive coding over RIVAL hypotheses scored against real exogenous data (not a scalar coherence score); buildable now via re-wiring existing parts (predictive_coding.py + SCV rival-LCCP candidates + corpus-precondition cue-weight scope). P_deflated=0.42, 3-arm must-fail test pre-registered.
sub_agents: research:sonnet x4 lit-scan (grid-cell/geometry, grounding/N400, predictive-reading, learning-signal)
plain_language: We asked: since our hand-built attempts at reading/reasoning kept turning out to be either rigged-by-construction or unable to learn, what does the brain actually do differently? Found the brain's answer is a mix, not one clean story: some of its structural wiring for generalizing is pre-built before experience, and the rest is genuinely learned by predicting what happens next and comparing against reality. The biggest correction to our own thinking: we assumed grounding the system in sensorimotor experience was the missing ingredient, but the strongest brain-science models of learning actually work fine on abstract, non-sensory data too -- so grounding is not required, just one way to get a rich enough signal. The real missing piece across all three of our failed attempts is that none of them compared MULTIPLE competing guesses against what actually happens next in real text -- they either had no comparison at all, or compared one guess to a fixed answer-key. We now have a specific, cheap redesign that reuses parts we already built, with an honest pre-registered test that could fail it.

summary: deep_drill_all_negatives_3x_unifying_root: 3-angle drill across 7 VET-confirmed negatives (N1-N7). Finding: TWO distinct roots, not one -- Root1 (N1 factorization compgen, N2 CLUTRR, N5 KG-reasoning) = free-algebra/construction-determined, truly closed, brain-shared (systematicity is real+early-scaffolded but combination vocabulary is always learned in the brain, never handed as an oracle). Root2 (N3 reader 0.557, N4 SCV thematic-fit, N6 cleanup-swap HARD-FAIL, N7 CPCL honest-null) = learning-signal preconditions, but this session already tested a DIFFERENT candidate against EACH of 3 separable sub-preconditions and got 3 different outcomes: rivalry (N4, open+cheapest, retest-first), representational SNR headroom (N6, closed for the decision rule -- argmax is Bayes-optimal for random codebooks per Hopfield/Gardner-Derrida/coding theory, confirmed by brain dentate-gyrus sparsify-upstream-not-smarter-CA3-decoder -- but OPEN for the code itself via sparsify+orthogonalize/redundancy/multi-cue), corpus/target discriminability (N7, honest null, diagnosed corpus-coarseness, open via hard-negative-mining/diversity-staging/structured-target per fresh lit-scan). Prior single-crux SYNTHESIS framing (one missing learning loop) is corrected to three separable, independently-testable preconditions.

plain_language: We took every recent failed experiment (7 of them) and asked: is there one single reason they all failed, or several? Answer: two reasons. Three of the failures happened because we handed the system a shortcut answer instead of making it actually learn (those are permanently closed, not fixable). The other four all involve a genuine missing learning signal, but each one is missing something different -- one needs the system to compare rival guesses against each other, one needs a better internal code (not a smarter decision rule), and one needs richer training text. The cheapest, most promising next experiment is already designed and ready to run.

summary: brain_foundation_map_and_overlooked_components: correspondence map (9 items) confirms/extends the two same-day drills (learning-signal contrastive-loop gap remains most load-bearing, now shown to also need a second neuromodulatory gating axis; binding+structural-code both hand-stipulated vs brain learned-from-data; comprehension has a NEW second gap -- flat/single-timescale vs Hasson-lineage hierarchy of temporal receptive windows, independent of the already-known rule-vs-predictive gap). Exhaustive Job-2 sweep (11 categories, 4 parallel Sonnet lit-scans, ~91 citations) surfaces 3 net-new TOTAL-GAP load-bearing items neither companion note touched: metacognition/confidence (highest product relevance -- auditable-after-the-fact != trustworthy-in-advance), attention/selective-gating (total gap, predicts failure once real noisy corpora replace curated toy sets), and multi-timescale hierarchical predictive processing (structurally separate build from the contrastive-loop fix, not a substitute). Runners-up: neuromodulation (3 non-redundant gating axes per Yu and Dayan 2005, but collapses into the correction-loop gap until that exists), inhibition/sparsity/normalization (real trade-off not one-sided), curriculum/staging (re-weighted toward load-bearing given the substrate own already-established 99k-word data-scarcity constraint), homeostatic plasticity (near-term stability risk once the CPC loop starts producing real updates). Cheap decisive test proposed: threshold an existing signal (cleanup match-score or CPC residual) as a confidence readout, pure readout no new architecture, HARD-PASS/FAIL pre-registered.
plain_language: Did a deep brain-science literature review comparing what our transparent reasoning system already has to what real brains have, split into two jobs: matching up the pieces we already built against their brain equivalents, and hunting for brain mechanisms we may have missed entirely. Matching: our fixed math-based memory-binding and our hand-designed word-meaning maps are both stipulated once and never change, while the brain both learns and continuously re-derives its equivalents from experience -- confirming our own most important recent finding (we are missing a self-correcting learning loop) and adding a new twist (comprehension needs not just that loop but also a layered, multi-timescale structure, a second missing piece, independent of the first). Missed-entirely: three real gaps we had not previously flagged at all -- (1) no way for the system to know when it is probably wrong and should say so (this matters a lot for our trustworthy-AI positioning, since being transparent about how an answer was built is not the same as knowing in advance you are about to give a wrong one); (2) no attention or relevance-filtering at all (processes everything equally, which brain science predicts will cause real trouble once we feed it messy real-world text instead of curated examples); (3) no layered, multiple-timescale structure in its prediction module, needed separately from (and in addition to) the already-known fix for its non-training first attempt. Proposed a cheap first test: check whether a signal we already compute can serve as a rough confidence signal, no new architecture needed.

summary: CPCL null 4x drill: best predictive target=entity-recurrence/coherence (Centering/entity-grid) not bag-of-words; richer-corpus is likely scapegoat (ALBERT NSP-vs-SOP precedent, fix=scoring-design not data); brain prediction-distinctiveness-vs-competitors is an unstudied gap for graded-reader text; loop-redesign + learned codebook (Random-Indexing/BEAGLE glass-box) converge on same skip-gram-equivalent mechanism, build together (codebook first). Cheap Test A pre-registered: re-target CPCL continuation_vec to entity-recurrence + within-lesson shuffle, reuse existing harness, before any corpus change.
